formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Douglas is a 46 year old single man who currently resides in level three supported accommodation at Herston Lodge. Adult Guardian are appointed decision makers for personal matters, but not including healthcare. Douglas has a diagnosis of Chronic Disorganised Schizophrenia, which is complicated by an intellectual impairment (including marked language impairment and illiteracy). He is currently maintained on a depot, which is administered by Dr Nyst at Herston Lodge on a monthly basis. Douglas has been a longstanding client of INBMHS for many years with multiple inpatient admissions. He has limited family and social supports, with the parents ceasing all contact. Douglas has a limited understanding of and insight into his illness and this has resulted in a long history of non-compliance with prescribed treatment. Historically there has been a history of violence with a number of documented assaults for which it appears have been unprovoked, as well as periods of low mood, with associated suicidal ideation.Engaging with Douglas can be difficult as his intellectual impairment is quite pronounced. He is a very poor historian and is very concrete in his thinking, often unable to identify links in everyday activities, such as reasons why things are done the way they are. This makes communication difficult, and often only ever superficial in nature. When unwell, Douglas presents as disorganised, thought-disordered and appears to be responding to internal stimuli. These symptoms are present to a lesser degree when he is well.Background: - Born in New Zealand- Moved to Australia at age two years with family- Grew up on family farm in Victoria- Diagnosed with Chronic Disorganised Schizophrenia at age 17 years in Goulburn, Queensland- Lived with parents until age 28 years, when he moved into supported accommodation.- Commenced on an antidepressant in 2011 following expressing suicidal thoughts.- Discharged from hospital to Pinjarra Lodge in 2012, but subsequently evicted due to smoking.- Lived at Green Meadow Court in Windsor 2012 - 2014.- Moved to Herston Lodge in 2014 after eviction from other facilities.- MHS advised Douglas' mother had passed away but request that this not be told to Douglas.Physical Health: - previous surgical intervention for rectal prolapse.Previous Medications: - Risperdal Consta- Clozapine - up to dose of 675mg. Ceased due to continued non compliance.- Lithium- CitalopramForensic History: - Breach of bail +++- Contempt- Enter dwelling to commit indictable offence.4 P'SPresenting:Douglas is a 45 year old man who lives at Herston Lodge.Long history of mental illness, with minimal supportsDouglas has a diagnosis of schizophrenia and an intellectual impairment, with marked language impairment and illiteracy.Psychotic symptoms persist at baseline despite maximising pharmacological interventions.Douglas most recent hospital admissions was in May 2018 and he has a long history of relapse due to poor adherence with medications.Precipitating:Non-adherence with medicationPsychosocial stressorsPerpetuatingLimited insight into illness and how to stay wellLimited social supportsMinimal meaningful occupations.ProtectiveResides in supported accommodationReceipt of Disability Support Pension under Public TrustUnder Adult GuardianHas a support worker from Uniting Care who supports him to attend the local PCYC and go shopping.

*** Case review copied from the previous as there are nil changes; some amendments made in the Summary of Care sectionLachlan is a 54 year old single man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia, dating back to the late 1990s. He currently lives alone in a Dept of Housing unit in New Farm, and receives a Disability Support Pension (manages own finances). He was treated by RBWH under a Forensic Order from 13/07/15 (hx of treatment under ITO prior) and was stepped down to a TSO on 23/01/2018 .He has some support / ongoing relationships with family (visits brother Phillip daily in his own unit, some phone contact with sister and brother living overseas), however since the passing of his father in May 2017, has become further socially isolated. Prior to his father's passing, Lachlan spent the majority of his time visiting / providing support and care to his father. Visiting his father at the family home and then in the nursing home had become his daily routine over the previous few years. He has since taken on a care and support to his brother Phillip who has a serious mental illness and is a client of this service also.Lachlan's mental state has been stable on his current depot treatment (shared care with GP under ATLAS program), since an increase in dose to 150 mg Paliperidone and then a change from four to three weekly, the residual symptoms of "coincidences"(ideas of reference) and monitoring conspiracy have ceased. In the past he has believed he is in someway being monitored by Facebook, despite not having an account. While he usually reported these residual symptoms regularly, he denied any associated distress or fixation and could manage to challenge these ideas successfully.When unwell, Lachlan presents with grandiose and persecutory delusions. He has made threats to kill his brother and father when unwell, and has a history of actual violence towards family members (over 10 years ago). His risk of violence is currently low when at baseline, but increases significantly when unwell.Lachlan has a family history of illness (brother also dx Schizophrenia, open to Southern CCT; unknown psychiatric hx of other family members). He was formally diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2001, after developing prodromal symptoms while living and working in England from 1992 - 2000. His first admission to RBWH was around 2000, upon return from England. He was previously treated under an ITO (MHA 2000), and remained quite stable for many years on a depot antipsychotic. Lachlan's ITO was subsequently revoked in 2007, and he was treated as a voluntary patient before being discharged to full care by his GP (May 2010).Following discharge from MHS/ to GP care in May 2010, Lachlan continued to be managed by his GP as a voluntary patient. However, after a period of approximately 2 years (and unbeknownst to prev. treating team), he disengaged from treatment (now reports this was due to his perception and GP reports that he was "doing well", and therefore he did not perceive need for medication). Lachlan's last hospital admission was between 31/07/13 - 13/08/13, when he was brought to the hospital by police under an EEO, having been arrested for attempted robbery, public nuisance and assault at University of Queensland (some of index offences of current Forensic Order). He had been experiencing persecutory delusions that people at the uni were sending messages on their mobile phone about him, and may be filming him. He then attempted to confiscate a phone from a female student and became aggressive to another female student in retaliation for what he perceived they were doing. At this time it became apparent that Lachlan had ceased his depot from his GP approximately 12 months prior. His father also reported he had become quite possessive of things in the kitchen, and experiencing ideas of reference from the newspaper a few months before the incident. Additional charges also became apparent later that year (re: separate incident), of unlawful stalking, following repeated unwanted contact and monitoring of ex-leader of Qld Liberal party/ well-known Queenslander Sir Liew Edwards, and wife Lady Jane Edwards (Lachlan now reports wanting to speak to him about political topics, ask his opinion about things etc). During this admission, he was treated with Paliperidone (injection) as he refused to have oral medication. He was discharged on an ITO, treated with Paliperidone 150mg 4/52.A Forensic Order was made on 13/07/2015 due to unsoundness of mind in relation to the charges incurred following the incident at UQ and additional charges related to unlawful stalking (between 01/06/13 and 21/12/13).Lachlan has very few social contacts, engaging in mostly solitary activities. He has recently been attending University of 3rd Age courses, however, does not make social connections there. He walks twice per day and goes to the movies on his own. He visits his brother daily. He has completed the SCIT group, however did not make any friendships.

<span style="font-size: 16px;">Nicholas has a 23 year history of paranoid schizophrenia with comorbid polysubstance abuse. Initially diagnosed at the age of 19 when Nicholas lived in Victoria. In 2007 he decided to move to Queensland to be closer to his parents. From 1994 until 2007 Nicholas was largely managed in the community. Collateral regarding Nicholas' treatment during this time was primarily gained from his mother Nikki. Nikki describes a lifelong pattern of temporarily good engagement with medication and mental health appointments, with an associated high level of functioning in the community (working as a mechanic, riding his motorcycle, maintaining private rental accommodation).Unfortunately this is interspersed with episodes where Nicholas withdraws from all supports, becomes non-compliant with medications and subsequently deteriorates with regard to his level of functioning. Nikki describes Nicholas at these times as paranoid, verbally and physically aggressive, homeless and unemployed, and states that typically he will come to the attention of police and be brought into an inpatient mental health institution.From May 2007 until early 2010 Nicholas was managed through the community mental health service as a voluntary client on 50mg Risperidone depot, with case management. He was able to engage with employment via 'Breakthru' and rode his motorcycle to work as a mechanic assistant. He had contact with his mother, and was able to maintain private rental accommodation. In 2010 Nicholas transitioned to the GP shared care program. At this point he failed to attend Dr's appointments from August 2010 onwards. He had cut all contact with his parents and subsequently moved from his private rental accommodation to a boarding house (Ellie Bennett). He then was asked to leave Ellie Bennett due to his confrontational and verbally aggressive behaviour which appears to have been driven by some persecutory delusions regarding his treatment by management at Ellie Bennett (eg. that they were making false accusations about him smoking in his room). He stopped his depot in November 2010.He came to the attention of mental health again in 2011 when attending court on some charges of public nuisance but was assessed by court liaison staff as psychotic. In March 2012, Nicholas care was transferred to HHOT. Since that time he regularly attended his outpatient appointments, and received his depot. However, he remained poorly kempt, thought disordered, and disorganised with ongoing paranoia. Nicholas moved into a Department of Housing unit in Spring Hill in November 2012.2013 He had incorporated his MIRT case manager into his delusional system, believing the clinician to be collaborating with the government to prevent him getting rent assistance, among other things. He believed there was another Nicolas Churches (with no H) who was an impostor and was stealing his benefits etc. He was quite irritable and verbally aggressive. He refused to let his Mental Health Clinician (MHC) leave his unit as he wanted him to wait on the phone to speak with Centrelink. Nicholas was commenced on a trial of Clozapine, with good result. After discharge blood results show incomplete adherence to his medication regimen despite the MIRT follow up.A Complex Care Review Committee (CCRC) was held on 13/2/14 to discuss with a larger group of clinicians the best way to move Nicolas forwards whilst taking risk issues into account. Most outcomes were not taken up by Nicholas as he felt that his current treatment suited him and stated that he is happy with his current levels of support. 2015 Nicholas' social situation became untenable. Upon finding out that the Department of Housing (DOH) were due to make a routine inspection, he told his MHC that a male acquaintance had moved himself and all of his possessions into his unit. The DOH Housing Officer's inspection report stated that the unit was 'in a state of squalor' and was waist high in junk. This necessitated a multi-agency response to rectify the situation. Nicholas was extremely scared of the male acquaintance as he had threatened physical harm should he move any of his possessions. It also became apparent that Nicholas had been giving this man money. Partners in Recovery arranged for the disposal of the rubbish and the clean up of the unit. QPS had to be on site at the start of each day of the clean up to ensure that the man was not there as there was concern that he may be physically aggressive. DOH agreed on a transfer to another unit. He moved to New Farm. He had been treated for Hep C but seems to have remained infected. He is currently receiving treatment for Irritable Bowel Syndrome:- Chron's Disease via PAH. Continues with his blister pack medications and 2/52 depot via a GP clinic. He is visited intermittently by his mother and uncle.

Joanne is a 37 year old woman currently residing in BHC community housing who presented to RBWH (and subsequently had 2 admissions in January 2018) with a relapse of her paranoid schizophrenia.Background:Joanne has had numerous admissions to psychiatric hospitals, over a period of many years (since 1992). She has been trialled on oral anti-psychotics, typical and atypical depots, and Clozapine. Treatment has been complicated by non-compliance with oral medications, an itinerant lifestyle, and substance abuse. When unwell, Joanne presents with symptoms which include derogatory auditory hallucinations, ideas of reference, persecutory delusions, agitation and irritability, suicidal ideation and an increase in impulsive and disorganised behaviour.Joanne has had her diagnosis of Schizophrenia for over 25 years. It is unclear whether there is a family history of mental illness, but Joanne's childhood was characterized by abuse and disrupted family attachment as she was put into care at age 11 and had her first child at age 14. Joanne has four children who have all been adopted by her Aunty in NSW. Joanne also began misusing drugs at an early age which likely contributed to the onset of her psychotic illness, the treatment of which was further compounded by a history of itinerance and non-adherence. While Joanne has not discussed her trauma history with her PSP, it appears likely that past trauma contributes to her vulnerability in the community and escalates her risk of aggression when unwell. Joanne continues to maintain that she is not usingsubstances and thus further rapport building is needed to support her consideration of it's impact on her mental health.Joanne's mental state and rapport with HHOT have continued to improve since discharge from hospital but can still fluctuate intermittently - possibly due to substance use, although Joanne denies this. Joanne is adherent to both oral and depot medications and initially received her depot from Dr. Solari at Joanne's request, but recently has accepted her depot from HHOT. Joanne expresses a strong dislike of the IMI medication and with being under the Treatment Authority. To support Joanne to build rapport with HHOT staff, her requests to have depot from a GP and from female staff have been supported. While Joanne's insight regarding the need for antipsychotic medication has not significantly improved, her engagement with mental health staff has improved and she has always self-presented when her injection is due.Joanne will continue to require support from QH Mental Health and treatment under the Mental Health Act 2016 as she would be at high risk for disengagement from treatment at present. With continued support to maintain adherence to prescribed medications, Joanne will return to study (USQ Information & Technology) / employment and hopefully end the past cycle of itinerance and homelessness.

Historically Jessie would train/dance and teach for long periods of time, it was expected that she wouldn’t eat during this period, Jessie was also restricting in an attempt to control her weight. Meal portions are also smaller in their home and they follow certain food rules including not eating specific foods at night due to thoughts of weight gain. At this stage Jessie is still exercising through teaching dance more than the average person, although she finds this difficult to acknowledge, also finds it difficult not replacing her ceased activity of dance training with another form of exercise. Jessie is supported by her partner Rob, she also has a circle of close friends whom are supportive. Jessie is employed as a dance teacher and enjoys same. formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Jett is a 15 year old female, socially identifying as male, currently a student in year 10 of KGSHS. Jett presented to hospital in crisis with escalating family tensions leading to self-harm and suicidal gestures. This follows previous treatment for depression, anxiety and ADHD by private psychiatrist Dr Sarah Steele.During this admission, the treating team did not observe a pervasive depressive disorder. It was difficult to clearly separate Jett's reported feelings of low mood, anxiety and anger from the social context of family breakdown, circumstances of protracted admission, and the uncertainties of discharge destination. Jett's reported symptoms were at times noted to be incongruent to the observed affect of reactivity, laughing, socialising on the ward etc.Jett’s presentation is perhaps understandable as being the result of long standing family conflict of high expressed emotion, confused/inconsistent boundary setting and loss of consistent parenting/ role modelling. This began several years ago when his parents separated, leading to hostile and bitter disputes that inevitably has impacted Jett and his siblings. The breakdown is reported to have been precipitated by an extra marital affair between Jett’s mother and another woman, which then ultimately ended with this same woman then leaving to start a relationship with Jett's father (and whom remains his partner to date).Jett's period of school refusal of six months in 2016 played a significant role in the relationship breakdown with his mother, as she reportedly did not consent for Jett to attend KGSHS (mother wished Jett to continue attending Steiner school). During this six month period (in the care of his father), Jett spent significant time on the internet where he used social media as a distraction, and where Jett reports he ultimately formed his new identity. Jett had recently become increasingly preoccupied with spending time online to interact with his current boyfriend. Jett's recent conflict with his father was in part related to the change in limit setting around internet access, as his father became more concerned about the online content Jett was accessing, as well as the influence of social media on his self harming behaviours. Jett perceived this new limit setting by the father as being solely the influence of his new partner, and this led to increasing conflict.Jett appeared to have limit ability to mentalise and showed a rigid thinking style. His ongoing resentment towards father/mother was not able to be shifted, and this significantly impeded any chances of conflict resolution or problem solving. Jett did not appear able to consider the immediate consequences of his various behaviours which were emotionally reactive and impulsive. Jett's current situation in residential care is considered undesirable by the treating team. and it is likely that Jett will have some difficulties adjusting to these conditions. Although the relationship between Jett and his father was strained, Jett appears to have still been affected by the process of relinquishing care (rejection) and the limited access he now has to see his sisters (whom are protective). Given this, Jett is likely at risk of experiencing ongoing distress and therefore self harm risks are likely elevated in the immediate future. Attempts to normalise other aspects of Jett's life such as contact with siblings and ongoing participation in school are likely to be protective factors going forward. Supportive psychotherapy and focussed work which allows Jett to develop skills to deal with emotional distress would be recommended.

Presenting SymptomsAlanah presents with:1. flashbacks and nightmares,2. sleep disturbance,3. weight loss,4. poor relationships with each parent,5. depression and anxiety,6. deliberate self-harm and low self-esteem, and7. frequent suicidal ideation with numerous significant suicide attempts, most recently involving ingestion of approximately 100 paracetamol tablets, attempting to jump off the Storey Bridge and attempting to hang herself. These are triggered by perceived rejection and interpersonal conflict.Predisposing FactorsAlanah’s symptoms present in the context of neurodevelopmental vulnerability, perfectionistic and internalising temperament, and adverse early life experiences. There is a biological predisposition to mental illness including Ms Clear’s anxiety, depression, and personality vulnerabilities, and Mr Pitman’s alleged alcohol misuse. There is further genetic loading from the maternal family with history of bipolar disorder, anxiety, depression, and emotional avoidance. Suggestion of intergenerational attachment difficulties are also present in the maternal family with two of Alanah’s maternal aunts being sexually abused by their own maternal grandfather, and an intergenerational history of cut-off relationships within the maternal family. There are allegations that Mr Pitman was verbally, emotionally, and occasionally physically violent towards Ms Clear throughout their marriage however collateral information suggests that the parental relationship was most likely characterised by high expressed emotion and distance, both emotional and physical with Mr Pitman frequently working long hours or out of town. As her parents became less able to communicate effectively with each other, it appears that Alanah was actively placed in the role of go-between. Consequently, in order to serve her parent’s emotional needs, Alanah may have begun to sacrifice her own individuation and growth, and instead, unfairly taken on some of her parent’s stress and played the “peacemaker” role. It is thought that the difficulties experienced within the parental relationship during Alanah’s early years has contributed to Alanah’s hypersensitivity to others, her tendency to disconnect from emotions, feelings of low self-worth, and a tendency to self-blame. Being raised in a family in which the adults may have been emotionally unavailable due to their own individual vulnerabilities is likely to have left Alanah feeling frightened, and mistrusting of adults ability to meet her needs, with a negative view of herself and the world including the belief that she is not important and has little or no control over her life, resulting in low self-esteem and feelings of anxiety and depression.Precipitating FactorsThe current presenting issues arise in the context of Alanah entering adolescence, parental separation, and two separate alleged sexual assaults. Alanah’s core beliefs that others are untrustworthy or that the world is unsafe are likely to have been reinforced by these events which all occurred within a 12-month period. Alanah's presentation are usually triggered by perceived rejection and interpersonal conflicts with her parents or partner at the time.Perpetuating FactorsContextual factors maintaining Alanah’s difficulties include her mother’s criticism, intrusiveness, low parental self-efficacy, as well as the poor social support for Alanah and her mother. Her parents’ own reduced capacity to regulate emotions is hypothesised to have modelled that emotions are scary and difficult to control. It is suggested that when Alanah feels strong emotions, she attempts to have others, particularly professionals, manage these by being admitted to hospital. Alanah's difficulties are also perpetuated by a reluctance to engage in skill based learning and preference to discuss her trauma. This preference leaves Alanah in a vulnerable position where she is unable to independently problem solve situational crises.Protective FactorsAlanah is currently engaged in the DBT Program which provides a structured an ongoing support base from which Alanah can draw from. This includes a weekly individual therapy appointment, a weekly DBT group and phone coaching available 24 hours a day. She is currently residing in her own unit within Clayfield which she returned to post discharge. Alanah has also commenced a Diploma of Early Childhood Education and Care and works as an educator under supervision during more of the week.

Emily is a 19 year old single female who lives with her parents in Kenmore. She is the oldest of 4 children (two brothers, one sister), and is currently studying mathematics at UQ. She comes from a devout Catholic family. Emily has previously expressed being same sex attracted. Emily has been a psychotherapy patient since June 2017 and has currently participated in 34/30 sessions. Psychotherapy was recommended by Dr Hirst following an inpatient admission on RBWH H-floor in March 2017. Emily was admitted with a serious suicide attempt by overdose of paracetamol, citing increasing stressors associated with academic workload at university.Emily has reports a long history of anxiety and depressed mood, which began not long after her younger brother died of a brain tumour in 2012 when Emily was 13 years old. Although she reports she had always been a shy and somewhat anxious child previously, the social anxiety at school increased significantly and became associated with school avoidance and intense episodes of distress which required close parental support. Emily soon began utilising self harm by cutting at around 15 years of age which she reports helped her manage her distress. Despite these difficulties, Emily was a high performing student who achieved an OP 1. She conceptualises all of her problems with anxiety as being related to self derived academic pressures and dismisses the idea her her brother's death has played a role. Following graduation from high school, Emily reported experiencing less anxiety, and more difficulties with low mood with suicidal thoughts. She continued to cite academic stress and feeling overwhelmed with work load as the primary driver of her difficulties.Emily reports an unremarkable early childhood and believes she met her developmental milestones. She grew up in a devout Catholic environment which she states was loving and supportive. She denied any concerns around abuse of any kind. She developed severe headaches at the age of 6 which resulted in multiple hospitalisations and a diagnosis of Benign Intracranial Hypertension, which resolved over a one year period. I speculate that such a significant illness around this has impacted the way in which Emily experiences and communicates distress. The loss of her brother whom her parents state she was close to, is of great significance. Emily herself plays down the significance with a complete isolation of affect. There are several unknowns associated at this time, and I wonder about how the family dealt with the brother's terminal illness, how this impacted the family dynamic as a whole, whether there was abnormal grieving, how a 13 year old Catholic girl views death, or whether Emily felt she was in some way responsible. Notably she is he only person in the family who has become atheistEmily demonstrates strong obsessional and perfectionist personality traits. She strongly identifies with her academic self and appears to struggle with factors outside of her control which might impact her academic performance (eg group work). She has a limited ability for mentalisation. She has an inflexible style of thinking and struggles to recognise and communicate her emotional distress. She demonstrates a limited ability understand her parents concerns, which has in the past led to increased family tensions around her safety. In this sense she appears to be developmentally stuck as an early teenager. Emily has some social difficulties as a result of these psychological issues and she overall has superficial friendships. She reports strong anxiety at the idea of having intimate relationships.Emily's family continues to be supportive and she had positive relationship with siblings. Her university studies are both a a protective factor and and ongoing source of potential distress.

Stable accommodation was an issue for Natalie in the past as she was noted to have had frequent difficulties tolerating flatmates (noted to be secondary to paranoia). Natalie also often has problems with clinicians as she finds it difficult to trust people. Natalie's treatment was transferred to the RBWH following her move to a transitional housing unit in the RBWH catchment area in 2009.Psychiatric HistoryNatalie was diagnosed with Schizophrenia in approximately 2004. She had 3 lengthy mental health admissions at the Princess Alexandra Hospital in 2008. Natalie has had multiple involuntary mental health admissions whilst under the care of RBWH and has trialled various medications including Risperdal Consta, Quetiapine, Olanzapine and Flupenthixol. Natalie was commenced on Clozapine in 2011. Natalie's ITO was revoked by the MHRT on 17.07.12. Natalie maintained compliance to treatment under supervision of her psychiatrist (Dr. Michael O'Sullivan) and mental health clinician (Julie O'Sullivan) up until December 2012, then informing her treating team she would no longer be takingclozapine. This lead to a deterioration in mental state over subsequent months. Natalie's care was transferred from Pine Rivers Hospital after a month long voluntary admission. She was not complying with the treatment plan (was self-adjusting her medication doses), was guarded and suspicious with nursing staff, withdrawn and was not participating in any of the patient programmes. It was decided then, given her complicated mental health history,failure to respond to least restrictive treatment and associated risks when psychotic, that she should be transferred to RBWH under involuntary assessment with re-introduction of Clozapine. Natalie was commenced on Clozapine immediately on admission with lithium support for neutrophils. Natalie was guarded, suspicious and did not interact with treating team. Positive symptoms were not elicited voluntarily, but indicators could be seen in her behaviour - e.g. calling Police to ward to report her clothing had been stolen by her parents. Eventually she demonstrated improvement, with increased interaction with treating team, a notable change in affect reactivity and most tellingly, she began making contact with her parents again (although somewhat guarded in doing so). Natalie was referred to MIRT on discharge under an ITO to continue with her care in the community. Natalie was initially difficult to engage in therapy and was followed up by MIRT from May 2013 until July 2014. Natalie's care was transferred from MIRT to the INBMHS Southern Team in July 2014.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: BackgroundMr. Brodie Nicol is a 56 year old single gentleman who currently lives alone in a privately owned unit in Auchenflower. Brodie is currently unemployed and receives the disability support pension. Brodie receives a HASP support package which is provided by Open Minds and MACS who provide daily assistance for medication management, domestic tasks, meal preparation and social activities such as PCYC gym, library visits and computer training. MACS visit each evening and supervise Brodie's medication which is kept in a locked box. Brodie has good family support and sees his family regularly. Brodie enjoys going to restaurants and cafes and the movies. He is well linked in with his GP. There is no known alcohol or illicit substance use.Psychiatric HistoryBrodie first came to the attention of psychiatric services in 1986 (age 28yrs) when his mother convinced him to see a psychiatrist. He had developed delusions concerning muscle pain in his thighs. This had been rigorously investigated by orthopaedic surgeons and neurologists with no organic aetiology ever found. The original diagnosis was mono symptomatic delusions / Schizophrenia. Brodie ceased seeing his psychiatrist in 1988 as he felt she had not understood his problems and was not helping him. Prior to this time, he had functioned very highly. He went to a private school and was described as being very intelligent, conscientious and obsessional. Brodie was a good athlete and was training in running to state representative standard. He obtained an honours degree in mathematics and was undertaking a doctorate, until he developed his muscle pain in 1986. Since then he has not continued his education and has not pursued any form of career. Around 1990, Brodie left Australia and travelled the world looking for relief for his somatic concerns. He sold his home (which was given to him by his parents) and severed all ties with family and friends.This enabled him to travel the world seeking a "cure" for his muscle pain. The countries visited included New Caledonia, Finland, Japan, Hong Kong, Italy, Egypt, South America and the United States. It was during his travels in Uruguay in 1992, that he shot and injured two lawyers as a result of untreated persecutory delusions, as described in the Forensic Assessment at the time. Brodie was transferred from a psychiatric facility in Uruguay back to Australia and underwent a protracted admission to the RBWH mental health unit (December 1992 – June 1993) where a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia was confirmed. Following discharge he was managed by the RBWH Community Mental Health Service. Brodie's level of disturbance remained relatively minimal until he required four admissions to the RBWH between 1997 and 1999. He absconded to Noumea in 2000 where he attempted to engage a lawyer. Whilst there, he made a serious suicide attempt inflicting deep lacerations to both wrists. In 2001 when Brodie's treatment history was discussed with a staff psychiatrist at RBWH, the situation was recalled as follows: Brodie had absconded overseas and was unable to be traced, he then made a premeditated attempt on his life was only found as another hotel guest noticed blood seeping out beneath his room door. He was transferred back to Australia three days later and placed under an Involuntary Treatment Order whilst an inpatient at the RBWH before being transferred to the Medium Secure Unit (MSU) of The Prince Charles Hospital. Brodie remained at MSU from January to November 2001 and then transferred to the Community Care Unit (Somerset Villas), RBWH where he has resided until 2013. During the intervening years, he has required two brief inpatient admissions to the RBWH (October 2004 and March 2006).To date, Brodie has had a poor treatment response to a number of antipsychotic medications including Quetiapine, Risperidone, Amisulpride, Olanzapine and Aripiprazole. Brodie was treated with Clozapine for many years, however, had a medical admission in 2015 with LRTI and further deterioration in cardiac function resulting in the need to cease Clozapine. Since Brodie's diagnosis, he has expressed repeatedly that he does not believe he has a mental illness and should not be on medication. As a result of his poor insight, there have been chronic issues around non-adherence with medication, and his illness is such that the risk of harm to himself and others is significant when he is unwell. Serious concerns remain that Brodie would become non-adherent with treatment if he were not under an ITO, leading to deterioration in his physical and mental wellbeing. However, he continues to hope to eventually come off his ITO and all psychotropic medications in the future. Brodie has periodically engaged a number of lawyers, to attempt to challenge his ITO and have it revoked. Brodie was referred to the Community Southern Team, Inner North Brisbane Mental Health Service in August 2013 for ongoing community mental health follow-up. The Southern Team's former Team Manager, K. Carney submitted a notification to the Gun Registration Board.Early Warning Signs:Pacing, becomes dishevelled, rubs his head excessively, mumbling to himself.

Scott is a 49 year old single man, living at level 3 supported accommodation Herston Lodge since April 2014. He is currently on DSP, and manages his own finances. He has a long forensic history including stabbing his brother Grant in 2008 with a hunting knife and stalking. Scott reports a long-standing history of familial conflict, itinerant lifestyle and homelessness. Mental Illness dates back to 2004 with episodes of non-compliance and being lost to follow up in Victoria.A Forensic Order was made in 2014, after Scott accrued numerous charges due to events which ensued due to him leaving Victoria and fleeing to Queensland in a stolen vehicle. Charges include: Drive uninsured vehicle, Drive unregistered vehicle, Fail to stop, Going armed in public so as to cause fear, Obstruct police, Offences involving registration, Unlawful use of a motor vehicle x 2, Serious assault on police, Stealing, Unlawful possession of a weapon, Use registration plate of another vehicle, Fail to supply specimen of breath for analysis, Willful damage. In the years leading up to his index offences, Scott had a number of inpatient admissions, triggered usually by non-compliance with oral medication. His first known presentation to MHS in Victoria (2004) was in the context of disclosing bizarre ideation to Police when he was served with an intervention order (re: a young shop assistant he was alleged tohave stalked after developing a morbid interest in her - no other details known). Police referred him for assessment at that time. He was admitted to hospital and commenced on treatment, oral Risperidone. He had a number of subsequent admissions, usually due to non-compliance with oral medication, and having become self-isolative and breaking off contact from family. In 2008, while living with his brother Grant, Scott experienced paranoid delusions that he was being "hunted" because he had "important military intelligence". He eventually stabbed his brother Grant due to psychotic ideas. On another occasion, it was reported that Scott then stole his brother's vehicle following a dispute over money. He was arrested after a siege during which he had armed himself with a hunting knife, axe and shovel. He served a total of six months in Melbourne Assessment Prison / Metropolitan Remand Centre, being released on a two year community corrections order. At that time, he went to live with his twin brother Mark in Ballarat. In 2009, Scott was admitted to the Ballarat Mental Health Unit, after becoming guarded and paranoid in the context of psychosocial stressors and non-compliance with medication. He was recommenced on oral medications and discharged back to his brother's address, but had another admission in 2011 again in the context of poor oral medication compliance. Scott continued to live with his brother Mark, until in February 2011 he had an altercation with his brother regarding accommodation. Scott reports his brother "kicked him out", and he became homeless. At this time, he was lost to follow-up, and treatment. Scott reports he was destitute and became increasingly paranoid and later became concerned that his brothers would arrange for him to be "locked up". It was at this time Scott decided to leave Victoria, and travel to Queensland.While on remand at Arthur Gorrie Correctional Centre, Scott disclosed persecutory beliefs in relation to his perceived longstanding harassment by his older brother and the police. He was experiencing grandiose delusions regarding the British monarchy stating he was "the son of Edward VIII". His mental state further deteriorated and he became increasingly hostile, refusing treatment, eventually resulting in transfer from correctional custody to High Security Inpatient Services in August 2012. He initially refused medication and food, but eventually cooperated with depot medication. Scott was officially discharged from AGCC on 27th February 2014, after being granted Bail. He was discharged to level 3 supported accommodation (Herston Lodge, his current address), and his ITO transferred to RBWH where he continued treatment and regular review.A Forensic Order was made on 25th August 2014 following a finding of unsoundness of mind.In June 2017 Scott's FO was revoked and a TSO was made by the MHRT.Scott remains fixated on his priority goal of relocating to Victoria however seems reluctant to engage in any problem-solving or steps to work towards this (incl. temporary leave to visit family, applying for transfer via legal avenues as previously advised as only available option). He is aware of an outstanding warrant for his arrest upon his return to Victoria and views this as a barrier to him temporarily visiting family, he states that he will not leave his belongings in QLD and visit Victoria in case he ends up in prison and therefore will lose his room at Herston and his belongings. He is willing to return to Victoria with his belongings once he is able to leave Qld.Scott remains amotivated to engage in any meaningful activities, employment or other means of support while he remains in Queensland stating this is a waste of time and money because Qld is not his home. He remains socially isolated articulating that he is not like the other people in Herston Lodge, he doesn't fight or use drugs, so he does not wish to socialise with them. He has very limited and irregular contact with family, and reports that even if he were to relocate to Victoria, he would not want his family overly involved in his day to day living or supports. He does not give the treating team permission to contact his family to assist with planning for transfer back to Victoria.Despite being able to attend to all ADLs and live independently, Scott resides in level 3 supported accommodation, due to not wanting to set himself up permanently in Queensland, or go to additional effort with maintaining a household or other commitments while temporarily in Queensland.Scott continues to externalise blame and feels justified in his offending. Scott believes lack of accommodation and income as well as lack of support as he has here, would explain and justify returning to offending behaviours.Scott attends all required appointments. He can become frustrated and anxious if he has to wait for any time for his depot or if his preferred staff are not available to give his depot. While he has said he would be willing to engage with mental health services upon his return to Victoria (or post-revocation of TSO) to some degree, he does not guarantee he would continue with his current prescribed treatment. Scott believes that so long as he is able to maintain stable accommodation and income he would have no issues in future and would not require ongoing medication.Scott's level of insight and engagement in his treatment and particularly identification of early warning signs and relapse prevention has improved over the years. He has started to consider what supports he would require long-term to maintain his current mental state and level of functioning upon return home to Victoria. He has also demonstrated an increasing level of insight regarding this and recently has identified some illness specific factors (paranoia, "fantasies"), whereas he previously attributed only external stress to his deterioration on the past (lack of family support, lack of income, homelessness).

Cameron is a 14 yo lad, living with his mother and step grandfather. Cameron has had a long history throughout his childhood of referral to community CYMHS teams for anger and aggression, low mood, and increasing suicidal expression and suicidal acts within the context of school. Cameron struggles with interpersonal relationships and has frequently become dysregulated with his peer group. From the start of this year, Cameron was becoming increasingly non-compliant and disengaged from his school work, increasingly escalating to the point he had repeatedly tried to self-asphyxiate byplacing his school bag around a high beam and placing the handles around his neck. This had led to multiple presentations to ED and a 1 week inpatient admission in May 2017.Cameron's formative years, stemming back to conception have been highly vulnerable. Cameron was conceived through rape, exposed to high risk medications in the first trimester (Katherine learnt she was pregnant whilst an inpatient at Prince Charles Hospital being treated for Bipolar/BPD, later diagnosed with PTSD). Katherine experienced her own vulnerabilities by virtue of her own trauma history. Katherine had been involved in identifying her friends who had been fatally involved in a road traffic accident. This was in addition to Katherine's own history of physical abuse from her father, leaving home and school in adolescence, being transient and estranged from her family. Katherine describes her relationship with her mother then as being distanced and reported to have not been emotionally available to Katherine. Clearly Katherine's experience of appropriate modelling from her own family of origin and attachment will have greatly impacted on her parenting style and relationship with Cameron.From early childhood, Cameron had had involvement from Mercy Services and DoCS further to concerns around lack of parental supervision, poor hygiene and neglect, leading to being made subject of a Custody Order and taken into out of home care at 5 yo until 8 yo. This disruption in his early years, would clearly have impacted on Cameron's sense of safety. Cameron has been described by his mum as clingy at times who with her own level of personal vulnerabilities, would likely have impacted on her capacity to meet Cameron's needs, being available to offer him co-regulation and develop his sense of safety, at such time.It is noted in collateral information obtained from Terri, that Cameron's mother had experienced domestically violent relationships in the early years, although the level to which Cameron was exposed is still to be determined. Whether this was in utero or in early childhood may suggest an impact on brain development and epigenetic changes. Similarly, this may have impacted on the ability to model effective communication styles and conflict resolution particularly around interpersonal conflict. Katherine's ability to contain and soothe Cameron may have been compromised at such high stress times. This in turn may have compromised Cameron's ability to learn to self-soothe and experience comfort.During Cameron's time in DoCS care, Cameron was subject to sexual assault by his carer's son thus further traumatising Cameron and confirming his internalised view of the world being unsafe and inability to trust others to keep him protected. This coupled with multiple placement breakdowns possibly further reinforces his own fragile sense of self and increased perceptions of rejection and abandonment, shame and poor self-esteem.Developmentally, Cameron has his own biological vulnerabilities adding to the complex picture with pre-existing diagnosis of pervasive developmental Disorder - ASD & ? ADD. Cameron is also reported to have a level of Intellectual Impairment and is currently completing Grade 3 work, although it is unclear from contradictory reports if this is about his level of ability or about engagement within an academic routine. Equally Cameron requires ongoing assessment for his speech and language difficulties to clarify and identify his limitations and supports required. It is possible that Cameron has learned to use such escalations as a means to communicate overwhelming feelings and frustrations without having an already existing emotional language.Cameron at 14 years of age physically appears much older than his years due to a tall and larger frame. Cameron is currently engaged in a specialised education programme which is aimed at a much younger age range – 7-8 yo which possibly is equally impacting on his sense of self and self-esteem.There has been a long-standing concern relating to Cameron's ability to self-regulate with escalations in how Cameron will express himself through high levels of risk taking. Cameron is impulsive and has a low tolerance threshold with a developed pattern of avoidance through externalising. As such the current concerns have escalated with a more intense focus and expectation that Cameron will adhere to High School learning and compliance with school routine. This is in discord with Cameron's wish and a need to focus on and withdraw to his computer games. Clearly Cameron'sdisengagement from school and lack of motivation to engage in daily life skills has compromised his adolescent development in individuation and independence. At such times when either school or family attempt to encourage engagement or place limitations around computer use Cameron will either ignore or escalate through suicidal threats and acts as a means to exert control of this environment.Other precipitating factors are likely to be initiated by the fact that the family home is currently in a state of renovation which has been described as disruptive for all concerned. There are expectations placed on Cameron to keep his room tidy and assist around the home when this is in an equally cluttered and disorganised state, possibly leading to confusing and mixed messages. Similarly there have been some disruptions to the dynamics within the home with Katherine's cousin moving in with his partner.The family have struggled to maintain a sense of routine around Cameron with escalations in his mood at the start of the school week, when he appears tired following a weekend. Without a sense of security through routine, Cameron may feel unsettled triggering his world view of fear and unreliability, stemming from his early history of uncertainty.Cameron's emotional escalations and poor coping strategies promotes removal from school and academics. This has become a repeated pattern of behaviour with Cameron expressing suicidal threats and acts to gain control over returning home and accessing his computer. Cameron’s own physical size, presence and lack of reciprocal social interactions can possibly perpetuate his interpersonal relationships negatively and sense of power which can possibly be anxiety provoking if feeling unsafe. Similarly this uncertainty for Cameron about his family's health issues may further be exacerbating his lack of sense of safety and worry for his future.It is reasonable to believe that Cameron has suffered cumulative harm from the events of his early formative years. Early attachment problems, trauma and developmental issues are pivotal to Cameron's ongoing behavioural and emotional problems. BackgroundMrs. Margaret Glenwright is a 57 year old married retired lady who lives with her husband & one of three adult sons who has down syndrome, in their home in Kenmore. Margaret & her husband are self-funded retirees & used to own an electrical business. Margaret enjoys playing tennis, yoga & socialising with friends on a weekly basis. Margaret has a diagnosis of schizophrenia & is currently treated under a Treatment Authority.Psychiatric HistoryMargaret has a diagnosis of schizophrenia which has been sub-optimally treated for many years due to disengagement from services & reluctance to take medication. Margaret has a history of discontinuing treatment, & she has been non-compliant with medications since disengaging from a brief trial of Paliperidone depot via a private psychiatrist 2 to 3 years ago. Margaret has previously had delusions that a media presenter was in love with her & a history of leaving the family home & booking herself into a hotel for unclear reasons but this appears to be related to the belief that these people were in love with her. Margaret's family attempted to re-engage Margaret with her private psychiatrist, however, Margaret did not attendappointments. Margaret was referred to the RBWH Acute Care Team on 23.6.15 following concern from her GP and family.Margaret presented with persecutory delusions & auditory hallucinations, & was acting on her delusions by sending text messages to a disconnected phone number protesting her innocence of claims that she believes the media are making up against her. Margaret began discussing her delusional beliefs with friends & there was a significant risk of damage to her reputation & of misadventure & vulnerability. Margaret's delusions about the media had been present for years & reportedly had worsened over the last 6-9/12. Margaret had been increasingly preoccupied with sending text messages & writing in a journal about her delusions. ~3/12 ago she started talking to herself with repetitive themes saying "I'm not scratched", "It's all lies", "I hate Elizabeth, I hate them". This was a new symptom. Margaret had stated that her sister was dead & that the family believe she killed her sister. Her sleep had worsened & her son could hear her in the bathroom talking to herself at 3am. She has shown less interest in her usual activities such as tennis, yoga & manicures. Margaret was also requiring more prompting than usual to engage in family activities. She has always taken time to process things that are said to her, but this had also gotten worse.Margaret was briefly treated by ACT who commenced her on an ITO in 2015 and referred on to Southern team. Abilify and paliperidone were both trialled with limited success for Margaret and delusionally driven behaviours continued - texting the ABC, constant AH's. Margaret's husband reported that she continued to be pre-occupied and not in touch with reality. Her delusions were quite fixed though there had been some improvement in her anxiety and sleep. Margaret was reviewed by Dr. Iti Agrawal on 8.10.15 and commenced on Olanzapine 2.5mg nocte for 3-4 weeks in addition to the Paliperidone depot. In the following months, Margaret presented with a significant improvement in her mental state. Although her delusions persisted, she was much less preoccupied with this and her thoughts are more organised. Auditory hallucinations disappeared and Margaret was sleeping much better. Margaret was linked with her GP for the monthly depot administration and was enrolled in the ATLAS program for extra support around this.

Cate is a 36 yo lady who was referred to the GP-Psych service at RBWH after presenting to her GP with negative and depressive thoughts in the context of a stressful work environment. She was assessed by Dr Hirst, who diagnosed her with Complex PTSD and recommended her as a candidate for ongoing psychotherapy.Cate has a developmental history that is significant for prejudicial events that may be contributing to her current presentation. She is the second of four children to a Catholic couple and attended primary school without issue until the age of 12. Her parents were reasonably devout Catholics, and the whole family attended Church on a regular basis during Cate's early childhood. Around the age of 11 or 12, Cate's parents became involved with a branch of the Catholic community known as Latin Mass. Cate describes this community as somewhat cult-like and states that her environment from that point on became surrounded by religious fanatics and doomsday predictions. The Latin Mass community also believed that traditional Catholic schools were inadequately catering to their expectations of what children should be taught in school and so Cate's parents began to home school her and her other siblings in order to align themselves with the beliefs of the other members in the community. This sudden departure from their normal way of life was a major upheaval in Cate's early childhood and she spent most of her home-schooling days wishing that she could return to "normal" school again.At the age of 16, Cate's father became ill with appendicitis and was unwell at home for several days. He refused to seek medical attention at this time, despite the requests from his family due to his strong religious beliefs and this ultimately led to his untimely death as a result of complications associated with untreated appendicitis. Cate was a witness to these events and bore the brunt of her mother's anger and grief after his death as she was the oldest daughter and most emotionally available of all the children.At age 17, after completing her education, Cate pursued a Bachelor of Education at university. She left the family home against the wishes of her mother and attended university, where she states that she felt the "most free" she has ever allowed herself to feel. During this period of her life, Cate did not actively practice Catholicism and made efforts to distance herself from the Catholic community. This experience was her first exposure to romantic relationships and also involved heavy alcohol consumption. Cate denies having ever tried any illicit or recreational drugs at any stage of her life.

Vanessa is a 32 year old mother of a 3yo daughter, Estelle and 15month old son, Edmund. She has a supportive husband, Luke; mother, mother-in-law and sisters. She had no thoughts of harm to the foetus or to her daughter.Work stressors appear t be the precipitating factor in Vanessa's decline in mental state. Being pregnant at the time may have also increased her vulnerability. There was a strong affective component in the presentations with mood congruent depressive delusions. There is a strong family history for Bipolar Affective Disorder. Treated with mood stabilising medications. She was treated under a TA and had 4x ECT and olanzapine.Vanessa has a supportive husband, Luke and supportive sisters and mother and mother-in-law. The children are not attending childcare.Vanessa continues to remain settled following her decision not to return to work until next year. She is sleeping well and has a good appetite. She reports her mood as good and enjoys activities such as going out with friends.Vanessa has agreed to see the psychologist through our service.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: owns Mazda3Edward (Eddie) is a 49 year old single man with a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia. According to Eddie he had been experiencing auditory hallucinations from the age of 17, after he reported suffering an acquired brain injury. He described constantly hearing threatening voices talking to him and about him. He reported intermittent cannabis and amphetamine abuse during his late teens and twenties, but claimed that he had not abused substances for over 5 years until just before the index offence. Collateral information from Eddie’s ex-girlfriend indicated he was experiencing auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions consistently between 2000 and 2004. Eddie had also reported that a psychologist at an employment agency had once recommended that he see a mental health service, but he did not follow through due to impaired insight.Following the index offence, Eddie spent approx. 7 months in prison before being transferred to High Secure Unit at the Park. He was treated on Olanzapine by PMHS, after initially refusing any anti-psychotic medication. After his transfer to HSU, he was commenced on Clozapine trial (November 2005). This led to a gradual resolution of positive psychotic symptoms and Eddie progressed well through CSU, accessing 5 nights LCT per week to supported accommodation by October 2010. There was one incident with a co-resident of the supported accommodation resulting in suspension of leave for 9 months. He continued to progress and was transferred to Somerset Villas Community Care Unit in October 2012. He progressed relatively well at CCU and his mental state remained stable. He demonstrated an overall high level of functioning and established routines, at times rather rigid. Eddie applied for public housing in 2014, with the view that he could commence a gradual transition from CCU. S - Rachelle is a 48-year old single woman currently living with her partner in a private unit in Spring Hill. Rachelle has a diagnosis of late onset paranoid schizophrenia. Rachelle has been managed by CCT-Southern since her discharge in Nov 2017 where she had a 5 week admission in the context of bizarre behaviours at the Hilton Hotel where she had been staying. QPS was alerted when Rachelletold staff she was their boss and fired them. She stated that the manager had poisoned her coffee. When QPS arrived, Rachelle claimed that she was a sergeant of police and an undercover Federal agent. She informed QPS that they were fake and she was going to fire them. She tried to arrest them. Rachelle was BIB under an EEA as she did not cooperate and needed to be handcuffed. On assessment at RBWH, Rachelle stated that she was studying for an exam and needed quiet at the Hotel as there was construction going on next door to her unit. She was irritable and guarded, expressing delusional beliefs. Her insight was impaired, refused treatment and was admitted under a TA. During this admission, Rachelle's treatment was changed to depot Paliperidone as she had refused orals and had previous success with Risperidone. Her mental state improved steadily upon commencement of depot Paliperidone 100mg and was discharged with close case management and psychiatric follow up in the community.Previous to this, Rachelle was admitted to RBWH in 2015 for 3 weeks under an ITO, treated for a delusional disorder with risperidone. She was followed up in the community for 3 months before ITO revoked. Her delusions at this time revolved around her mother assuming Rachelle's identity, people at work being fake and her husband was replaced by an imposter. Collateral from her family suggest intermittent psychotic episodes about every 2 years often associated with stress, which apparently resolved without treatment. She was managed by the Acute Care Team since August 2017 after family became concerned by her withdrawing from them and her behaviour becoming more erratic. She believed her cousin ( who does not live in Brisbane, was "mooning" her.) However, Rachelle remained guarded and was reluctant to engage.B- As Rachelle has responded well to treatment, her insight into her mental illness continuing to improve and her current functioning almost back to premorbid functiong, her treatment authority was reversed in May 2018. Rachelle continues to actively work on her recovery using CBT-P, mindfulness and EWS. Her monthly Paliperidone depot has been reduced to 75mg (due to increased prolactin levels) and will be transitioning to 3 monthly Invega Trinza in Aug 2018 under GP shared care with a plan to discharge. However, Rachelle has recently been made redundant from her contract position in an IT Learning company due to funding loss and has requested to remain an open consumer. Rachelle has agreed to a referral to Mylestones IEP and continue to engage closely with case management and regular psychiatric reviews.A - Rachelle is a 48 yo woman who presented with an acute psychotic episode in the context of multiple recent stressors on a background of late onset schizophrenia. She had a recent relationship breakdown, stress from course work related to a Masters in IT and withdrew from her family and friends. This tends to be a pattern with Rachelle when her mental health deteriorates. She maintains a very high level of functioning in the community when well, and is slowly engaging with her estranged family and close friends. She has responded very well to the Paliperidone depot, actively uses CBT-P to maintain her recovery and has developed good insight into her schizophrenia illness. She presents with no affective or psychotic features despite recent loss of employment. She is agreeable to continue with treatment and monitoring with CCT.

Lance has seriously self harmed as a result of command hallucinations telling him to kill himself. Lance also experiences paranoia and high levels of associated anxiety and frequently seeks PRN to manage this. Lance also has a hx of binge drinking as a method of managing distress and when intoxicated can become aggressive and usually will require presentation to hospital to contain risks. This matter was heard in 2017 and charges were dispensed with due to Lance having a mental health defence. Presenting - Chronic AH, paranoia and mood fluctuation (primarily anxiety) resulting in distress and acting impulsively at times. Will often act on AH telling him to harm himself or consume large amounts of alcohol leading to aggressive behaviour and/or self harm. Personality vulnerabilities which result in high sensitivity to abandonment and perceived rejection from others often resulting in self harm. When in acute psychotic relapse Lance may present almost cationic, perseverative and with significantly reduced self cares. Predisposing - CSA, witnessed DV growing up, early cannabis use, MVA resulting in loss of role/employment/relationships. Lance is quiet a sensitive and creative soul who grew up in a very masculine environment that did not allow for his full expression. Lance identifies as a member of the LGBTI community however, this is not accepted by family and co-residents currently. Precipitating - relapses are precipitated by interpersonal conflicts particularly with his family, perceived rejection/abandonment, accessing the community - particularly crowded places, stressful events and treatment resistant symptoms that causes distress, alcohol use and intimate partner relationships ending or lack of intimate partner relationships, past traumatic memories that appear unexpectedly, poor sleep and non-compliance with treatment (although this has not occurred for many years, medications supervised). Mood and psychotic sx tend to have a cyclic nature fluctuating over about a two week cycle, starting off good then deteriorating suddenly by the end of 2/52 for this reason Lance is receiving fortnightly ECT which appears to have reduced presentations to hospital and admissions. Lance will generally have a topic that he is dealing with sometimes for several months, it may involve a past relationship, an issue with a co-resident, not having a partner and past regrets. Lance at times, does not respond well to limit setting and will become irritable and/or angry if limits are placed on him particularly around drinking. Perpetuating - ongoing intermittent alcohol use, maladaptive schemes - low self esteem/worth, disproportionate guilt at times, lack of intimate partner relationship which is troubling for Lance, low frustration tolerance, reliance on PRN. Coping style is medication orientated although Lance has learned many non-medication strategies over the years which he currently uses. Protective - Lance utilises many strategies to cope with chronic sx including listening to music, doing art work, cooking, going for walks. He is activity orientated and enjoys socialising with others at local new farm neighbourhood centre. Well supported by family and Open Minds. Compliance with treatment and willing to work with treating team. Able to express his emotions and his creative side. Formulation: Lance has a treatment resistant illness which he manages with a combination of medication, psychological strategies and supports. Illness is complicated by acquired brain injury, substance misuse and personality vulnerabilities.

Her ITO was changed to community category on discharge.Admission 24/11/17 - 18/12/17:Venika presented with acute paranoid delusions and hallucinations regarding female spirits that she can feel and see. Venika is a highly educated woman, she is compliant and responding well to treatment, and has a husband who is very supportive of her. Her insight and judgement remain poor, and she will require case manager follow up to monitor for any side effects from her medications, liaise with her partner regarding further concerns, as well as ensuring medication compliance continues on discharge. Tina is a 52 year old, single woman, who lives in a studio BRIC Housing Unit in New Farm. She is currently unemployed and receiving Newstart Allowance, but is looking for casual work in the hospitality industry. Tina has recently applied for Disability Support Pension in the context of a recent diagnosis of Schizophrenia (Late Onset), on a background of past treatment for depression. Tina has been quite guarded with assessing Clinicians and Doctors when discussing information about her past, and the information that has been provided has been inconsistent. The Treating Team are unclear whether these discrepancies relates to the acute nature of Tina's contact with Mental Health Services and/or whether the inconsistencies exist as a form of protective strategy for Tina in dealing with the traumatic nature of the things she has experienced in her life. Collateral from an assessment that was completed in 2011 suggests that Tina was born in Brisbane, and that she had also lived interstate. At the time of her first contact with Mental Health Services Tina identified as Indigenous. Her indigenous status was also documented as being confirmed by Centrelink. She had readily engaged with the Indigenous Health Worker at that time. Tina had also reported a prejudicial childhood, and identified as being a victim of physical and sexual abuse in institutional care as a child. She provided a timeline of being cared for by her grandmother, and later her aunt and uncle, before being taken into Foster Care. However, when Tina was question by a Doctor on the 09/03/17 she is reported to have denied any Indigenous heritage, advising staff that she had been brought up in Texas by her American father, and that she had moved to Australia when she was 17 years old. She stated that her mother has never been in her life. Tina has also indicated previously that she was once married, (now divorced) and that she has two adult children and two grandchildren. Ina recent review by the Community Care Team Registrar Tina denied having any family in Australia. While Tina has only recently been referred to the RBWH Community Care Team (Southern), the treating team are looking forward to building a therapeutic rapport with Tina, and hope to learn more about her as a person and her experience of life.Past Hospital Admissions:G Floor, RBWH MHS (9 - 16 March 2017).Tina was originally referred to the Homeless Health Outreach Team (HHOT) on the 6/02/17 by a Community Support Agency called Micah after staff had observed Tina exhibiting odd behaviours and in the context of her abruptly leaving accommodation in Wynnum West where she had recently placed after an extended period of living on the streets. Tina was located by HHOT and was observed responding to internal stimuli in the Brisbane CBD. Upon interaction, Tina appeared to be experiencing paranoid symptoms. She was placed under the Mental Health Act and transported to hospital for an involuntary Assessment.On medical review Tina was reporting persecutory delusions (reports being violently assaulted at food vans in front of everyone including food van staff and no one assisting her and that Indigenous women on the streets were yelling at her) and distressing auditory hallucinations. She denied her Indigenous heritage and reported that she was raised in Texas by her American father. Previous history has suggested that she responded well to anti psychotic treatment in the past. Her illness appeared to be affecting her ability to maintain permanent accommodation leading to chronic homelessness. She was refusing voluntary admission or trial of medication and was posing a risk to self and others.Once in hospital Tina was diagnosed with Schizophrenia (late onset), and commenced on a monthly long acting anti-psychotic medication. After a short admission, accommodation was arranged at Pindari Women's Hostel and she was discharged back into the community, with HHOT follow up. Tina remained at Pindari Women's Hostel until 08/05/17, when she relocated to a Bric housing group room in Kent St, New Farm. Tina reports feeling safe and settled in new accommodation and plans to remain there until her Disability Support Pension application is approved.Past Engagement with Mental Health Services:Tina had one brief engagement with RBWH Homeless Health Outreach Team in 2011 when she was referred by Pindari Womens' Hostel. At the time of referral she presented with persecutory delusions, pressured speech, racing thoughts and increased anxiety. She was commenced on quetiapine (100mg) with a view to increase the dose but she was lost to the service when she relocated to the Gold Coast to live. The clinical notes on file indicate that Tina responded well to the trial of quetiapine.Rosemount Mental Heath Unit:Tina report that she has previously been an inpatient of Rosemount Mental Health Unit where she was diagnosed with depression and prescribed fluoxetine. Unfortunately there is no information available to the service currently to confirm or deny this admission.
