Occupational Influence:Caitlin participated in a range of occupations during her childhood such as dancing (ballet, tap, jazz), playing the piano,playing the violin, being in the school band and short distance running. Caitlin excelled at all of these and was seen as beingexceptional, she self reports themes of perfectionism from an early age. These occupations formed Caitlin's early identityand representation of others perceptions of her and her ability / skills, ultimately synthesizing doing, being, becoming andbelonging to support an evolving sense of self. In her early teenage years Caitlin experienced rapid weight loss whichresulted in a long hospital admission this interrupted her capacity to engage in her valued roles and placed her in anenvironment that had a negative impact on her image (children's hospital). During this stay Caitlin was diagnosed withAnorexia Nervosa, further investigations were conducted for Celiac's but came back negative at this stage. Caitlin reportsthis part of her life commenced a representation of being only a "number," which had the control to give or take away hersense of self by removing access to valued occupations.Caitlin had several hospital admissions through her teenage years which continued to interrupt her education and other roles,this experience caused a greater sense of loss and further instilled a view that she was perceived as an Anorexic and later aCeliac. Expressing emotional states to others to raise these concerns was not readily received by the environments Caitlinwas experiencing. Further trauma was experienced at the age of 16years through being sexually assaulted by a "friend", thisincident went unreported and assisted further in critical self appraisal. Caitlin attempted to forget the incident by goingoverseas to Canada to see family (Canadian heritage), the trip was unsuccessful and Caitlin was returned to Australia whereshe experienced further hospital admissions due to being medically compromised and of significantly low weight.Occupational Presentation:Currently Caitlin no longer engages in these early formed occupations and reports this as being a process of loss and grief.Forming a new valued identity that isn't based on childhood occupations and degree level study is difficult and is met withguilt and shame. Ongoing restrictive eating patterns are embedded in feelings of shame and guilt and assist Caitlin innumbing interoceptive sensory responses and enable her to feel undesired by others "if i keep myself as ugly and tiny aspossible people wouldn't want to go there". Her continued battle with Celiac's can illicit pain, lethargy and depressive feelingscausing Caitlin to have difficulties with maintaining a balanced routine and commitment to her roles. Caitlin remainsultimately positive and can relate well too others. She is motivated to sustain functional capacity and improve this into thefuture. Caitlin recognizes that her ability to communicate significant life events and emotional states attached to these is anissue and limitation to maintaining nutritional balance at times.Occupational Focus:Develop positive self-identity through continued engagement in meaningful roles (work, yoga).Further develop eating habits to assist in supplementing weight to reduce likelihood of admission.Forming new valued social relationships.Reviewing new hobbies and interests - mindfulness based activities, reading.Spending quality time with family

Brendan is a 47 year old man who presents with schizoaffective disorder complicated by long standing substance abuse. It is notable the Brendan's contact with police and mental health services started at the same time in his early thirties. Prior to this it appears that Brendan was able to lead a functional lifestyle, although substance use commenced at the age of 28 with MDMA when he was living in the United Kingdom. Brendan has had periods of stability, for example between 2005 and 2010 when he had no admissions or formal contact with police. In 2010 Brendan's alcohol use increased, he was non-compliant with oral medication and begun using amphetamines and his behaviour began to deteriorate, escalating when he began heavily using methamphetamine in 2015. These behaviours included inappropriate sexual behaviours and, more recently, stalking behaviours towards females in addition to threats and suicidality. Brendan's history is indicative of poor coping mechanisms in that he uses avoidance and substance use to manage stress and distress, and has considered suicide in the past. Brendan's presentation is complex with possible personality vulnerabilities underpinning some of his behaviours.

Presenting - Brodie is a 23 year old freelance artist and bartender who lives in share accommodation with 3 others. He has a bachelor of Fine Arts degree and is currently single. He is the oldest of two children, he has a younger sister. Parents are married. He was referred to RBWH DBT program by Headspace after presenting with suicidal ideation and self harming behaviour (cutting) in the context of interpersonal relationship challenges. He has a hx of presenting with mood fluctuations, initially though tot be consistent with an emerging bi-polar illness but changed to BPD with narcissistic personality features. Brodie can present with nihilistic beliefs and ideas such as that he should not live and should kill himself. Such episodes of low mood generally occur as a reactive response to a triggering experience in his interpersonal life or in response tochallenging emotions. Brodie also engages in regular alcohol use and there is a strong hx of alcoholism in Brodies family.Predisposing - Brodie reports parental neglect in childhood with both parents working a lot and Brodie spending a lot of time on his own watching Disney movie's. He reported a very lonely childhood and has hinted at abuse in early childhood but details are unknown. Strong negative experience of primary school, including bullying and poor interactions with females with significant bullying from girls in his grade 4 class. Reports loss of self esteem as a result. Also reports strong negative experience with grade 3/4 female teacher "she made my life horrible." Brodie has always wanted a partner and since grade 2recalls only wanting to "have a wife, sleep next to her and share everything." Strong family hx of mental illness on Father's side with some member's suffering from schizophrenia and an uncle with BPAD who completed suicide. Family hx of alcohol abuse in father and grandfather.Precipitating - Brodie reported that he was in love with a woman (who subsequently rejected him due to being a lesbian) who suffered from trauma and psychosis and reported the exact date of 22/06/15 when he fell in love with her. From his description, on that date they were working together and made a deep emotional connection with each other (or perhaps that was what Brodie perceived). This woman had a female partner at the time and had not been in a sexual relationship with Brodie, they continued to meet as friends and Brodie held a belief that he was the closet person in her life. He acknowledged that “I remind her constantly that I want more from her.” He also reported “I really believe I am the only person who could be with her....I need to be needed and welcomed.” Brodie reported wanting a relationship full of passion and highs and lows, not just two people quietly loving one another. He had never been in a long term sexual relationship, although reported to have casual sex in the past. Brodie also uses alcohol to cope with difficult emotions and manage distress. Binge drinking results in increased emotional vulnerability to periods of low mood and associated suicidal ideation and urges to self-harm. Other emotionally vulnerabilities include history of restricting food intake to maintain ideal weight and poor sleep associated with alcohol misuse.Perpetuating - Brodie currently identifies as transgender and is actively engaged in taking HRT however, he remains highly ambivalent about making a transition. Brodie acknowledges that he has developed a poor sense of himself due to BPDand often feels confused about who he is and what he wants. It is worth noting that Brodie has had significant issues with women and appears to hold some suppressed anger (as per Headspace psychiatrist's formulation) towards the women in his early life that chastised, bullied or rejected him. Brodie has also struggled to form intimate relationships with women. Identify disruption along with alcohol abuse and interpersonal challenges continue to be the main perpetuating factors to Brodie's emotional vulnerability and subsequence parasuicidal behaviours.Protective - Brodie is currently participating in DBT program and has not self harmed for over 6 months. He has enjoys developing mastery in several areas of his life and this drive provides some protection from suicide and associatedparasuicidal behaviour. Brodie also cites his family as a protective factors and states he would never take his life as he would be abandoning them. Despite ongoing identity confusion, Brodie does strongly identify as the "wounded helper" and "protector" of his family and friends and this role does give him some meaning. In addition, Brodie is proud to be a freelance artist and has been commissioned to provide several murals around Brisbane City which allows for a feeling of success and mastery in this area of his life.IMP:Brodie is a 23 year old man with a diagnosis of BPD and chronic dysthymia associated with relative parental neglect in childhood. He is at increased risk of Bipolar due to strong family history but this has been ruled out as an appropriate diagnosis currently. There appear to be features of both borderline and narcissistic traits. Apart of engaging in parasuicidal behaviours Brodie's sense of self and identity were particularly impacted during his development and this continues to be a source of distress for him to this day. Although not a violent person there are multiple past prejudicial experiences associated with females and his past history of idealised love which may place him at risk of developing erotomanic delusions. Gender dysphoria and poor sense of self remain ongoing vulnerabilities and possible impediments to recovery.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Janice is a 68 year old female who is currently residing at Merriwee Court Residential Aged Care Facility. During her early years, Janice started hoarding food and has always had poor hygiene, not wishing to engage in self-care tasks. Janice completed grade 10 at school and worked as a nurse. She trained at Royal Brisbane Hospital and worked at Prince Charles Hospital. Following her first episode of severe mental illness Janice became de-registered and has not since re-engaged in nursing. She officially stopped working at age 60.Janice lived with her mother her whole life until her mother became unwell and was placed in residential aged care. Her mother passed away approximately four years ago. Janice did not visit her mother following RACF placement and did not attend the funeral. Janice's father passed away many years ago. Naomi is a 26 year old female who lives in shared accommodation. She is employed as a sex worker for an organization called Montecitos. She has been in an on/off relationship with her partner (Thomas) for multiple years. She has no children.Presenting:She was brought into RBWH by QAS on an EEA after being found trespassing on a neighbour's property. She reported she heard screaming and thought that a child was being assaulted. She could smell burning flesh and heard loud noises. She also reported that she had recently stopped smoking cannabis and was having trouble sleeping. She described losing 3 weeks in time and her friends were concerned for her. On examination she was noted to be dishevelled with agitation and elevated mood. She was thought disordered with psychotic symptoms of delusions and hallucinations. She was commenced on risperidone 3mg and placed on a TA.Post Discharge, Naomi frequently complained of perceived side effects (i.e., fatigue; difficulty concentration) of the Respiridone, and despite a reduction and psycho education she became increasingly distressed and non-compliant. She was seen in clinic (25/10/2017) and found to have severe depression with intermittent thoughts of suicide (nil plan or intent) in the context of medication non-compliance (preoccupied with perceived AEs). Admitted to H floor where she was commenced on Citalopram (to manage depressive symptoms) and Paliperidone depot (due to non-compliance with Risperidone) with good result.Predisposing: Naomi experienced a prejudical childhood with no evident protective adult figures. She was a victim of childhood sexual abuse by her biological father, and described her mother as highly critical (i.e., "conservative Christian", "very black and white") and emotionally and physically unavailable (Naomi recalls having to raise her little sister due to her mother being bed ridden with chronic fatigue). Naomi reported an inconsistent education, moving between schools frequently due to travelling around Australia with her mother and sister (reason for this is unclear). As a young adult, she was required to return to living with her father for a period and soon after first began using substances. She reported a history of "heavy" daily cannabis use from this time. Shortly after this period she was introduced to sex work in the context of an abusive relationship, where she was vulnerable to further abuse and exploitation. Overall, Naomi has experienced persistent adversity throughout her childhood development which may have increased her reactivity during times of stress in adulthood, particularly when there is inconsistent nurturing or modelling of pro-social stress-management, problem solving and emotion regulation skills. Such adversity increases her susceptibility to severe and long-term consequences such as disruptions to development of her identity, disruption to her ability to control emotions and form trusting relationships, being vulnerable to abuse or exploitation, substance abuse, and subsequently mental illness.Precipitating: Frequent substance use (including cannabis, methamphetamines and cocaine).Perpetuating: A lack of self-identity and self-worth, underdeveloped adaptive coping strategies and exposure to peer and occupational groups that endorse this behaviour are factors in continued drug use, which increases her vulnerability to psychotic experiences. Naomi reports an unstable relationship with her "on and off" again partner Tom (who she has describes as "emotionally abusive") which may contribute to her fluctuations in mood. Protective: Naomi is future focussed (plans to commence nursing TAFE next semester) and is engaging well in case management.

Management of symptoms was largely maintained through routine and distraction in educational and social activities.- During adolescence Ellen’s school burnt down and she experienced a period of time being home-schooled. Ellen recalls having a lot of unstructured time available and began researching various diseases with interest triggered after routine immunisations. 25yo F female presenting with manic episode in the context of hallucinogen use. This is on the background of no previous similar presentations (according to Suellen herself and collateral information) and a possible family history of BPAD. On presentation, Suellen presented as acutely manic and psychotic - overfamiliar, tangential, elevated and grandiose, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, risky behaviours, hallucinations, nihilistic delusions. It is difficult to determine whether her mania/psychosis was purely secondary to drug use or represents the first presentation of a primary mental illness. Suellen reported she has used hallucinogens on a regular basis (weekly) for the last year. Given that she has never previously behaved this way in the context of drug use (for this amount of time), the latter was considered more likely. However, it was noted that Suellen's mental state did improve rapidly with treatment and this may support the hypothesis of a drug precipitated episode. Regardless of the underlying pathology, Suellen was extremely unwell when she first came into hospital and was at risk of self harm (both intentional and misadventure), damaging her relationships, her reputation and finances. Given the risks involved, Suellen requires a longitudinal period of observation and assessment in the community to ensure relapse prevention.

Agnes is a 15-year-old female who was transferred to the Adolescent Mental Health Unit, RBWH, from LCCH on the 17/05/18 on a Treatment Authority for continued re-feeding secondary to Anorexia Nervosa. Agnes has an approximate one year history of anorexia which appears to have been precipitated by the transition into adolescence, the perception that she was 'bigger' than her peers and the desire to be the same weight as them (who are shorter than her), as well as receiving negative comments from her mother made about her food choices. Such factors appear to have resulted in subsequent dieting behaviour and restriction of ‘unhealthy’ foods alongside dissatisfaction with her body. Subsequently, these patterns of behaviour were associated with significant weight loss, dropping from approximately 72kg to 57kg, she experienced increased obsessionality associated with food, body shape and weight, alongside further body dissatisfaction (disliked her thin frame but was unable to consume more in order to gain weight), reduced energy, and poor motivation. Agnes was also suffering a range of medical symptomatology including dizziness and disorientation on standing, chest pain and problems with shortness of breath. She denied purging, laxative use, or significant bingeing but compulsive exercise was thought to be a symptom in her presentation. With respect to predisposing factors, Agnes has a genetic vulnerability to developing an eating disorder as evidenced by her mother also having suffered from one when she was younger. She also displays psychological character traits including obsessionality and perfectionism that have also likely made her vulnerable to developing an eating disorder. Furthermore, significant family factors including a history of marital discord, inconsistencies within the parental relationship, and conflict with regards to her treatment plan have likely served as both predisposing and perpetuating factors. Protectively, Agnes is an intelligent and likeable young lady who appears genuinely motivated to recover and reports improvement in her anorexic cognitions. In addition, despite the parental and family system difficulties, it is clear both parents love their daughter and want her to recover and there was evidence of increased parental capacity to re-feed and understand her illness.

Corey is a 29 year old, single male of mixed race (Aboriginal/Vietnamese), who lives alone in Community housing unit (DOH) in Clayfield but has a supportive family. Corey has previously maintained part time employment, but is currently in receipt of the Disability Support Pension and is currently focused on his recovery rather than recommencing paid employment. Corey has a long history of Paranoid Schizophrenia and Generalised anxiety disorder on a background of childhood trauma. He has a history of polysubstance abuse (cannabis and alcohol) which usually occurs in the context of peer pressure/social interaction. He has successfully abstained from smoking marijuana since his last hospitalization at the end of August 2017. Corey is currently managed on a Community Treatment Authority which is currently considered the least restrictive means of treatment, but there have been periods where he has been successfully managed as a voluntary patient in the community. Corey is currently managed on a monthly Paliperidone injection, oral aripiprazole tablets and sertraline. Since his discharge from hospital Corey has been focussed on a goal of transitioning off his paliperidone injection to an aripiprazole depot. He reports that this medication had been really helpful for him in the past when he was on Clozapine and he believed that this medication alone would be the best treatment for his illness. His treating team have been working towards this goal since his discharge from hospital. Corey's mother Tracey is his identified Carer and Allied person, and usually will attend all of Corey's mental health appointments. There is a family history of Schizophrenia, with Corey's Uncles (maternal side) both having this diagnosis. Background: June 2007 - First presentation at Fraser Coast Mental Health Service with hallucinations, delusions. HDU care needed because he was aggressive towards staff. This episode was apparently precipitated by marijuana. Mother has two brothers with a functional psychiatric illness. He was subsequently started on Clozapine .He found a job in QUT under an employment program . He was functioning well with Clozapine. Towards the end of 2008 his ITO was revoked. Jan-Feb 2009 Corey decided to stop Clozapine himself. He was on monthly follow up at the Valley clinic then. In spite of repeatedly urging him he refused to take Clozapine again. To his credit he continued toremain off illicit drugs and attend his appointments with the doctors at Valley on a bimonthly basis. Nov 17th 2009 Corey was brought in to PEC by Leah Cassidy, Indigenous Employment Officer for QUT. Corey had been reported as experiencing auditory hallucinations for the last week. Corey was verbose &thought disordered. Conversation was rambling and in-sightless. He expressed delusional believes of being part of the SES, witness in a criminal proceeding etc. He was put on an Involuntary Treatment Order. Heremained in the locked ward (high dependency unit) for almost 3 weeks due to violent behaviour, which required occasional seclusion.June 2016 Admitted voluntarily to G Floor RBWH with a deterioration in his mental state. Corey was subsequently placed on an ITO during admission, due to not having capacity, when he was unwell. This wasrevoked on discharge. Initially on admission, Corey presented as grossly disorganised, with severe FTD and thought blocking at times.It is likely his relapse was due to planning to cease smoking, with subsequentdose reduction of Clozapine, however Corey continued to smoke the same amount. Upon increase of the Clozapine dose, Corey's mental state improved to baseline. He was no longer perplexed, with good thoughtstream. He had mild tangential FTD. His affect remains blunted. Corey shows good insight and decision making regarding his illness and ongoing treatment. At discharge, he was globally low risk. Since discharge Corey was engaging well with his treating team and remained a voluntary patient. His mental state remained well with Clozapine dose and he was doing very well in all aspects of his lifeJuly - August 2017Corey was referred to the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital by his case manager after disclosing ceasing his Clozapine almost three weeks earlier. He reported a number of side effects to Clozapine thatwere no longer tolerable. He had discussed this with his treating team who had planned to reduce the dose slowly. He had continued with oral Aripiprazole and Sertraline. He presented voluntary and participated in review with the Psychiatric Registrar. On review he was noted to be tangential at times, and voiced some delusional content; he was disorganised, with perceptual disturbance. Despite this he was found to have good insight and was admitted as a voluntary patient. On review the next day on the ward Corey was found to have worsening of thought disorder with significant thought blocking and thought latency and tangential content. He was unsure about starting Clozapine due to the side effects and was wanting leave. Due to historical risks when unwell and current mental state with non compliance with medications Corey did not have capacity to consent to treatment and was placed on a Treatment Authority. This was confirmed on consultant review the following day.During this admission Corey was transitioned back to a long acting antipsychotic injection (Paliperidone) at his request. Corey disclosed that his decision to discontinue his clozapine occurred in the context of an episode of bed wetting Corey had while he was staying overnight at his Cousin's house and for which he found embarrassing. Corey also identified concerns about the ongoing sedation associated with this medication and it's negative impact on his quality of life. He was aware that his functioning would likely deteriorate as a result of discontinuation of Clozapine, but indicated that this was his preferred means of treatment at this time. Family were supportive of his decision. August 2017 - currentRBWH - Southern CCTSince discharge from hospital, Corey has been well engaged in treatment. His mental state continued to improve in the months following his discharge from the inpatient wards. Shortly after meeting his new Community Treating Psychiatrist Corey identified that his goal was to transition from the Paliperidone injection to his preferred injection aripiprazole. Corey was agreeable to a slow transition (over a period of 12 months) to the medication as Treating Psychiatrist wanted to minimise the likelihood of Corey becoming unwell. Corey believed that the aripiprazole injection was going to be the best medication for him as he identified that when he was on it with Clozapine in the past it had given him more energy and he didn't put on as much weight as he had since recommencing the Paliperidone injection. Corey sees a private psychologist (under MHCP) in the community to discuss past trauma issues perpetrated towards him when he was a child.

The same pattern of non-compliance with treatment occurred and in October he was admitted to Acute Ward at Gold Coast Hospital. BackgroundD'Jamel Boumzar is a 56 year old divorced male who currently lives alone in a studio apartment at a Brisbane Housing Company property in Fortitude Valley. D'Jamel is originally from Algeria, having had lived in several countries before settling in Australia after meeting his Australian ex-wife.He has 3 children with his ex-wife: 14 year old son lives with ex-wife, 20 year old son who lives independently and a daughter in her early 20s who lives in Sydney with her partner and 3 young children.D'Jamel has some contact with ex-wife and keeps ongoing close contact with oldest daughter who is his primary contact. He is under the Public Trust and Adult Guardian.D'Jamel's daily activities are limited to mostly sleeping or walking around the Fortitude Valley and Brisbane City suburbs. D'Jamel speaks multiple languages and reportedly thinks in French before translating and communicating in English.D'Jamel presents with a diagnosis of Schizophrenia, unspecified (treatment resistant) and is currently treated as a voluntary client. He is an open client of the Southern Team, Inner North Brisbane Mental Health Service (INBMHS) since June 2014.D'Jamel has multiple medical issues and is currently treated with medication (webster pack): Hepatitis C, Diabetes Mellitis Type 2, Liver Cirrhosis, Ischaemic Heart Disease. In February 2018 D'jamel experienced a R) parietal/occipital CVA and is reported to have resulted in hemianopia and significantly reduced vision in his left eye. Following discharge from GARU, D'jamel received treatment from Community-based Rehabilitation Team to support him in his recovery.Psychiatric HistoryD'Jamel was first referred to mental health service, HHOT in July 2013 by Relationships Australia, as he reported suicidal ideation during a counselling session addressing his gambling. He attempted suicide by jumping from William Jolly Bridge on 31.08.13 in response to auditory hallucinations post eviction from OzCare, sustaining a T12 fracture. He had also previously attempted suicide by ingesting rat poison in 2009 in the context of marriage breakdown stress. D'Jamel had numerous PEC crisis presentations presenting with suicidal ideation and deterioration in mental state regarding precipitating factors: conflict with ex-wife regarding access to see his children, narcotic abuse, and gambling.D'Jamel has had a number of admissions for his physical and mental health relapses. He was diagnosed with Paranoid Schizophrenia in 2014 and has a history of opioid dependence, depression, PTSD, and personality vulnerabilities: cluster B traits. D'Jamel had previously been prescribedopiate replacement therapy and was a long-term recipient of methadone for 16 years via Biala.D'Jamel was previously managed by HHOT due to periods of homelessness in 2013 before transferring to Southern CCT in June 2014 for ongoing case management.D'Jamel experiences ongoing chronic auditory hallucinations which are derogatory in nature. He is able to identify and utilise several strategies to manage his symptoms, including increasing the TV volume, listening to radio, putting on ear plugs, and pacing. He is also able to identify the role medication plays in managing his symptoms. When unwell, D'Jamel's auditory hallucinations increase in frequency and duration, becoming command in nature ("jump off the bridge", "you are a coward", "you don't deserve to live"). Early warning signs also include sleep disruption, irregular sleep cycles, and disorientation to time, date and appointment schedules. As D'Jamel has acted on such hallucinations in the past, he is aware to present to PEC should symptoms worsen and strategies fail to relieve symptoms. D'Jamel had a prolonged admission to RBWH Mental Health Centre from 2.11.16 - 13.01.17 due to worsening of auditory hallucinations that become command in nature.Poor sleep cycles has been a significant precipitating factor to D'Jamel's mental state deteriorating quite rapidly. D'Jamel also has akathesia as a side-effect from depot.D'Jamel identifies his children as a protective factor whenever he experiences suicidal ideation. D'Jamel is insightful of his positive and negative symptoms impacting on his social functioning and intermittently preventing him from participating in community activities.D'Jamel started Aripiprazole depot 400mg 4/52 in October 2016 at Valley MH clinic. He continues to be adherent with treatment, however often requires phone call reminders to attend appointments. A trial of clozapine in 2016 resulted in the development of dysphagia. Clozapine was subsequently weaned and ceased.

Brittany was a 17 year old female from Bundaberg who was referred following an intentional impulsive overdose of approximately 30 of her mother's Amitryptyline tablets on the 14/07/18. Brittany reported that the overdose was immediately precipitated by conflict with her mother and on the background of an approximate four year history of suicidal thinking, self-harm, and mood related problems that first emerged in the context of her parents separation. Brittany described a range of culminating psychosocial stressors and a worsening of her mood state prior to her overdose including stress associated with school performance, chronic relationship difficulties with her mother and perceived emotional abuse, disruption in her peer group with the loss of her closest friend earlier in the year, and grief and loss related to the death of her grandmother in 2017. Brittany also disclosed having been the victim of a rape in April 2018 (on the background of a sexual assault at age 7) and that since this time has felt increasingly anxious as well as using increased substance use in an attempt to numb her emotional state and block her memories. As a result of such factors, Brittany has been experiencing problems related to poor sleep, tiredness, reduced motivation, and increased emotionality. Maintaining factors relate to Brittany's use of avoidance behaviours (including substance use) to try and cope with her difficulties, a lack of social support, disrupted sleep patterns and tiredness exacerbating poor coping, and continued exposure to psychosocial stressors without access to respite away from same. Protectively, Brittany is a prosocial and intelligent young women who has demonstrated significant resilience. She displays increased openness to engage with supports as well as shows improving insight into her use of maladaptive coping mechanisms. Despite the conflict, her mother is supportive of her daughter and is now more informed and aware of the stressors for Brittany.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Presenting - Carina is a 24 year old single female on DSP living in department of housing accommodation with a current primary diagnosis of Intellectual Impairment (IQ) 60, borderline PD, with differential diagnosis of psychosis (NOS). She was referred to Southern Team - CCT for case management following in excess of 70 hospital presentations in 2016-17 and becoming the highest user of Ferny Grove QPS in the same year. Carina's history of engagement with mental health services is characterised by frequent crisis presentations to hospital with somatic complaints and suicidal ideation/attempts (by non-lethal means) and DSH in the form of superficial self-harm. There is also documentation of her complaining of intermittent internal and external auditory hallucinations (derogatory voices, including of Satan; and historically the voice of her pastor's daughter), and these can improve with distraction.Predisposing - Carina is the second eldest of 4 daughters. She reportedly left home at age 17 or 18 for reasons which are not clear. Carina has maintained intermittent contact with her mother and currently has phone contact every couple of weeks. Clinical documentation indicates that Carina has reported physical abuse by her step-father in the past. As well, Carina has reported experiencing sexual violence. Carina resided primarily in crisis accommodation when she moved out of home and has made multiple links with community non-government agencies. Accommodation arrangements appeared to end abruptly, prompted either by eviction or of Carina's choice to leave, often in short notice. Carina has used drugs and alcohol opportunistically and is a smoker.Precipitating - Carina's re-entry into mental health system was precipitated by a breakdown in housing situation and care arrangements resulting in increased need for care co-ordination. Carina has significant difficulty regulating her emotions, poor interpersonal skills and limited capacity to tolerate distress. Thus her presentations are often precipitated by interpersonal conflicts with neighbours or family resulting in poor emotion regulation and distress. This is further complicated by low IQ and chronic health/somatic issues. Carina requires significant supports to maintain her independence in the community which was not being achieved prior to referral to CCT. Carina requires lots of support to solve problems, manage interpersonal difficulties and maintain structure/routine.Perpetuating - Low IQ, interpersonal conflicts/poor social skills, lack of available suitable accommodation facilities/support, boredom and somatic complaints. Although Carina was assessed by DSQ as requiring 24 hour supported accommodation there is no such accommodation available, thus Carina will continue to experience periods of instability due to inadequate supports. Other factors that continue to perpetuate presentations to hospital are boredom and ongoing somatic issues relating to poor lifestyles choices particularly diet resulting in chronic constipation (abdo pain) and issues associated with cerebral palsy including pain and falls.Protective - Carina is very likeable and when willing to engage can actually do very well living independently in the community with support, she has a 25 hours per week package of support from Footprints and has recently started engaging in multiple groups/activities which has significantly reduced her contact with MHS. She has grown to be more resilient over the years and is a strong advocate for herself. Historically Carina has demonstrated improved ability to utilise her identified strategies and her presentations to emergency services have significantly decreased over time.Formulation - Carina has established diagnoses of borderline PD & intellectual disability with significant past history of multiple traumas that include physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She has often presented with psychotic symptoms and currently experiences hallucinations in a number of modalities leading to an additional diagnosis of psychosis NOS. She has limited coping strategies but has learnt to be more resilient over the years; she continues to have a low tolerance to distress resulting in acute presentations in a dysregulated state as well as psychotic symptoms, that I would formulate as a psychological defence mechanism, namely exteriorisation of a critical component of the psyche, in response to feelings of vulnerability. She belongs to a group characterised by chronic elevated risk (acute risk moderate) to self in view of the mental disorder diagnosis, personality disorder, ID, hx of traumas, ongoing interpersonal conflict with a neighbour, limited insight, limited adaptive coping mechanisms; ongoing risks being contained by current drug treatment (partial at best), regular MHC monitoring and psychosocial interventions (by NGO, support from neighbours, police input, GP support

Sally is a 63 year old single lady living in BRIC Housing. She is on the DSP and has Public Trust manage her finances. Has been in the mental health system since a teenager, with previous diagnoses of eating disorder and schizoaffective disorder. Sally has a diagnosis of Borderline personality disorder. Sally is well known to MHS with multiple prior presentations of deliberate self harm (DSH). Extensive CIMHA hx. Has a presentation management plan. Frequent calls to QAS at night due to self harm ideation, or post self harm via cutting forearms with broken crockery, glass bottles or scissors. In recent times Sally has also taken to attempting to set herself or her unit on fire, although attempts to date have been minor.As per her diagnosis, Sally has difficulty in regulating her emotions and frequently becomes emotionally dis-regulated, which escalates to DSH. Precipitants to DSH usually involve issues of abandonment or rejection and/or interpersonal relationship difficulties. Sally for example fears that care givers or family are or will withdraw support and that she will end up alone. Evenings are a particularly fraught time for Sally due to chronically poor sleep and nightmares that cause significant distress. Sally states that she becomes increasingly anxious at night feeling that she "has no-one" and she reports a continual feeling of emptiness. The majority of Sally's presentations to DEM occur at night. Sally has been given extensive support around sleep hygiene and at times provided with medication support to assist sleep with varying results.Sally has a substantial package of care from Footprints that involves daily contact and assistance with social support, transport, cleaning and attending to self cares where required. Sally is also linked with Catholic Pastoral care where she attends weekly. Clancy McDonald (ED nurse - Frequent Presenters project) is also involved to help track and support frequent presentations. Stakeholder meetings are held regularly to discuss ongoing care needs. Sally presents less to PEC when she is well linked in with external services, however presents multiple times in periods of stress due to feeling any rejection by family, acquaintances and caregivers. Sally has shown that she finds change with CM difficult and that often her self harming and distress/chaos will increase for a short period of time however will settle with time and consistency.Sally has multiple medical issues including poor mobility and chronic pain associated with her hip. Sally is currently linked with OPD Orthopedics and hopes to have a hip replacement sometime into the future (pre-surgery appointment scheduled for 10/08/18). Sally is, for the most part, is able to self care with occasionally need from support, particularly if there has been episodes of deliberate self harm and Sally is requiring dressing and bandaging support. Sally is reviewed by her MHC every week and is offered DBT informed therapy at these weekly sessions. Sally has a history of cancelling these sessions however. MHC is available 8-4:30pm for phone support to manage crisis and offer support to manage distress. Sally can then access after hours support via MHCall. Sally is also reviewed by her treating psychiatrist every 4/52, again attendance at these appointments can be poor at times also.

Occupational Influence – Occupational Identity:Jamie was raised in a family unit that lived separately where his parents referred to themselves as “best friends”. Jamie lived with his mum full time and his father would visit regularly. Jamie is the youngest and is one of five children. He has four siblings Toby who he shares both biological parents with, Cass and Temika who are his half sisters, and shares the same mother and Matthew a half-brother who he shares the same father with. Jamie has contact with all his siblings apart from Matthew who he reports having no contact with from about the age of 8 years old. He was a premature baby but reports he wasn’t aware of any other complications at birth or experienced delayed developmental milestones.Jamie recalls forming a secure attachment with his mother was difficult as she did not display love and affection and offered little validation and minimal physical contact. He describes his mother as kind and caring. Jamie describes his father as quite negative, he was physically and verbally abusive to his brother Toby, and he witnessed theseassaults, but reports he is his fathers “favourite” child.School for Jamie in the primary years was “good”, he was an intelligent child and achieved academically. In high school Jamie recalls this being a difficult time with some bullying, minimal friends and he “struggled to find a place” in the system. He reported feeling that something was different from commencement in high school and by the age of 13 was consciously aware that he was gay. This discovery for many years was wrapped in feelings of guilt and shame about who he was and to acknowledge this publicly took 11 years. He experienced his first gay relationship in secret with a friend from school at the age of 16. This relationship continued in secret for over a year and ended after his friend accidentally drowned after graduation from high school. Jamie recalls it was exceedingly hard to grieve appropriately for the loss of his friend and partner as their family’s and wider community were not aware of their gay relationship “how can you grieve your love for someone when no one knows the truth”. After leaving school at the age of 17 Jamie worked for MacDonald’s and moved to a manager role fairly rapidly; during this job he met the mother of his children (Ashely) who he recalls as being a “cool chick”, she fell pregnant after a one sexual encounter and gave birth to their eldest Daughter Ella after a 6-month pregnancy. Ella required ongoing hospital care post birth and Jamie reported he felt he had an obligation to “stick around” but did not feel “trapped”. This relationship lasted for 5 years and had an “on, off” aspect, within the middle of the 5 years theyconceived another child “I wanted Ella to have a sibling”.His parent’s relationship changed in 2013 when Jamie was 19, he reports his mother met a new man and when she advised his biological father he became hostile towards her. Comments about his mother were made openly and these were degrading towards her, his father made it very clear that he felt rejected by her as Jamie’s mother for years had insisted on telling the family unit that she didn’t want to have a husband / partner. This change in his parent’s relationship also occurred around the birth of his first child Ella and family contact with both parents was hostile and anxiety provoking during this period. During the relationship with Ashley, Jamie was aware he was gay but continued to struggle on with the partnership. He recalls that during this time Ashley became very controlling alienating him from his family and female friends and only consenting to Jamie “doing” things with her. In 2017 Jamie made the decision while intoxicated with alcohol to disclose to his family and close friends that he was gay, he felt this decision was also driven by thoughts around ending his life if he couldn’t identify with this part of himself “I was sick of living in a world of regret…. What had I got to lose”. His family were accepting of this disclosure, but this further ruptured an already tenuous relationship with Ashley.Occupational Presentation – Occupational Competence:Jamie struggles to form stable relationships often seeking validation of a partner’s feelings to manage chronic anxiety around his emotional needs. He has a well formed stable routine that centres around the primary role of work and regular contact with his daughters, but it lacks other occupational experiences. Ongoing mediation with Ashley around contact with his children continues to cause distress and increase emotional dysregulation. Jamie moved to Brisbane in March 2017 and within the first few days broke up with his partner Chris, it was at this point Jamie reports being sexually active with multiple short-term partners labelling this as a “rampage”. After this 9-month experience Jamie met Josh and identifies he committed himself to this relationship but ultimately attempted to change aspects of his self-identity to align with Josh’s wishes. This environmental influence further impacted on Jamie’s sense of self and elicited an increase in seeking validation from Josh to manage his emotional needs. Proceeding the break-up from Josh, Jamie’s routine and capacity to articulate his needs diminished and he experienced a short admission to mental health. Jamie also articulates that alcohol has played a big role in his routine and is a strategy he uses for avoiding ongoing anxiety. Jamie continues to use social media platforms to gain validation from others during times of distress.Occupational Focus - Occupational Adpation: Develop a positive self-identity through continued engagement in meaningful roles (work, father). Forming new valued social relationships that are not built on seeking validation. Reviewing new hobbies and interests. Develop skills to assist with emotional regulation and decrease parasuicidal behaviour through exploring practical strategies founded in the modality of sensory approaches. Develop a routine that reduces access to electronics that interfere with developing a robust sense of self.

Presenting SymptomsAlanah presents with:1. flashbacks and nightmares,2. sleep disturbance,3. weight loss,4. poor relationships with each parent,5. depression and anxiety,6. deliberate self-harm and low self-esteem, and7. frequent suicidal ideation with numerous significant suicide attempts, most recently involving ingestion of approximately 100 paracetamol tablets, attempting to jump off the Storey Bridge and attempting to hang herself. These are triggered by perceived rejection and interpersonal conflict.Predisposing FactorsAlanah’s symptoms present in the context of neurodevelopmental vulnerability, perfectionistic and internalising temperament, and adverse early life experiences. There is a biological predisposition to mental illness including Ms Clear’s anxiety, depression, and personality vulnerabilities, and Mr Pitman’s alleged alcohol misuse. There is further genetic loading from the maternal family with history of bipolar disorder, anxiety, depression, and emotional avoidance. Suggestion of intergenerational attachment difficulties are also present in the maternal family with two of Alanah’s maternal aunts being sexually abused by their own maternal grandfather, and an intergenerational history of cut-off relationships within the maternal family. There are allegations that Mr Pitman was verbally, emotionally, and occasionally physically violent towards Ms Clear throughout their marriage however collateral information suggests that the parental relationship was most likely characterised by high expressed emotion and distance, both emotional and physical with Mr Pitman frequently working long hours or out of town. As her parents became less able to communicate effectively with each other, it appears that Alanah was actively placed in the role of go-between. Consequently, in order to serve her parent’s emotional needs, Alanah may have begun to sacrifice her own individuation and growth, and instead, unfairly taken on some of her parent’s stress and played the “peacemaker” role. It is thought that the difficulties experienced within the parental relationship during Alanah’s early years has contributed to Alanah’s hypersensitivity to others, her tendency to disconnect from emotions, feelings of low self-worth, and a tendency to self-blame. Being raised in a family in which the adults may have been emotionally unavailable due to their own individual vulnerabilities is likely to have left Alanah feeling frightened, and mistrusting of adults ability to meet her needs, with a negative view of herself and the world including the belief that she is not important and has little or no control over her life, resulting in low self-esteem and feelings of anxiety and depression.Precipitating FactorsThe current presenting issues arise in the context of Alanah entering adolescence, parental separation, and two separate alleged sexual assaults. Alanah’s core beliefs that others are untrustworthy or that the world is unsafe are likely to have been reinforced by these events which all occurred within a 12-month period. Alanah's presentation are usually triggered by perceived rejection and interpersonal conflicts with her parents or partner at the time.Perpetuating FactorsContextual factors maintaining Alanah’s difficulties include her mother’s criticism, intrusiveness, low parental self-efficacy, as well as the poor social support for Alanah and her mother. Her parents’ own reduced capacity to regulate emotions is hypothesised to have modelled that emotions are scary and difficult to control. It is suggested that when Alanah feels strong emotions, she attempts to have others, particularly professionals, manage these by being admitted to hospital. Alanah's difficulties are also perpetuated by a reluctance to engage in skill based learning and preference to discuss her trauma. This preference leaves Alanah in a vulnerable position where she is unable to independently problem solve situational crises.Protective FactorsAlanah is currently engaged in the DBT Program which provides a structured an ongoing support base from which Alanah can draw from. This includes a weekly individual therapy appointment, a weekly DBT group and phone coaching available 24 hours a day. She is currently residing in her own unit within Clayfield which she returned to post discharge. Alanah has also commenced a Diploma of Early Childhood Education and Care and works as an educator under supervision during more of the week.

The overdose appeared to have been precipitated by a culmination of psychosocial stressors including school exams and pressure to do well, recent parental separation and disharmony, relational problems, as well as intensifying negative cognitions regarding her self-worth and a global worsening of her mental state and ability to cope. During her admission Tahlia exhibited worsening eating patterns and on discharge, she continued to restrict her oral intake and purge if provided with the opportunity. As a result, postural tachycardia began to emerge and she required a medical admission to LCCH. Prior to Tahlia's initial admission she had been seeing a sports psychologist previously and also a private psychiatrist, Dr. Evans, over the past few months. She was prescribed fluvoxamine and quetiapine at the time of her admission but reported limited benefit and her parents remained concerned that these medications had worsened her mental health. This was ceased during her admission.Tahlia described first experiencing performance anxiety at around age 13 years in the context of athleticism and sporting pursuits in which she was a state representative in triathlon. Since that time she has had a history of injury and disengagement from her sport. Tahlia reported experiencing a strong sense of pressure to perform at a high standard and perceived that those around her were highly critical of her performance. Increasing concerns related to body shape and weight and the development of eating disordered behaviour coincided with her injury and disengagement from competitive sport. Such difficulties also appear to have occurred in the the context of temperamental sensitivities and need for validation and love, in association with a series of losses in earlier life, longitudinal exposure to high pressure performance situations, perceived criticism regarding her ability, and suspected perceived invalidation of her emotions. Current maintaining factors appear to be in line with poor coping, difficulties in expressing and communicating emotional content, continued exposure to psychosocial stressors, a poor sense of self-worth with current focus on shape and weight to derive same, and continued disharmony and inconsistencies within the parental relationship.Tahlia currently lives with her mother, Kylie, and older brother, Xavier. Just prior to her first admission her father had left the home. Tahlia is enrolled in Genesis Christian College and is in Year 12. Reportedly, she has to work hard to achieve her current grades which is in comparison to her brother who is described as very intelligent. She has not been back to school since her first admission.

BackgroundMr. Brodie Nicol is a 56 year old single gentleman who currently lives alone in a privately owned unit in Auchenflower. Brodie is currently unemployed and receives the disability support pension. Brodie receives a HASP support package which is provided by Open Minds and MACS who provide daily assistance for medication management, domestic tasks, meal preparation and social activities such as PCYC gym, library visits and computer training. MACS visit each evening and supervise Brodie's medication which is kept in a locked box. Brodie has good family support and sees his family regularly. Brodie enjoys going to restaurants and cafes and the movies. He is well linked in with his GP. There is no known alcohol or illicit substance use.Psychiatric HistoryBrodie first came to the attention of psychiatric services in 1986 (age 28yrs) when his mother convinced him to see a psychiatrist. He had developed delusions concerning muscle pain in his thighs. This had been rigorously investigated by orthopaedic surgeons and neurologists with no organic aetiology ever found. The original diagnosis was mono symptomatic delusions / Schizophrenia. Brodie ceased seeing his psychiatrist in 1988 as he felt she had not understood his problems and was not helping him. Prior to this time, he had functioned very highly. He went to a private school and was described as being very intelligent, conscientious and obsessional. Brodie was a good athlete and was training in running to state representative standard. He obtained an honours degree in mathematics and was undertaking a doctorate, until he developed his muscle pain in 1986. Since then he has not continued his education and has not pursued any form of career. Around 1990, Brodie left Australia and travelled the world looking for relief for his somatic concerns. He sold his home (which was given to him by his parents) and severed all ties with family and friends.This enabled him to travel the world seeking a "cure" for his muscle pain. The countries visited included New Caledonia, Finland, Japan, Hong Kong, Italy, Egypt, South America and the United States. It was during his travels in Uruguay in 1992, that he shot and injured two lawyers as a result of untreated persecutory delusions, as described in the Forensic Assessment at the time. Brodie was transferred from a psychiatric facility in Uruguay back to Australia and underwent a protracted admission to the RBWH mental health unit (December 1992 – June 1993) where a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia was confirmed. Following discharge he was managed by the RBWH Community Mental Health Service. Brodie's level of disturbance remained relatively minimal until he required four admissions to the RBWH between 1997 and 1999. He absconded to Noumea in 2000 where he attempted to engage a lawyer. Whilst there, he made a serious suicide attempt inflicting deep lacerations to both wrists. In 2001 when Brodie's treatment history was discussed with a staff psychiatrist at RBWH, the situation was recalled as follows: Brodie had absconded overseas and was unable to be traced, he then made a premeditated attempt on his life was only found as another hotel guest noticed blood seeping out beneath his room door. He was transferred back to Australia three days later and placed under an Involuntary Treatment Order whilst an inpatient at the RBWH before being transferred to the Medium Secure Unit (MSU) of The Prince Charles Hospital. Brodie remained at MSU from January to November 2001 and then transferred to the Community Care Unit (Somerset Villas), RBWH where he has resided until 2013. During the intervening years, he has required two brief inpatient admissions to the RBWH (October 2004 and March 2006).To date, Brodie has had a poor treatment response to a number of antipsychotic medications including Quetiapine, Risperidone, Amisulpride, Olanzapine and Aripiprazole. Brodie was treated with Clozapine for many years, however, had a medical admission in 2015 with LRTI and further deterioration in cardiac function resulting in the need to cease Clozapine. Since Brodie's diagnosis, he has expressed repeatedly that he does not believe he has a mental illness and should not be on medication. As a result of his poor insight, there have been chronic issues around non-adherence with medication, and his illness is such that the risk of harm to himself and others is significant when he is unwell. Serious concerns remain that Brodie would become non-adherent with treatment if he were not under an ITO, leading to deterioration in his physical and mental wellbeing. However, he continues to hope to eventually come off his ITO and all psychotropic medications in the future. Brodie has periodically engaged a number of lawyers, to attempt to challenge his ITO and have it revoked. Brodie was referred to the Community Southern Team, Inner North Brisbane Mental Health Service in August 2013 for ongoing community mental health follow-up. The Southern Team's former Team Manager, K. Carney submitted a notification to the Gun Registration Board.Early Warning Signs:Pacing, becomes dishevelled, rubs his head excessively, mumbling to himself.

BackgroundMs. Natalie Day is a 34 year old single lady who currently resides in a Department of Housing unit in Ascot. Natalie was a previously high functioning lady who finished year 12 and commenced an arts course at university, later enrolling in Speech Therapy and working as a jazz singer. Her illness has been complicated in the past by polysubstance abuse including heroin and marijuana. Her other co-morbidities include Hepatitis C. Stable accommodation was an issue for Natalie in the past as she was noted to have had frequent difficulties tolerating flatmates (noted to be secondary to paranoia). Natalie also often has problems with clinicians as she finds it difficult to trust people. Natalie's treatment was transferred to the RBWH following her move to a transitional housing unit in the RBWH catchment area in 2009.Psychiatric HistoryNatalie was diagnosed with Schizophrenia in approximately 2004. She had 3 lengthy mental health admissions at the Princess Alexandra Hospital in 2008. Natalie has had multiple involuntary mental health admissions whilst under the care of RBWH and has trialled various medications including Risperdal Consta, Quetiapine, Olanzapine and Flupenthixol. Natalie was commenced on Clozapine in 2011. Natalie's ITO was revoked by the MHRT on 17.07.12. Natalie maintained compliance to treatment under supervision of her psychiatrist (Dr. Michael O'Sullivan) and mental health clinician (Julie O'Sullivan) up until December 2012, then informing her treating team she would no longer be takingclozapine. This lead to a deterioration in mental state over subsequent months. Natalie's care was transferred from Pine Rivers Hospital after a month long voluntary admission. She was not complying with the treatment plan (was self-adjusting her medication doses), was guarded and suspicious with nursing staff, withdrawn and was not participating in any of the patient programmes. It was decided then, given her complicated mental health history, failure to respond to least restrictive treatment and associated risks when psychotic, that she should be transferred to RBWH under involuntary assessment with re-introduction of Clozapine. Natalie was commenced on Clozapine immediately on admission with lithium support for neutrophils. Natalie was guarded, suspicious and did not interact with treating team. Positive symptoms were not elicited voluntarily, but indicators could be seen in her behaviour - e.g. calling Police to ward to report her clothing had been stolen by her parents. Eventually she demonstrated improvement, with increased interaction with treating team, a notable change in affect reactivity and most tellingly, she began making contact with her parents again (although somewhat guarded in doing so). Natalie was referred to MIRT on discharge under an ITO to continue with her care in the community. Natalie was initially difficult to engage in therapy and was followed up by MIRT from May 2013 until July 2014. Natalie's care was transferred from MIRT to the INBMHS Southern Team in July 2014.

However, after a period of approximately 2 years (and unbeknownst to prev. treating team), he disengaged from treatment (now reports this was due to his perception and GP reports that he was "doing well", and therefore he did not perceive need for medication). He then attempted to confiscate a phone from a female student and became aggressive to another female student in retaliation for what he perceived they were doing. At this time it became apparent that Lachlan had ceased his depot from his GP approximately 12 months prior. His father also reported he had become quite possessive of things in the kitchen, and experiencing ideas of reference from the newspaper a few months before the incident. Additional charges also became apparent later that year (re: separate incident), of unlawful stalking, following repeated unwanted contact and monitoring of ex-leader of Qld Liberal party/ well-known Queenslander Sir Liew Edwards, and wife Lady Jane Edwards (Lachlan now reports wanting to speak to him about political topics, ask his opinion about things etc). He has recently been attending University of 3rd Age courses, however, does not make social connections there. He walks twice per day and goes to the movies on his own. He visits his brother daily. formulationOverallClinicalImpression: The impression was of a deterioration in mental state precipitated by a urinary tract infection.This deterioration was characterised by both psychotic features (thought disorder, thought blocking, and ruminating on dead relatives) and affective symptoms (manic symptoms reported the week prior to admission, and depressive symptoms in the initial stage of the admission, including dysphoria, possible depressive cognitions and suicidal ideation).The diagnosis was of a mixed affective state and Nola responded to a combination of treatment of her UTI, as well as Lithium (which was withheld for a day during the admission due to an AKI which was withheld for 3 doses during the admission due to an AKI; level on discharge was 0.4 but should be re-checked by the GP).Obtaining a clear history from Nola was challenging as she appeared somewhat suggestible.A review of Nola's history suggested repeated presentations featuring diagnostic challenges due to the unqualified nature of her intellectual impairment, atypical psychotic symptoms which are at times difficult to differentiate from a delirium or intellectual impairment, and the complicating mood component to her illness.However, Nola did improve throughout the admission and on discharge her affect was bright and reactive, there was no evident thought blocking or thought disorder, she denied any perceptual disturbances, and there were no depressive cognitions or suicidality. Collateral reports indicate that in the 7 months he had been without his depot he had slowly stopped caring for himself and had becoming increasingly socially withdrawn and aggressive. Scott is a 49 year old single man, living at level 3 supported accommodation Herston Lodge since April 2014. He is currently on DSP, and manages his own finances. He has a long forensic history including stabbing his brother Grant in 2008 with a hunting knife and stalking. Scott reports a long-standing history of familial conflict, itinerant lifestyle and homelessness. Mental Illness dates back to 2004 with episodes of non-compliance and being lost to follow up in Victoria.A Forensic Order was made in 2014, after Scott accrued numerous charges due to events which ensued due to him leaving Victoria and fleeing to Queensland in a stolen vehicle. Charges include: Drive uninsured vehicle, Drive unregistered vehicle, Fail to stop, Going armed in public so as to cause fear, Obstruct police, Offences involving registration, Unlawful use of a motor vehicle x 2, Serious assault on police, Stealing, Unlawful possession of a weapon, Use registration plate of another vehicle, Fail to supply specimen of breath for analysis, Willful damage.In the years leading up to his index offences, Scott had a number of inpatient admissions, triggered usually by non-compliance with oral medication. His first known presentation to MHS in Victoria (2004) was in the context of disclosing bizarre ideation to Police when he was served with an intervention order (re: a young shop assistant he was alleged to have stalked after developing a morbid interest in her - no other details known). Police referred him for assessment at that time. He was admitted to hospital and commenced on treatment, oral Risperidone. He had a number of subsequent admissions, usually due to non-compliance with oral medication, and having become self-isolative and breaking off contact from family.In 2008, while living with his brother Grant, Scott experienced paranoid delusions that he was being "hunted" because he had "important military intelligence". He eventually stabbed his brother Grant due to psychotic ideas. On another occasion, it was reported that Scott then stole his brother's vehicle following a dispute over money. He was arrested after a siege during which he had armed himself with a hunting knife, axe and shovel. He served a total of six months in Melbourne Assessment Prison / Metropolitan Remand Centre, being released on a two year community corrections order. At that time, he went to live with his twin brother Mark in Ballarat.In 2009, Scott was admitted to the Ballarat Mental Health Unit, after becoming guarded and paranoid in the context of psychosocial stressors and non-compliance with medication. He was recommenced on oral medications and discharged back to his brother's address, but had another admission in 2011 again in the context of poor oral medication compliance. Scott continued to live with his brother Mark, until in February 2011 he had an altercation with his brother regarding accommodation. Scott reports his brother "kicked him out", and he became homeless. At this time, he was lost to follow-up, and treatment. Scott reports he was destitute and became increasingly paranoid and later became concerned that his brothers would arrange for him to be "locked up". It was at this time Scott decided to leave Victoria, and travel to Queensland.While on remand at Arthur Gorrie Correctional Centre, Scott disclosed persecutory beliefs in relation to his perceived longstanding harassment by his older brother and the police. He was experiencing grandiose delusions regarding the British monarchy stating he was "the son of Edward VIII". His mental state further deteriorated and he became increasingly hostile, refusing treatment, eventually resulting in transfer from correctional custody to High Security Inpatient Services in August 2012. He initially refused medication and food, but eventually cooperated with depot medication. Scott was officially discharged from AGCC on 27th February 2014, after being granted Bail. He was discharged to level 3 supported accommodation (Herston Lodge, his current address), and his ITO transferred to RBWH where he continued treatment and regular review.A Forensic Order was made on 25th August 2014 following a finding of unsoundness of mind.In June 2017 Scott's FO was revoked and a TSO was made by the MHRT.Scott remains fixated on his priority goal of relocating to Victoria however seems reluctant to engage in any problem-solving or steps to work towards this (incl. temporary leave to visit family, applying for transfer via legal avenues as previously advised as only available option). He is aware of an outstanding warrant for his arrest upon his return to Victoria and views this as a barrier to him temporarily visiting family, he states that he will not leave his belongings in QLD and visit Victoria in case he ends up in prison and therefore will lose his room at Herston and his belongings. He is willing to return to Victoria with his belongings once he is able to leave Qld.Scott remains amotivated to engage in any meaningful activities, employment or other means of support while he remains in Queensland stating this is a waste of time and money because Qld is not his home. He remains socially isolated articulating that he is not like the other people in Herston Lodge, he doesn't fight or use drugs, so he does not wish to socialise with them. He has very limited and irregular contact with family, and reports that even if he were to relocate to Victoria, he would not want his family overly involved in his day to day living or supports. He does not give the treating team permission to contact his family to assist with planning for transfer back to Victoria.Despite being able to attend to all ADLs and live independently, Scott resides in level 3 supported accommodation, due to not wanting to set himself up permanently in Queensland, or go to additional effort with maintaining a household or other commitments while temporarily in Queensland.Scott continues to externalise blame and feels justified in his offending. Scott believes lack of accommodation and income as well as lack of support as he has here, would explain and justify returning to offending behaviours.Scott attends all required appointments. He can become frustrated and anxious if he has to wait for any time for his depot or if his preferred staff are not available to give his depot. While he has said he would be willing to engage with mental health services upon his return to Victoria (or post-revocation of TSO) to some degree, he does not guarantee he would continue with his current prescribed treatment. Scott believes that so long as he is able to maintain stable accommodation and income he would have no issues in future and would not require ongoing medication.Scott's level of insight and engagement in his treatment and particularly identification of early warning signs and relapse prevention has improved over the years. He has started to consider what supports he would require long-term to maintain his current mental state and level of functioning upon return home to Victoria. He has also demonstrated an increasing level of insight regarding this and recently has identified some illness specific factors (paranoia, "fantasies"), whereas he previously attributed only external stress to his deterioration on the past (lack of family support, lack of income, homelessness).

Presenting concerns relate to Jessica's severe and enduring eating disorder which at times has been life threatening. Jessica continues to attribute her food choices to aspergers and subsequent sensory preferences, and strongly denies the presence of an eating disorder. She currently presents with a range of eating disorder behaviours on a background of complex trauma. In an acute presentation Jessica will present medically compromised and with cognitive impairment. Jessica also has been treated for depression by several GP's in the past and identifies as having a depressive illness. She has presented with suicidal ideation with plan and intent and has a history of suicide attempt and deliberate self harm. Therefore Jessica may present with an intense wish to die, and constructs her weight loss in the context of acute presentation as an act of self harm and wish to die. Jessica has also presented with a desire to commit petty crimes in the hopes she can "rot in jail." At baseline, Jessica is bright and bubbly, she will make eye contact and be making a real effort to look after herself and be engaging in a range of activities including work related activities, volunteering with RSPCA and attending several support groups.Predisposing factors include a history of significant childhood trauma she reports that her mother was physically and emotionally abusive towards her. Jessica also reports she was sexually abused by the mother's boyfriend and by the groundskeeper at school from pre-school to high school and when she told her mother about the sexual abuse but she didn't believe her. She left home when she was 16 yrs old and went to live with an aunt and uncle for a year while she completed year 11. At the end of the year her aunt was murdered by her husband, it is not known to writer if Jessica witness any violence in the home in the lead up to this event. Following this her grandmother and grandfather passed away in the space of a year from cancer. She has had no contact with her mother since she moved out of home when she was sixteen and does not know her biological father. Jessica has reported, at times, an intense lack of self worth and self esteem and that restricting her food and weight has been a means of controlling areas of life that have felt out of control and as a means of managing stress or anxiety.Factors that precipitate a relapse are multiple and include the enduring nature of Jessica illness, poor insight, stress, and likely ongoing eating disordered cognitions that remain unchallenged due to avoidance. Jessica reports the reason for low weight and admission in 2016 was due to decline in mood with coinciding desire to die (via food restriction) as a result of depressive illness. She believes also to have Asperger's syndrome which she reports maintains her eating disorder and low weight due to fixed ideas about eating/not eating certain foods and not accessing a variety of foods due to inflexible thinking. Jessica has a history of substance abuse, but reports no recent history.Perpetuating factors including limited insight into eating disorder and the length of time Jessica has been living with an eating disorder. Chronicity is considered a perpetuating factors with respect to eating disorders. Other perpetuating factors include eating disorder cognitions and lack of engagement in treatment to target cognitions specifically.Jessica's protective factors currently include engagement in valued activities including volunteering, casual employment at a primary school, going on holidays and being under a treatment authority which her private psychiatrist, Dr. Theodorus, has agreed to now manage. Jessica also has established a consistent support network. Jessica is currently engaged with a private psychologist. She is resourceful and a strong advocate for herself.
