In subsequent years, she has had several hospital admissions for the medical management of a diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa (with obsessive-compulsive traits and cluster b traits) interspersed with interventions which have included psychodynamic therapy, DBT, CBT-E, and nutritional (dietician) support.Isabel was admitted to RBWH (25/07/2017) after being referred by Dr Warren Ward (after her first consultant outpatient appointment) in the context of restrictive intake, compulsive exercise and resultant postural tachycardia. She was admitted under the medical team for stabilisation of her postural tachycardia and was treated with NGT feeds. She was reviewed by CL psychiatry during the admission, who noted Isabel had been quite distressed and removed her NGT on a number of occasions. She was commenced on a treatment authority (to facilitate her treatment) and transferred to H floor Eating Disorders Unit (09/08/2017). Following discharge from the ward in January 2017 (4 month admission), Isabel was continued on a community Treatment Authority and followed up assertively in the community.Upon presentation (to the CCT), Isabel weighed 51.6kg and stood 164cm tall. Isabel reported being significantly distressed in regards to her current weight and expressed a desire to achieve a BMI of 17 (despite significant evidence suggesting she was unable to maintain medical stability at this weight). In addition to caloric restriction (1500 calories a day), she reported engaging in excessive exercising (15000 steps). She denied any use of laxatives, diuretics, or diet pills.Following a routine outpatient clinic by Dr McMahon (26/04/18), Isabel was readmitted due to significant weight loss (i.e., calorie restricting & excessive exercise) resulting in her second consecutive weight below 51kg (her readmission weight). Isabel was escorted to RBWH DEM for medical clearance then admitted to the H floor Eating Disorders Unit for nutrition and weight restoration (2 month admission). After Isabel reached her goal BMI of 21, she was discharged home (with community follow-up).Formulation:Isabel possessed many of the personality traits associated with the etiology and maintenance of Anorexia Nervosa (i.e., anxious, perfectionistic, over-investment in a thin physique, achievement driven). Throughout her life, Isabel was somewhat socially anxious, and felt particularly anxious in interpersonal conflicts, which led her to be people-pleasing and perfectionistic. She was also somewhat dependent in her significant relationships, which made her even more vulnerable to distress in the context of conflict, because the continuity of the relationships felt so desperately important to her. Her traits were likely triggers into the development of an eating disorder because she engaged in dietary restraint at a time when she was experiencing a sense of powerlessness. Her powerlessness stemmed from her orthopaedic condition (i.e., intoeing) which led to ongoing school bullying; it was further exacerbated by the separation of her parents, and the stress of her brother who was reportedly "in and out" of MH wards. These events made Isabel very anxious and upset. Isabel reported using ED behaviours (dieting, calorie-counting, and exercising) to "numb" unwanted negative emotions which were negatively reinforced (i.e., as escape behaviours). Additionally, when her family members responded to the news of her illness with concern and involvement, this reinforced for her the idea that the eating disorder could get her the attention she was craving at the time. Furthermore, as she lost a significant amount of weight (originally modest weight loss through swimming and later dieting that led to a dramatic weight loss), she also appeared to have an increased sense of control and self-esteem. She also reported receiving reinforcement for her weight loss early on in the form of positive comments about her physical attractiveness. Over the course of her illness, Isabel has demonstrated great difficulty in challenging her ED cognitions due to her rigid thought patterns and high levels of anxiety about not adhering to her compulsions. Due to her long-standing illness and need for hospital admission, Isabel has become institutionalised and her identify is strongly linked to her eating disorder, further perpetuating her illness.

Case managers undertook a home visit with the assistance of QPS. Her daughter and son were notified. At the home visit there was no sign of Alison, her car or her dog. Her son used a chainsaw to break into a door between the garage and the house. Nothing untoward was noted in her house. She was later found by Police at Kilcoy. She had gone there to stay in a caravan park. She reported a longstanding desire to relocate toKilcoy and reported that she had frequently stayed at the caravan park in the past. She indicated later that she had thought she was about to have her driver's licence taken from her and so avoided her OPD appointment with Prof Byrne. This was not the case, as there has been no concern about her driving.She was admitted to the RBWH Mental Health Centre for several days of observation. During this time she underwent multiple mental state examinations and a physical examination. No significant changes in her mental state or behaviour were observed on the ward. She was discharged home. During this admission, it was reiterated to Alison that the conditions of her Forensic Order required her to notify staff whenever she was planning overnight trips away from home. Alison went missing again during the week commencing 8th February 2016 (the exact date is uncertain). She did not answer the telephone when case managers attempted to contact her and she was not at home when they visited. It subsequently emerged that she had once again driven to Kilcoy. On this occasion she had reportedly repeatedly visited a house about 20km outside Kilcoy (near Somerset Dam). It is our understanding that the home owner called QPS and Mrs Anderson was taken to the Caboolture Hospital. She was subsequently transferred to the RBWH on 16th February 2016. BackgroundMrs. Margaret Glenwright is a 57 year old married retired lady who lives with her husband & one of three adult sons who has down syndrome, in their home in Kenmore. Margaret has a history of discontinuing treatment, & she has been non-compliant with medications since disengaging from a brief trial of Paliperidone depot via a private psychiatrist 2 to 3 years ago. Margaret has previously had delusions that a media presenter was in love with her & a history of leaving the family home & booking herself into a hotel for unclear reasons but this appears to be related to the belief that these people were in love with her. Margaret's family attempted to re-engage Margaret with her private psychiatrist, however, Margaret did not attend appointments. Margaret was referred to the RBWH Acute Care Team on 23.6.15 following concern from her GP and family.Margaret presented with persecutory delusions & auditory hallucinations, & was acting on her delusions by sending text messages to a disconnected phone number protesting her innocence of claims that she believes the media are making up against her. Margaret began discussing her delusional beliefs with friends & there was a significant risk of damage to her reputation & of misadventure & vulnerability. Margaret's delusions about the media had been present for years & reportedly had worsened over the last 6-9/12. Margaret had been increasingly preoccupied with sending text messages & writing in a journal about her delusions. ~3/12 ago she started talking to herself with repetitive themes saying "I'm notscratched", "It's all lies", "I hate Elizabeth, I hate them". This was a new symptom. Margaret had stated that her sister was dead & that the family believe she killed her sister. Her sleep had worsened & her son could hear her in the bathroom talking to herself at 3am. She has shown less interest in her usual activities such as tennis, yoga & manicures. Margaret was also requiring more prompting than usual to engage in family activities. She has always taken time to process things that are said to her, but this had also gotten worse.Margaret was briefly treated by ACT who commenced her on an ITO in 2015 and referred on to Southern team. Abilify and paliperidone were both trialled with limited success for Margaret and delusionally driven behaviours continued - texting the ABC, constant AH's. Margaret's husband reported that she continued to be pre-occupied and not in touch with reality. Her delusions were quite fixed though there had been some improvement in her anxiety and sleep. Margaret was reviewed by Dr. Iti Agrawal on 8.10.15 and commenced on Olanzapine 2.5mg nocte for 3-4 weeks in addition to the Paliperidone depot. In the following months, Margaret presented with a significant improvement in her mental state. Although her delusions persisted, she was much less preoccupied with this and her thoughts are more organised. Auditory hallucinations disappeared and Margaret was sleeping much better. Margaret was linked with her GP for the monthly depot administration and was enrolled in the ATLAS program for extra support around this.

Carolyn is a 51 year old woman, working fulltime as a librarian, divorced, mother of three, living with her two youngest children Nick (12) and Saskia (16). She has a past diagnosis of PTSD resulting from domestic violence within her relationship with her ex husband and father of her three children as well as a history of MDD and anxiety. She was referred to the registrar psychotherapy program by her daughter's psychiatrist Dr Victoria Gladwell (day program north - CYMHS) in the context of her family stesses and past relationship problems with her mother and ex husband impacting her current relationships. All three of her children have chronic health problems and have all been impacted to some degree by their fathers reported controlling and hyper critical ways. Her oldest child Rebecca (19) has severe Ehlers Danlos syndrome, Saskia has ASD, does not attend school and is engaged with CYMHS, Nick has epilepsy and sturge weber syndrome. Carolyn reports difficulty in engaging in romantic relationships, ongoing difficulties in her relationship with her mother, anxiety regarding uncertainty of her future given her children's health problems and significant guilt around the impact of her relationship with her ex husband on the mental health and happiness of her children.Carolyn was raised in rural NSW with a loving father and a mother tending toward controlling behaviour over Carolyn, her adopted brother and her father though largely able to meet her needs. Carolyn reports internalising messages early on of placing other peoples needs before her own and feelings of guilt. Carolyn reports she was a high achieving student and feeling a need to do this to earn approval from her mother. In her early adulthood she discovered her father is not her biological father, a fact he is also aware of but that the two of them have never discussed. Carolyn did well at university and gained work as a librarian after where she met her future husband Mark. they lived in a variety of countries together for his work and had their two oldest chidlren before returning to rural NSW. Carolyn describes a highly controlling and emotionally and verbally abusive relationship with her husband with angry and rejecting behaviour toward her and her two youngest children. Her parents helped her to leave the relationship and after many years of court Carolyn won sole custody of the three children.Presentation to psychotherapy was precipitated by a number of relationship factors. These include: ongoing difficulties with her middle child's mental health; Nicks recent development of epilepsy and diagnosis of Sturge Weber syndrome; a sexual relationship with an acquaintance which Carolyn remains reluctant to define and unable to articulate what she wants from on an emotional level; and conflict between her and her parents leading to them moving out of the home the had all purchased together.Difficulties are maintained by ongoing challenges in the relationship with her mother and her middle childs ongoing mental health issues.Protectively Carolyn is intelligent, likeable and able to build and maintain friendships. She provides relative financial stability for her family, there are no drug or alcohol issues and her employment is stable. She loves and enjoys her children. She has been able to appropriately respond to new financial stressors in such a way as to address them quickly and decrease their impact.

21 yo young female presented with escalating impulsive suicide attempts in the context of situational crisis - perceived rejections from rental applications, housemates, potential employment. This is on a background anxiety disorder diagnosed at age 14, for which she reports self medicates with alcohol and has recurrently lead to recurrent abuse resulting in increased impulsivity and suicidality.Strong genetic loading for GAD, mother on escitalopram and younger sister had admission for GAD. Parents work full time (Dad is a housing project manager, mom works with special need children), potentially emotionally unavailable and poor attachment. Maddi was a victim of sexual assault and bullying as a teenager, reports she was shamed for falling victim of assaults. She experienced a period of hearing impairment from the age of 14 -16 due to jaw malformation impacting on structure of her ear canal, and required facial reconstruction during this period. Furthermore, her best friend completed suicide on her 18th birthday, Maddi reports she was the last person contacted and has unresolved guilt. Recently, she moved from Sydney to pursue her long term aspiration as a police officer, unfortunately she sustained a shoulder dislocation while attending police academy, which precipitated her first suicide attempt via overdose driven by fear of not being able to continue training. She was subsequently discharged from service due to unstable mental state, for which she managed reasonably well with adequate professional psychological support, until relationship break up with boyfriend in June, which re-triggered ruminations around multiple losses in recent years, and precipitated acute suicidal ideation. She was diagnosed with adjustment disorder and commenced on escitalopram, she experienced side effects of agitation and anxiety, thus recently changed over to sertraline without cross titration. Maddi feels this has further destabilise her mental state, leading to increased sensitivity to rejection.It is hypothesised that Maddi's anxious temperament, in addition to trauma history, has led to maladaptive coping mechanism towards losses and perceived rejections, and failure at her chosen career has caused further identity disturbances. Maddi is psychologically minded and display good intellectual insight into her mental health needs. She willing to engage with therapy and has supportive family in Sydney, who has been heavily involved in her current episode of care. She is premorbid high functioning and highly driven to maintain independent and regain her identity.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Raymond is a 71 year old Caucasian gentleman who lives independently in a two bedroom Public Housing unit at Wooloowin. He has a history of Paranoid Schizophrenia. He had no previous contact with the mental health services until September 1996 when he attacked his neighbours with a machete on the background of a long history of persecutory delusions. On receiving a mental health defence he was admitted to John Oxley Memorial Hospital from 1996 until 2001, when he began his transition back to the community. His diagnosis was initially considered to be Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features; hence he was given a course of ECT with good responses. However, later his diagnosis was changed to Schizophrenia, which has been confirmed by a Forensic Psychiatrist, during a regular review in August 2008. From 2001-2005 he was managed at the Continuing Care Unit (CCU), RBWH. Over the years Raymond has been compliant with his treatment, and has gradually continued to improve in affect, functioning and thought process. Following discharge from CCU he has been managed in the community. In the community he has been compliant with oral medications and has attended regular appointments with his psychiatrist and case manager. He denies any mood or positive psychotic symptoms. He has previously expressed some remorse for his actions. In February 2016, Raymond was transferred to RBWH OPMHS for ongoing care and case management. His allocated case manager is CN Keighley Dean. His mental state is currently stable.Had a MyAged Care Assessment on 24.08.2017 (Approved).

Edward (Eddie) is a 49 year old single man with a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia. He is currently engaged in a supported employment (Mylestones) three days per week and works voluntarily at Stepping Stones the other two week days in the kitchen.A Forensic Order was made on 7 June 2006 after Eddie was found of unsound mind by the Mental Health Court related to a charge of Murder on 24 October 2004.Prior to the Index Offence, Eddie had no history of mental illness recorded, but subsequent information suggested that he may have been suffering from an untreated psychotic illness for many years. According to Eddie he had been experiencing auditory hallucinations from the age of 17, after he reported suffering an acquired brain injury. He described constantly hearing threatening voices talking to him and about him. He reported intermittent cannabis and amphetamine abuse during his late teens and twenties, but claimed that he had not abused substances for over 5 years until just before the index offence. Collateral information from Eddie’s ex-girlfriend indicated he was experiencing auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions consistently between 2000 and 2004. Eddie had also reported that a psychologist at an employment agency had once recommended that he see a mental health service, but he did not follow through due to impaired insight.Following the index offence, Eddie spent approx. 7 months in prison before being transferred to High Secure Unit at the Park. He was treated on Olanzapine by PMHS, after initially refusing any anti-psychotic medication. After his transfer to HSU, he was commenced on Clozapine trial (November 2005). This led to a gradual resolution of positive psychotic symptoms and Eddie progressed well through CSU, accessing 5 nights LCT per week to supported accommodation by October 2010. There was one incident with a co-resident of the supported accommodation resulting in suspension of leave for 9 months. He continued to progress and was transferred to Somerset Villas Community Care Unit in October 2012. He progressed relatively well at CCU and his mental state remained stable. He demonstrated an overall high level of functioning and established routines, at times rather rigid. He engaged in activities including grocery shopping, going for walks, snooker, 10 pin bowling, Stepping Stones Club House and volunteering with Meals on Wheels (eventually ceased volunteering due to concerns re: having to disclose previous history of offence). He continued to engage in programs at CCU and adhered to required conditions of leave. He also complied with all random UDS, all of which returned negative results. Eddie applied for public housing in 2014, with the view that he could commence a gradual transition from CCU. He signed up to his current property with Dept of Housing in April 2015 and commenced his gradual transition. During May - November 2015 review period, Eddie completed his transition from CCU. He has remained living full-time in the community since this time. He initially received support from Communify to assist with the transition.In March 2017, Eddie's uds was positive for cannabis for the first time since the FO was made. It seems the drug use was related with the re-engagement with previous peers from the Park. Eddie continues to deny having used cannabis and reports results must be due to secondary smoke. He was counselled re: possible impact on his FO/ conditions, and has since reported he no longer associates with peers he knows use substances.Eddie can be guarded and reluctant to discuss any potential or actual stressors in an attempt to manage his impression to the treating team. He presents himself in an overly positive light, denying any problems at all or any fluctuations in his mental state. He also reportedly can behave in ways that may indicate he is anxious regarding return to employment (e.g. will find reasons not to explore possible options once they become available, or provide excuse as to why appointment time not suitable etc). He has failed attempts to gain independent work on two previous occasions and seemed to have no ability to reflect on the situation.He attends all appointments and has all tests as requested. There is no indication that he is non-compliant. He continues to live alone in Dept of Housing unit, he owns a car, Mazda3 which he has approval to drive, he has contact with his daughter via Face Book, but not his son who he is estranged from.Completed SCIT program (finished June 2017).Completed HEP C TIDE program treatment -Clear of virus, now Hep C negative.Currently attending work five days per week, three days paid, two days volunteer.Considering future study/vocational options.Continues to have contact with friends / peers, including friends from Stepping Stones.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Naomi is a 26 year old female who lives in shared accommodation. She is employed as a sex worker for an organization called Montecitos. She has been in an on/off relationship with her partner (Thomas) for multiple years. She has no children.Presenting:She was brought into RBWH by QAS on an EEA after being found trespassing on a neighbour's property. She reported she heard screaming and thought that a child was being assaulted. She could smell burning flesh and heard loud noises. She also reported that she had recently stopped smoking cannabis and was having trouble sleeping. She described losing 3 weeks in time and her friends were concerned for her. On examination she was noted to be dishevelled with agitation and elevated mood. She was thought disordered with psychotic symptoms of delusions and hallucinations. She was commenced on risperidone 3mg and placed on a TA.Post Discharge, Naomi frequently complained of perceived side effects (i.e., fatigue; difficulty concentration) of the Respiridone, and despite a reduction and psycho education she became increasingly distressed and non-compliant. She was seen in clinic (25/10/2017) and found to have severe depression with intermittent thoughts of suicide (nil plan or intent) in the context of medication non-compliance (preoccupied with perceived AEs). Admitted to H floor where she was commenced on Citalopram (to manage depressive symptoms) and Paliperidone depot (due to non-compliance with Risperidone) with good result.Predisposing: Naomi experienced a prejudical childhood with no evident protective adult figures. She was a victim of childhood sexual abuse by her biological father, and described her mother as highly critical (i.e., "conservative Christian", "very black and white") and emotionally and physically unavailable (Naomi recalls having to raise her little sister due to her mother being bed ridden with chronic fatigue). Naomi reported an inconsistent education, moving between schools frequently due to travelling around Australia with her mother and sister (reason for this is unclear). As a young adult, she was required to return to living with her father for a period and soon after first began using substances. She reported a history of "heavy" daily cannabis use from this time. Shortly after this period she was introduced to sex work in the context of an abusive relationship, where she was vulnerable to further abuse and exploitation. Overall, Naomi has experienced persistent adversity throughout her childhood development which may have increased her reactivity during times of stress in adulthood, particularly when there is inconsistent nurturing or modelling of pro-social stress-management, problem solving and emotion regulation skills. Such adversity increases her susceptibility to severe and long-term consequences such as disruptions to development of her identity, disruption to her ability to control emotions and form trusting relationships, being vulnerable to abuse or exploitation, substance abuse, and subsequently mental illness.Precipitating: Frequent substance use (including cannabis, methamphetamines and cocaine) and medication non-compliance.Perpetuating: A lack of self-identity and self-worth, underdeveloped adaptive coping strategies and exposure to peer and occupational groups that endorse this behaviour are factors in continued drug use, which increases her vulnerability to psychotic experiences. Naomi reports an unstable relationship with her "on and off" again partner Tom (who she has describes as "emotionally abusive") which may contribute to her fluctuations in mood.Protective: Naomi is future focussed (currently completing a Diploma in Nursing) and is engaging well in case management.

Occupational Influence / identity:Caitlin participated in a range of occupations during her childhood such as dancing (ballet, tap, jazz), playing the piano, playing the violin, being in the school band and short distance running. Caitlin excelled at all of these and was seen as being exceptional, she self reports themes of perfectionism from an early age. These occupations formed Caitlin's early identity and representation of others perceptions of her and her ability / skills, ultimately synthesizing doing, being, becoming and belonging to support an evolving sense of self. In her early teenage years Caitlin experienced rapid weight loss which resulted in a long hospital admission this interrupted her capacity to engage in her valued roles and placed her in an environment that had a negative impact on her image (children's hospital). During this stay Caitlin was diagnosed with Anorexia Nervosa, further investigations were conducted for Celiac's but came back negative at this stage. Caitlin reports this part of her life commenced a representation of being only a "number," which had the control to give or take away her sense of self by removing access to valued occupations.Caitlin had several hospital admissions through her teenage years which continued to interrupt her education and other roles, this experience caused a greater sense of loss and further instilled a view that she was perceived as an Anorexic and later a Celiac. Expressing emotional states to others to raise these concerns was not readily received by the environments Caitlin was experiencing. Further trauma was experienced at the age of 16years through being sexually assaulted by a "friend", this incident went unreported and assisted further in critical self appraisal. Caitlin attempted to forget the incident by going overseas to Canada to see family (Canadian heritage), the trip was unsuccessful and Caitlin was returned to Australia where she experienced further hospital admissions due to being medically compromised and of significantly low weight.Occupational Presentation / competence:Currently Caitlin no longer engages in these early formed occupations and reports this as being a process of loss and grief. Forming a new valued identity that isn't based on childhood occupations and degree level study is difficult and is met with guilt and shame. Ongoing restrictive eating patterns are embedded in feelings of shame and guilt and assist Caitlin in numbing interoceptive sensory responses and enable her to feel undesired by others "if i keep myself as ugly and tiny as possible people wouldn't want to go there". Her continued battle with Celiac's can illicit pain, lethargy and depressive feelings causing Caitlin to have difficulties with maintaining a balanced routine and commitment to her roles. Caitlin remains ultimately positive and can relate well too others. She is motivated to sustain functional capacity and improve this into the future. Caitlin recognises that her ability to communicate significant life events and emotional states attached to these is an issue and limitation to maintaining nutritional balance at times.Occupational Focus:Develop positive self-identity through continued engagement in meaningful roles (work, yoga).Further develop eating habits to assist in supplementing weight to reduce likelihood of admission.Forming new valued social relationships.Reviewing new hobbies and interests - mindfulness based activities, reading.Spending quality time with family

Candice is a 17 year old female who was brought into hospital by QAS on an EEA after being located at the Windsor train station expressing intent to end her life. Her acute deterioration was thought to occur in the context of a fight with a female friend, invalidation and rejection from peers, mounting school pressure, and recent maternal absence. Candice presents with a constellation of symptoms including episodic low mood and emotional dysregulation, anxiety, relational problems, and disordered eating. She also has a history of challenging and oppositional behaviour, temperamental difficulties including rigidity in thinking style and speech and language problems in childhood and it is thought that these factors also contribute to her current presentation and difficulty with emotional regulation. The difficult systemic factors occurring since her parents divorce alongside her transition through adolescence appear to have been significant precipitating factors with the former thought also to be a significant continuing perpetuating factor in this case. Protectively, Candice is also a young woman who has a keen sense of humour and has demonstrated functional capacity at school and in her work place. She is described as having a strong work ethic and reportedly works hard at school to achieve her future ambitions. Her strong willed temperament can therefore be recognised as a strength in this domain. Her parents also remain supportive and appropriately concerned which remains protective, although it is noted that this is waning and relationships are becoming increasingly strained leading to perceived/real rejection and invalidation. She also has a positive rapport with her community team and a willingness to help-seek.

He was acutely psychotic with paranoid persecutory delusions on presentation. He was homeless. He had been living with hisgirlfriend Tania but they had been evicted due to non-payment of rent. During this admission, Scott was commenced on zuclopenthixol depot and regular olanzapine. He also had 9 sessions of ECT (approved by MHRT) with rapid settling of his mental state. Clozapine was also discussed on multiple occasions however Scott was not willing to trial this at the time.07/07/13 - 15/07/13: Scott was admitted to RBWH after presenting to the Psychiatric Emergency Dept with agitation, confusion, difficulty sleeping and paranoia in the context of MDMA use 3 days earlier. He was also distressed over a disagreement he had with his girlfriend. Although he was initially settled, he began responding to stimuli and became both verbally and physically aggressive, kicking in a glass door panel on the ward. He later absconded and an ATR was issued. This was later recalled after he voluntarily presented to the Valley Clinic to see his Dr for review.06/10/13 - 10/10/13: Self-presented to Psychiatric Emergency Dept in crisis with anxiety and paranoia following conflict with his partner.For a few years Scott engaged relatively well with the team. His mental state deteriorated and began to think his partner was a Navy Seal and working for the government. He threw laptops over thebalcony and caused damage to a parked car. A DVO was taken out by QPS as a result. He was placed back on ITO on 15/12/15 after not agreeing to increase his seroquel medication, displayed fluctuating insight and fluctuating compliance withhis medication.After discharge, Scott declined referrals to any NGOs. He decided to work with his partner on her t-shirt business idea and obtained his security license (despite reportedly only completing 5 of the required 11 modules). He originally wanted to seek out security work (such as crowd control), however it was recommended to him at the time that the work wasn't suitable for him due to factors (such as stress, anxiety and poor anger management) that could affect his mental state. Scott's motivationto pursue this varied constantly, often influenced by Tanya who believed he should and could do security work.Scott was taken off his ITO in July 2016 by the MHRT. Scott disputes his intentions. It is reported that in the lead up to this event Tanya's mental state had also deteriorated and that Scott had become fearful for his safety. Scott's zuclopenthixol depot medication was increased to 500mg fortnightly, with Scott's agreement, to assist in stabilising his mental state during this time, however it was later decreased to 450mg after EPSE's developed. Daniel is a 41 year old single man who lives on his own in a boarding house in New Farm. He is currently in receipt of Newstart Allowance despite MHS providing him with a letter to support transfer to DSP. Has a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia which was first diagnosed in 2014 and for which Daniel has limited insight. He spends most of his day in bed, often not getting up until after 1:30pm and is unmotivated to look for work or to try and improve his psychosocial situation. He occasionally engages with other residents at the boarding house to drink beer and watch football, but his generally isolates socially. He resents that Mental Health Service has interfered with his life and ruined any chance of him living a happy and successful life.Background:Daniels was initially referred to INBMHS - SCCT via Nambour MHS in March 2014 following an involuntary inpatient admission (26/02/14 - 25/03/14), after presenting to the local HHOT team and then QPS when voicing delusional ideas of being sexually assaulted. Daniel described the first alleged incident occurring in Thailand when he was there with his girlfriend (and then fiancée) several years ago and described waking up on his hands and knees with a pillow case covering his face with a feeling of knowing that he had been sexually assaulted during the night. His girlfriend allegedly denied Daniel's version of events. Daniel also later alleged that he was sexually assaulted by his ex-wife's brother at a later stage. These beliefs have been unremitting throughout.Whilst in hospital Daniel was started on Quetiapine 200 BD plus PRN to assist with agitation and insomnia. He was also put on an alcohol withdrawal scale and prescribed thiamine vitamin supplementation. File notes state that a full assessment was unable to be done initially due to his mental state and that whilst on the ward Daniel was said to have kept a low profile, and was described as guarded and difficult to engage. Insight was said to be "non-existent". There was no FTD noted. Due to the lack of improvement in Daniel's mental state IM Paliperidone was commenced and an improvement in the intensity of hisbeliefs (about the rape/s) was noted and he felt he could put these events behind him though remains convinced of their veracity. Daniel chose to move to Brisbane to get away from the Sunshine coast and the negative social implications as he saw them in that region feeling that his reputation has been severely damaged by his MH admission and diagnosis, which he disputes.Since Daniel has engaged in Community Treatment with INBMHS his medication was increased due to limited improvement in his beliefs and in the hope of improving negative symptoms. This did not appear to improve Daniel's symptoms and it was hoped that a trial of Aripiprazole may be more effective in treating Daniel's illness. Daniel has now been transferred and maintained on Aripiprazole for over 12 months with no notable change in his presentation. He continues to gain weight which is more likely due to his lifestyle choices than the effect of the medication.Daniel continues to deny having a mental health diagnosis. Reports that would have to a lie to treating team and MHRT he has schizophrenia in order to come off the ITO. He is unwilling to engage in discussions with clinicians around delusions or hospital admissions. Maintains sexual assault occurred and sees little benefit in pursuing charges due to stigma associated with diagnosis. Daniel previously engaged in volunteer work three days per week but ceased this arrangement in 06/2016 following a deterioration in mental state. At subsequent reviews he was noted to express paranoid ideas about Bikies. Ceased work with St Vincent De Paul following an incident where a "bikie" came into work and caused him to become stressed, reporting that he was rather demanding and "wanted all things his way". Is now reluctant to return to unpaid work as believes should be getting paid for the work he does.

Agnes is a 15-year-old female who was readmitted to the Adolescent Mental Health Unit, RBWH, for continued re-feeding secondary to Anorexia Nervosa. Agnes has an approximate one year history of anorexia which appears to have been precipitated by the transition into adolescence, the perception that she was 'bigger' than her peers and the desire to be the same weight as them (who are shorter than her), as well as receiving negative comments from her mother made about her food choices. Such factors appear to have resulted in subsequent dieting behaviour and restriction of ‘unhealthy’ foods alongside dissatisfaction with her body. Subsequently, these patterns of behaviour were associated with significant weight loss, dropping from approximately 72kg to 57kg, she experienced increased obsessionality associated with food, body shape and weight, alongside further body dissatisfaction (disliked her thin frame but was unable to consume more in order to gain weight), reduced energy, andpoor motivation. Agnes was also suffering a range of medical symptomatology including dizziness and disorientation on standing, chest pain and problems with shortness of breath. She denied purging, laxative use, or significant bingeing but compulsive exercise was thought to be a symptom in her presentation. With respect to predisposing factors, Agnes has a genetic vulnerability to developing an eating disorder as evidenced by her mother also having suffered from one when she was younger. She also displays psychological character traits including obsessionality and perfectionism that havealso likely made her vulnerable to developing an eating disorder. Furthermore, significant family factors including a history of marital discord, inconsistencies within the parental relationship, maternal alienation from temperament, paternal alignment with features of the illness, and conflict with regards to her treatment plan have likely served as both predisposing and perpetuating factors. Protectively, Agnes is an intelligent and likeable young lady who does wish for her situation to be improved. In addition, despite the parental and family system difficulties, it is clear both parents love their daughter and want her to recover and there has been some evidence of increased parental capacity to re-feed and understand her illness.

Peter is a single male, divorced, father of three who has lived alone for several years in a private rental in Brisbane. He is somewhat isolated except for the support of his carers and friend Phil Dixon (who lives in NSW) and has occasional contact with his son David. In his younger years Peter was a very successful accountant running his own business as well as a range of other successful business ventures including owning a taxi fleet.He was diagnosed with BPAD in the late 1990s and has been managed by Dr Axel Estenson in the private system since this time. His illness has been quite disabling resulting in multiple admissions (at least one admission per year) to New Farm clinic, usually with manic episodes. He has had a couple of depressive episodes resulting in suicide attempts. During his manic episodes he would often spend large sums of money (on one occasion buying 3 BMWs and giving these away). In between episodes he continued to be somewhat grandiose often living outside his means and believing he had access to millions of dollars. His illness was complicated by narcissistic personality disorder, periods of heavy alcohol use and more recently concerns about his decline in memory (although consistently refused formal testing with Dr Estenson).At a result of his mental illness and excess spending during relapses his EPOA, Mike Alcorn (an old business friend) took over the management of his finances in 2003. In addition, he stopped work and has been on income protection since 2006 and now on the aged care pension.Mike Alcorn managed to secure carer support through DSQ about 7 years ago although the reasons for this are still unknown to us or to Dr Estenson. We suspect these might not have been entirely founded or necessary initially. However his carers, EPOA and psychiatrist noticed a decline in his cognition and functioning in the 6-12 months leading up to admission and needed quite a lot of prompting and assistance to self cares.At this admission there was a clear diagnosis of dementia based on imaging, history, cognitive testing and clinical presentation. His bipolar illness settled within the first couple of weeks and has remained stable for the last 4months. Peter clearly did not have capacity to make decisions related to his finances, health and lifestyle because of his dementia and chronic mental illness. As such an application was made to QCAT and Mike Alcorn was removed as EPOA and a guardian and trustee appointed.Peter remained under our care for nearly 5 months due to awaiting QCAT and appropriate placement as his previous EPOA ceased accommodation (reportedly as could no longer afford it). He was settled and with no management issues on the ward. The main concern during this admission (apart from the new diagnosis of dementia) was his 3 medical admissions with collapse, chest infection and urosepsis. Given deconditioned while in hospital a referral was made to aged care services for assistance prior to NGO footprints assisting Peter with private accommodation. While his primary issue is dementia his long standing history of severe bipolar warrants ongoing input from mental health services for the near future and management under a TA.

Kylie is a 16 year old female who is currently under a long term child protection guardianship order through child safety services. Since approximately August 2017 Kylie has demonstrated significant destabilisation in her emotional and behavioural state characterised by increasing suicidal ideation and associated behaviour, severe difficulties in regulating her emotional state, and heightened aggression. Her decompensation in mental health is thought to have occurred in the context of significant psychosocial stressors including having to be removed from her foster mother's care following allegations that she (amongst others) had made regarding the care that she was receiving and her foster mother's subsequent death by suicide. Kylie experiences significant guilt, anger, and grief associated with these events and has limited coping strategies to help her to manage such complex emotions. Her adjustment to these losses continues to perpetuate her difficulties and typically triggers relating to an acute episode of emotional and behavioural dysregulation include reminders/memories, perceived rejection, nightmares, guilty cognitions, fear, others' distress, limit-setting, and over-stimulation. It is also suggested that Kylie's behaviours are an attempt to provoke caring responses from her workers or seek containment from those around her as she is unable to do this herself. Additionally, Kylie has expressed a desire to feel the pain that her foster mother felt or indeed be with her foster mother through death, and in this way, her behaviour helps her to feel close to her foster mother. Kylie is also fearful of feeling vulnerable and controlled and it is suspected that her aggressive behaviour is often a form of her feeling powerful and in control. In addition to the losses that she has experienced, Kylie has also been placed into residential care and there have been significant adjustments that have been required as a result of this. Kylie struggles to manage interpersonal relationships and changes within her environment and therefore these factors continue to perpetuate her difficulties. Behaviourally, inconsistency within her care team and/or people's responses to her behaviour, including her aggressive behaviour, is also thought to be a maintaining factor in her presentation by virtue of inconsistent behavioural contingencies. Kylie's current presentation also occurs on the background of exposure to neglect and abuse in her infancy, emotional and psychological abuse longitudinally, and previous difficulties centring around Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Oppositional-Defiant Disorder, Developmental Delay. She has also previously attracted a diagnosis of Childhood Autism.

Joelle is a 47 year old widowed female of Caribbean descent. She currently resides alone in a private rental in Toowong. She is unemployed and in receipt of a Newstart allowance.First inpatient admission: Joelle was admitted to MHH (RBWH) from 25/05/2018 - 18/06/2018 under the Mental Health ACT (before being transferred to Nundah House on the 18/06/2018 and then MHI on the 16/07/2016) when she presented to her first OPD appointment in a highly distressed state. Her presentation was characterised by symptoms suggestive of bereavement complicated by a superimposed mood disorder with exacerbation of OCD traits and PTSD. Joelle reported a history of long-standing severe anxiety and mood symptoms that have intensified in the context of the death of her husband in October 2017. Unfortunately Joelle had exhausted all available psychological supports and was referred to CCT for case management due to the complexity of her presentation.Given Joelle's background of childhood instability characterised by an absence of parental figures, her trajectory into adulthood mental health difficulties was unsurprising. It is likely that an anxious-avoidant attachment style emerged during development in the context of separation from her sister, abandonment by her biological father and an insecure primary attachment with her mother, who appeared unable to consistently attune to Joelle's emotional needs and who was perceived as a harsh, critical parent figure. It is likely that these early experiences have led to development of core beliefs that "the world is unsafe" and "I am not good enough". These beliefs were likely reinforced when she met Craig (Deceased Husband), who held similar beliefs about the world being a hostile place. Their shared beliefs, together with Joelle's desire for acceptance and Craig's apparent comfort in a dominant role, appears to have shaped their relationship to one of dutifulness by Joelle towards her husband. Her relationship with Craig was also one of Joelle's first intimate attachments, which likely heavily influenced her reliance and compliance to his instructions.Joelle (and Craig) responded to core assumptions about the world being a hostile place with overcompensation - she did not trust people other than Craig and isolated herself from others. As a result, she and Craig lived a secluded life and remained each others' pillars of support. The recent death of Craig was considered a precipitant for Joelle's admission as it likely activated her abandonment schema and a reminder that she is alone with no support. How readily a person seek help is heavily dependent on the social structure of the family - and this is mostly assessed through attachment in childhood, which help shape an individuals personality and social development in adulthood. Given the early invalidating experiences that Joelle experienced (absence of nurturing response to her distress), it is likely she developed an avoidant attachment style (characterised by withdrawal when distressed), which has impacted her interpersonal relationships as an adult. In addition, she currently experiences a complicated grief response which is further exacerbated by social isolation and efforts to comply with Craig's final instructions of not trusting anyone. Avoidance of help-seeking and continued efforts to maintain an independent coping stance was reinforced by an absence of stable supportive networks.Joelle reported feeling like a "burden" and being "uncertain" about how to deal with emotions. These labels reflect a sense of incompetence or inadequacy that likely prevented her from engaging in approach behaviours to seek help. Whilst she evidently had pre-existing emotional difficulties, her recent loss, social isolation, and financial stressors seemed to have triggered her recent distress and decline in mental health. Combined with a rigid belief and commitment to her deceased husband's instruction that the world should not be trusted, it has left her with no further options to consider.Fortunately, Joelle has several intrapersonal protective factors that may buffer against future mental health deterioration. She is intellectual and motivated to continue studying, and has had some good experiences with previous psychological interventions. These elements may be utilised in her favour throughout intervention and recovery.

Donald in an 80 year old male who presents with BPSD following dementia diagnosis in 2015. Don is a highly intelligent individual who has worked as a professor and lecturer at QUT and as a property developer for a number of years. He is married with 2 adult children and grandchildren. In the last 5 years Donald's behaviour, memory, problem solving and judgement have been impaired secondary to Alzheimers dementia. It has resulted in multiple charges, financial loss (through inappropriate purchases of property) resulting in public trustee, tension between family members, deterioration in his self cares and other risky behaviours around the house (included trying to use a jackhammer to fix the water pipe) just prior to admission.Donald responded well to medication and after some time setting into the ward environment. There was no evidence of psychosis or mood disorder. While memory deficits, poor judgement and problem solving remained he was a delight to have on the ward. He was very cooperative with staff, engaged in painting and enjoyed telling stories of his past. Given the extent of his impairment QCAT approved guardianship and the decision was made (with recommendation from the treating team) for Donald to be discharged to a residential facility. Donald grieves the loss of his former self and struggles with his diagnosis and the decision of him having to move to an aged care facility. However overall accepts this and we have no doubt that with time and adjustment he will settle into his new environment.There are no imminent risks. However at risk of BSPD in future as the dementia progresses or with stressors/new environment and without medication.

Melissa is a 49 year old female who presents with psychotic symptoms and mood disturbance in the setting of BPAD and chronic cannabis use. Despite a somewhat adverse childhood (adopted and abused by brothers) and possible family history of mental illness was very high functioning for a long period. She completed medical school, worked as a doctor, married and had two children. There is clear evidence of manic and depressive episodes throughout her life and on longitudinal assessment diagnosis of BPAD has been made. Commencement of psychotic symptoms is unclear however have likely been there on and off for years. These are mostly in regards to her neighbour and conspiracies about the police not taking action around this. It is clear that Melissas life has been significantly impacted by her major mental illness becoming de-registered (by herself) as a medical practitioner, becoming estranged from her family and being financially vulnerable and at times living out of her car (to travel to Nimbin and escape stress of the neighbour). Melissa is clearly still a very intelligent person with some very alternative views. She would likely greatly benefit from treatment and follow up however is limited by her poor insight. Risks when unwell include poor self cares and emailing authorities and stalking of the neighbour. However no significant events have occurred when unwell, she is not suicidal and there is no aggression history making it difficult to argue ongoing use of a treatment authority. She has already stopped taking her oral medication and given not acutely unwell there is a change her TA may be revoked. If this happens she would still benefit from follow up and encouragement from treatment. Should she re-present, deteriorate or risks change would recommend more assertive treatment with a depot however did not seem warranted at this point.

Johann has been charged with 'stalking' a young lady outside the Beaudesert Shopping Centre after she refused to give him a cigarette (September 2013), and also with Public Nuisance (May 2014). Such threats serve their purpose and are rarely followed up with a commitment to action. These threats often occur at times of stress when Johann lacks the skills to cope in other ways.To establish dominance in a situation where he feels powerless or fearful. Such threats aim for immediate impact rather than progression to action, but may occasionally result in aggression if the threatener feels pushed to prove they mean it. Attendance improved somewhat throughout the course of treatment, however, Johann continues to require significant support to attend.

OverviewGraham is a 56 year single, unemployed man living independently in community housing at Hamilton receiving the DSP. He has a history of aggression, weapon possession and assaulting staff.Psychiatric History Graeme has a long history of mood disturbance dating back to at least 1992 when his GP diagnosed him with a chronic depressive illness. In 1995 he became interested in the possibility of adult ADHD, and was diagnosed with this at the Serfontein Clinic. He was trialled on dexamphetamines prescribed by his GP with little effect. He then began to exhibit paranoia including persecutory beliefs that people were conspiring against him and placing him under surveillance, taping his phone conversations and wanting to harm him. He began taping up the windows of his house and digging up the groundlooking for electronic bugs.His first psychiatric admission was to RBWH on 26/2/1996, when he was diagnosed with Drug Induced Psychosis (diff dx Schizophrenia). He was readmitted in May 1996 and diagnosed with Chronic Delusional Disorder and premorbid Schizoid Personality. During his third admission in June 1996 his diagnosis evolved to Paranoid Schizophrenia. In further admissions in 1998 he was diagnosed with BPAD with mania and psychosis, diff dx Schizoaffective Disorder.Since 2005 Graeme has had multiple admissions to hospital and has been consistently diagnosed with schizoaffective Disorder. His history of significant functional decline and delusions in the absence of mood symptoms is certainly consistent with a schizophrenic process. Graeme, however, disagrees with his diagnosis and is convinced that he has bipolar disorder and Adult ADHD. He has been serially non-compliant with oral medication in the past, and has previously required ATRs for avoiding depot medication. He continues to question the diagnosis of psychotic illness and does not believe that he requiresanti-psychotic medication, despite being seen by several psychiatrists who have concurred with his current diagnosticformulation and need for ongoing medication.Graham has self-presented to RBWH multiple times, and has also been admitted on many occasions following ATRs and EEOs. He has been on a TA since 2005 and has a forensic history including charges of common assault and carrying a knife in public to cause fear from May 2005.In July 2010 he was worked up for Clozapine. He was admitted to RBWH G-Floor ward from 27/9/10 to 30/9/10 for Clozapine initiation. His mental state was stable during this process, although he remained somewhat guarded and dismissive. He was admitted to ICU at RBWH on 13/10/10 and clozapine was ceased. In 2013, Graeme had 2 involuntary MH admissions in both Brisbane and Canberra.He was admitted to the RBWH on the 05/05/13 after presenting via QPS on an EEO following a MVA. It is reported that Graham reversed his car down a one way street at ~ 60 km / hr in attempt to run over something in his rear view mirror. Whilst in PEC Graham required IV neuroleptisation after assaulting a PEC nursing staff member. He was hostile, irritable, demanding and intrusive, requiring management in HDU, seclusion and multiple IM injections. During this admission Graeme was commenced on lithium, Olanzapine and his fluphenazine 75mg depot was recommenced. Olazapine was to be gradually reduced and stopped post discharge. She is a mother of two young children, daughters aged 12 and 10 years. Emily works as an Assistant in Nursing (AIN) at Young Care where she has worked for approximately 10 years. At time of presentation, Emily reported symptoms including dietary restriction, limited food groups, frequent chew/spit behaviours, over-evaluation of weight and shape, and fears of weight gain. In addition, Emily reported symptoms of an enduring low mood and generalised anxiety. Emily reported a difficult upbringing and described an invalidating childhood environment including parental emotional abuse at times. Emily described predisposing factors including being parentified from the age of five-years where she was required to care for her younger brothers and sisters. Additionally, Emily reported a maternal history of an eating disorder and depressive symptoms. Emily reported precipitating factors including the onset of her eating disorder after the birth of her second child, approximately nine years prior. Emily reports a number of psychosocial stressors including relationship difficulties and financial strain; these external stressors appear to perpetuate her eating disorder symptoms. Additionally, over-evaluation of weight and shape and fears of weight gain are perpetuating factors that result in dietary restriction. Protective factors include her relationship with her daughters, close family friend, supportive step-father (located in NZ), and stable work environment and colleagues.

And recent family reunion with her brothers has likely retriggered childhood traumas, as well as perceived favouritism by mother towards her brother, perpetuating feeling of hopelessness, helplessness and worthlessness. Maddison is a 15 year old female who was referred to the Adolescent Mental Health Unit (AMHU) by her CYMHS team due to increasing concerns regarding her risk to self, deteriorating mental state, and Maddison's acknowledgement that an admission may be of benefit. Maddison reported that her acute deterioration in mood had been precipitated by a relationship break-up and also her best friend terminating their friendship, on the background of long-standing mood problems and a series of interpersonal stressors and being the victim of bullying, both in person and online, since beginning high school. Predisposing factors seem to relate to a genetic vulnerability to mood disorder, possible disrupted attachment in early childhood, and exposure to high maternal anxiety. Additionally, it was also suspected that Maddison had longitudinally exhibited a more sensitive temperament as an infant, prone to high emotion, and that this, combined with the cumulative effects of aversive relational/interpersonal experiences may have led to Maddison developing core difficulties with emotion regulation.

Nikki describes a lifelong pattern of temporarily good engagement with medication and mental health appointments, with an associated high level of functioning in the community (working as a mechanic, riding his motorcycle, maintaining private rental accommodation).Unfortunately this is interspersed with episodes where Nicholas withdraws from all supports, becomes non-compliant with medications and subsequently deteriorates with regard to his level of functioning. Nikki describes Nicholas at these times as paranoid, verbally and physically aggressive, homeless and unemployed, and states that typically he will come to the attention of police and be brought into an inpatient mental health institution.From May 2007 until early 2010 Nicholas was managed through the community mental health service as a voluntary client on 50mg Risperidone depot, with case management. He was able to engage with employment via 'Breakthru' and rode his motorcycle to work as a mechanic assistant. He had contact with his mother, and was able to maintain private rental accommodation. In 2010 Nicholas transitioned to the GP shared care program. At this point he failed to attend Dr's appointments from August 2010 onwards. He had cut all contact with his parents and subsequently moved from his private rental accommodation to a boarding house (Ellie Bennett). He then was asked to leave Ellie Bennett due to his confrontational and verbally aggressive behaviour which appears to have been driven by some persecutory delusions regarding his treatment by management at Ellie Bennett (eg. that they were making false accusations about him smoking in his room). He stopped his depot in November 2010.He came to the attention of mental health again in 2011 when attending court on some charges of public nuisance but was assessed by court liaison staff as psychotic. In March 2012, Nicholas care was transferred to HHOT. Since that time he regularly attended his outpatient appointments, and received his depot. However, he remained poorly kempt, thought disordered, and disorganised with ongoing paranoia. Nicholas moved into a Department of Housing unit in Spring Hill in November 2012.2013 He had incorporated his MIRT case manager into his delusional system, believing the clinician to be collaborating with the government to prevent him getting rent assistance, among other things. He believed there was another Nicolas Churches (with no H) who was an impostor and was stealing his benefits etc. He was quite irritable and verbally aggressive. formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Kylie is a 16 year old female who is currently under a long term child protection guardianship order through child safety services. Since approximately August 2017 Kylie has demonstrated significant destabilisation in her emotional and behavioural state characterised by increasing suicidal ideation and associated behaviour, severe difficulties in regulating her emotional state, and heightened aggression. Her decompensation in mental health is thought to have occurred in the context of significant psychosocial stressors including having to be removed from her foster mother's care following allegations that she (amongst others) had made regarding the care that she was receiving and her foster mother's subsequent death by suicide. Kylie experiences significant guilt, anger, and grief associated with these events and has limited coping strategies to help her to manage such complex emotions.Her adjustment to these losses continues to perpetuate her difficulties and typically triggers relating to an acute episode of emotional and behavioural dysregulation include reminders/memories, perceived rejection, nightmares, guilty cognitions, fear, others' distress, limit-setting, and over-stimulation. It is also suggested that Kylie's behaviours are an attempt to provoke caring responses from her workers or seek containment from those around her as she is unable to do this herself. Additionally, Kylie has expressed a desire to feel the pain that her foster mother felt or indeed be with her foster mother through death, and in this way, her behaviour helps her to feel close to her foster mother. Kylie is also fearful of feeling vulnerable and controlled and it is suspected that her aggressive behaviour is often a form of her feeling powerful and in control. In addition to the losses that she has experienced, Kylie has also been placed into residential care and there have been significant adjustments that have been required as a result of this.Kylie struggles to manage interpersonal relationships and changes within her environment and therefore these factors continue to perpetuate her difficulties. Behaviourally, inconsistency within her care team and/or people's responses to her behaviour, including her aggressive behaviour, is also thought to be a maintaining factor in her presentation by virtue of inconsistent behavioural contingencies.Kylie has required numerous inpatient admissions since August 2017 due to heightened acute risk to self and/or behavioural disturbance including physical aggression towards others. It is noted that Grace reports that her OCD continues to be at the same level it has been for the past few years and is not intensifying in the hospital setting.PrecipitatingAt this stage Grace reports being unable to identify any acute precipitants for this deterioration, which is consistent with her most recent admission to LCCH. Her mother notes that the school had indicated Grace is not expected to complete any assessments but Grace expressed of not wanting to be singled out, preferred to complete assessments to achieve good grades. It appears Grace self-imposed this high expectation on herself resulting in stress. Previously she indicated some social difficulties, however did not elaborate on these. She reports that her dad has recently commenced a new job and she feels her current mental state is manageable.PredisposingThere is a marked family history of mental health that represents a genetic predisposition to development of mental health difficulties, with paternal history of anxiety and schizophrenia. Grace's anxious temperament is also considered a predisposing factor to mental health issues. Father reports recent deterioration of his own mental state with increase in perceptual phenomena in recent months, which has coincided around the time of losing his job. Despite this, Andrew reports a steady improvement in his mental health in recent weeks and has obtained casual employment usually working2-3 days per week.PerpetuatingPreviously Grace's use of avoidant behaviour has been hypothesised to perpetuate her OCD and anxiety. Grace is noted to have actively participated in her treatment plan with the treating team. Further Grace has not presented with any physical or emotional disruptions/deteriorations across the period of the medication change in dosage; reported the medication had worked for her in reduction in SI and DSH.

Presenting - Carina is a 24 year old single female on DSP living in department of housing accommodation with a current primary diagnosis of Intellectual Impairment (IQ) 60, borderline PD, with differential diagnosis of psychosis (NOS). She was referred to Southern Team - CCT for case management following in excess of 70 hospital presentations in 2016-17 and becoming the highest user of Ferny Grove QPS in the same year. Carina's history of engagement with mental health services is characterised by frequent crisis presentations to hospital with somatic complaints and suicidal ideation/attempts (by non-lethal means) and DSH in the form of superficial self-harm. There is also documentation of her complaining of intermittent internal and external auditory hallucinations (derogatory voices, including of Satan; and historically the voice of her pastor's daughter), and these can improve with distraction.Predisposing - Carina is the second eldest of 4 daughters. She reportedly left home at age 17 or 18 for reasons which are not clear. Carina has maintained intermittent contact with her mother and currently has phone contact every couple of weeks. Clinical documentation indicates that Carina has reported physical abuse by her step-father in the past. As well, Carina has reported experiencing sexual violence. Carina resided primarily in crisis accommodation when she moved out of home and has made multiple links with community non-government agencies. Accommodation arrangements appeared to end abruptly, prompted either by eviction or of Carina's choice to leave, often in short notice. Carina has used drugs and alcohol opportunistically and is a smoker.Precipitating - Carina's re-entry into mental health system was precipitated by a breakdown in housing situation and care arrangements resulting in increased need for care co-ordination. Carina has significant difficulty regulating her emotions, poor interpersonal skills and limited capacity to tolerate distress. Thus her presentations are often precipitated by interpersonal conflicts with neighbours or family resulting in poor emotion regulation and distress. This is further complicated by low IQ and chronic health/somatic issues. Carina requires significant supports to maintain her independence in the community which was not being achieved prior to referral to CCT. Carina requires lots of support to solve problems, manage interpersonal difficulties and maintain structure/routine.Perpetuating - Low IQ, interpersonal conflicts/poor social skills, lack of available suitable accommodation facilities/support, boredom and somatic complaints. Although Carina was assessed by DSQ as requiring 24 hour supported accommodation there is no such accommodation available, thus Carina will continue to experience periods of instability due to inadequate supports. Other factors that continue to perpetuate presentations to hospital are boredom and ongoing somatic issues relating to poor lifestyles choices particularly diet resulting in chronic constipation and diabetes. Issues associated with cerebral palsy including pain and falls.Protective - Carina is very likeable and when willing to engage can actually do very well living independently in the community with support, she has a 25 hours per week package of support from Footprints and has recently started engaging in multiple groups/activities which has significantly reduced her contact with MHS. She has grown to be more resilient over the years and is a strong advocate for herself. Historically Carina has demonstrated improved ability to utilise her identified strategies.Formulation - Carina has established diagnoses of borderline PD & intellectual disability with significant past history of multiple traumas that include physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She has often presented with psychotic symptoms and currently experiences hallucinations in a number of modalities leading to an additional diagnosis of psychosis NOS. She has limited coping strategies but has learnt to be more resilient over the years; she continues to have a low tolerance to distress resulting in acute presentations in a dysregulated state as well as psychotic symptoms. She belongs to a group characterised by chronic elevated risk (acute risk moderate) to self in view of the mental disorder diagnosis, personality disorder, ID, hx of traumas, ongoing interpersonal conflict within her community, limited insight, limited adaptive coping mechanisms; ongoing risks being contained by current drug treatment (partial at best), regular MHC monitoring and psychosocial interventions (by NGO, support from neighbours, police input, GP support.

41 yo female, Ethiopian refugee, arrived in Australia 2010, single mother of 2 young sons 13 yo, 6 yo, presented after overdose with suicide intent whist alcohol intoxicated in the setting of major depression, third presentation in 2018 with suicidality. Background of significant trauma histories with complex PTSD, where Mekdes witnessed killing of her father pre migration, spent 17 years at refugee camp since 14 yo where she was repeated raped, her first son result of sexual assault. She experienced difficulties adjusting and settling in a foreign country with different culture and language. It is hypothesized that her trauma history has invoked a sense of learnt helplessness and subsequent feeling of social rejection upon arrival in Australia. Biologically, Mekdes suffers from diabetes and chronic pain post MVA, which is at times disabling and further impacted on her capacity to look after her children, causing damage to her self esteem. Current episodes precipitated by relationship breakdown with brief ex husband 1 year ago, where Mekdes felt betrayed and exploited by an Ethiopian man she sponsored to come to Australia who left the marriage shortly after his arrival. Subsequently she disengaged with her local Ethiopian church causing increasing social isolation. More recently, her elder son was suspended from school, and Mekdes viewed this as her failure as a mother and reacted with increasing feeling of guilt, compounded by fear of DOCS involvement, retriggering past trauma of herself displaced from family as a child at a similar age. Her depression is perpetuated by ongoing interpersonal conflict with her children, which she becomes increasingly sensitive to, also suboptimal treatment of her depression with antidepressants at inadequate dose and possibly inappropriate form of psychotherapy for her complex histories that lead to worsening feeling of helplessness and hopelessness. This is compounded by alcohol abuse as a form to self medicate and perpetuated her depressive symptoms. Mekdes demonstrates resilience in the past, she is help seeking and highly motivated to remain as carer of her two sons. She identify her friends Maddie and Michelle as good support. She also receives weekly supports from NGOs to assist with her carer's role. Of note, it is important to explore cultural concepts of Mekdes's presentation to provide appropriate care, particularly cultural expectation of the mother role and possible association to shame and guilt as a single mother. Unfortunately Mekdes declined input from transcultural mental health at this stage.

Kylie is a 16 year old female referred for inpatient psychiatric management due to escalating risk to self and others. Since approximately August 2017 Kylie has demonstrated significant destabilisation in her emotional and behavioural state characterised by increasing suicidal ideation and associated behaviour, severe difficulties in regulating her emotional state, and heightened aggression. Her decompensation in mental health is thought to have occurred in the context of significant psychosocial stressors including having to be removed from her foster mother's care following allegations that she (amongst others) had made regarding the care that she was receiving and her foster mother's subsequent death by suicide. Kylie experiences significant guilt, anger, and grief associated with these events and has limited coping strategies to help her to manage such complex emotions. Her adjustment to these losses continues to perpetuate her difficulties and typically triggers relating to an acute episode of emotional and behavioural dysregulation include reminders/memories, perceived rejection, nightmares, guilty cognitions, fear, others' distress, limit-setting, and over-stimulation. It is also suggested that Kylie's behaviours are an attempt to provoke caring responses from her workers or seek containment from those around her as she is unable to do this herself. Additionally, Kylie has expressed a desire to feel the pain that her foster mother felt or indeed be with her foster mother through death, and in this way, her behaviour helps her to feel close to her foster mother. Kylie is also fearful of feeling vulnerable and controlled and it is suspected that her aggressive behaviour is often a form of her feeling powerful and in control. In addition to the losses that she has experienced, Kylie has also been placed into residential care and there have been significant adjustments that have been required as a result of this. Kylie struggles to manage interpersonal relationships and changes within her environment and therefore these factors continue to perpetuate her difficulties. Behaviourally, inconsistency within her care team and/or people's responses to her behaviour, including her aggressive behaviour, is also thought to be a maintaining factor in her presentation by virtue of inconsistent behavioural contingencies.

These difficulties appear to make it difficult for Jayden to make and keep friends. He reports that he has been told multiple times that he is annoying.There appear to be emerging personality vulnerabilities which appear to impact his tolerance of distress and his relationships.Precipitating this likely is related to the breakdown in his relationship with his girlfriend and social deprivation with the added loss of his only friend pre-relationship. There appears to be family conflict in relations to Jayden's adolescence. Jayden is likely a little delayed in this respect and there is certainly conflict with regards to Jayden's role confusion. There is rebellious behaviour which appears to be triggering in his mother and father, but primarily his mother. I suspect that some of the conflict that is being experienced in Sonya is secondary to the domestic violence that has been experienced at home.The ongoing discrepancies in what is being said to different health care professionals is likely the personality traits which are emerging, this currently represents a barrier to recovery, community case work is invariably focused on risk and managing this. His family are very much supportive of him engaging in treatment, they act protectively. Jayden attends school full-time and also works part-time.

Natalie maintained compliance to treatment under supervision of her psychiatrist (Dr. Michael O'Sullivan) and mental health clinician (Julie O'Sullivan) up until December 2012, then informing her treating team she would no longer be taking clozapine. She was not complying with the treatment plan (was self-adjusting her medication doses), was guarded and suspicious with nursing staff, withdrawn and was not participating in any of the patient programmes. Natalie was referred to MIRT on discharge under an ITO to continue with her care in the community. 25 year old male, single, a father of 2 children (5 years old - Ella and 3 years old - Zella). Works as a technician at the Retail company in Everton Park. He lives with a friend in Ferny Grove.
