Jamie lived with his mum full time and his father would visit regularly. Jamie is the youngest and is one of five children. He has four siblings Toby who he shares both biological parents with, Cass and Temika who are his half sisters, and shares the same mother and Matthew a half-brother who he shares the same father with. Jamie has contact with all his siblings apart from Matthew who he reports having no contact with from about the age of 8 years old. He was a premature baby but reports he wasn’t aware of any other complications at birth or experienced delayed developmental milestones.Jamie recalls forming a secure attachment with his mother was difficult as she did not display love and affection and offered little validation and minimal physical contact. He describes his mother as kind and caring. Jamie describes his father as quite negative, he was physically and verbally abusive to his brother Toby, and he witnessed these assaults, but reports he is his fathers “favourite” child.School for Jamie in the primary years was “good”, he was an intelligent child and achieved academically. In high school Jamie recalls this being a difficult time with some bullying, minimal friends and he “struggled to find a place” in the system. He reported feeling that something was different from commencement in high school and by the age of 13 was consciously aware that he was gay. This discovery for many years was wrapped in feelings of guilt and shame about who he was and to acknowledge this publicly took 11 years. He experienced his first gay relationship in secret with a friendfrom school at the age of 16. This relationship continued in secret for over a year and ended after his friend accidentally drowned after graduation from high school. Jamie recalls it was exceedingly hard to grieve appropriately for the loss of his friend and partner as their family’s and wider community were not aware of their gay relationship “how can you grieve your love for someone when no one knows the truth”. After leaving school at the age of 17 Jamie worked for MacDonald’s and moved to a manager role fairly rapidly; during this job he met the mother of his children (Ashely) who he recalls as being a “cool chick”, she fell pregnant after a one sexual encounter and gave birth to their eldest Daughter Ella after a 6-month pregnancy. Ella required ongoing hospital care post birth and Jamie reported he felt he had anobligation to “stick around” but did not feel “trapped”. This relationship lasted for 5 years and had an “on, off” aspect, within the middle of the 5 years they conceived another child “I wanted Ella to have a sibling”.His parent’s relationship changed in 2013 when Jamie was 19, he reports his mother met a new man and when she advised his biological father he became hostile towards her. Comments about his mother were made openly and these were degrading towards her, his father made it very clear that he felt rejected by her as Jamie’s mother for years had insisted on telling the family unit that she didn’t want to have a husband / partner. This change in his parent’s relationship also occurred around the birth of his first child Ella and family contact with both parents was hostile and anxiety provoking during this period. During the relationship with Ashley, Jamie was aware he was gay but continued to struggle on with the partnership. He recalls that during this time Ashley became very controlling alienating him from his family and female friends and only consenting to Jamie “doing” things with her. In 2017 Jamie made the decision while intoxicated with alcohol to disclose to his family and close friends that he was gay, he felt this decision was also driven by thoughts around ending his life if he couldn’t identify with this part of himself “I was sick of living in a world of regret…. What had I got to lose”. His family were accepting of this disclosure, but this further ruptured an already tenuous relationship with Ashley.Occupational Presentation – Occupational Competence:Jamie struggles to form stable relationships often seeking validation of a partner’s feelings to manage chronic anxiety around his emotional needs. He has a well formed stable routine that centres around the primary role of work and regular contact with his daughters, but it lacks other occupational experiences. Ongoing mediation with Ashley around contact with his children continues to cause distress and increase emotional dysregulation. Jamie moved to Brisbane in March 2017 and within the first few days broke up with his partner Chris, it was at this point Jamie reports being sexually active with multiple short-term partners labelling this as a “rampage”. After this 9-month experience Jamie met Josh and identifies he committed himself to this relationship but ultimately attempted to change aspects of his self-identity to align with Josh’s wishes. This environmental influence further impacted on Jamie’s sense of self and elicited an increase in seeking validation from Josh to manage his emotional needs. Proceeding the break-up from Josh, Jamie’s routine and capacity to articulate his needs diminished and he experienced a short admission to mental health. Jamie also articulates that alcohol has played a big role in his routine and is a strategy he uses for avoiding ongoing anxiety. Jamie continues to use social media platforms to gain validation from others during times of distress.Occupational Focus - Occupational Adaptation: Develop a positive self-identity through continued engagement in meaningful roles (work, father). Forming new valued social relationships that are not built on seeking validation. Reviewing new hobbies and interests. Develop skills to assist with emotional regulation and decrease parasuicidal behaviour through exploring practical strategies founded in the modality of sensory approaches. Develop a routine that reduces access to electronics that interfere with developing a robust sense of self.

Factors likely to have predisposed Polly to her current mental health issues include a genetic vulnerability to anxiety, temperamental factors associated with ASD, long-standing symptoms of anxiety, and her conductive hearing loss which causes Polly difficulty with hearing and communicating with others.Polly's transition into adolescence and high school may have acted as a distal precipitant for the worsening of Polly's mental health resulting in mood dysregulation and increased anxiety. The cessation of medication, and the change of coping strategies within the school environment may have precipitated Polly's recent overt distress and increase in suicidal ideation and thoughts of self-harm.Polly's diagnosis of ASD may influence her ability to effectively communicate, possible limited emotional-language and her limited willingness to seek support when at school may perpetuating her high level of risk. Polly's avoidance of school and particular tasks may also act to maintain her level of anxiety with attending school. Additionally, parental and systemic factors including carer's fatigue, delayed access to full school supports, and her mothers own experience of anxiety in relation to Polly's safety may also perpetuate Polly's current mental health issues.Protectively, Polly's family is highly knowledgeable, supportive and willing to engage Polly in support services. Polly is able to engage in some pleasurable activities and is able to seek support from her mother when at home. Once rapport had been established, Polly gradually engages in conversation about her emotions and she was able to collaboratively engage in safety planning.

BackgroundMr. Brodie Nicol is a 56 year old single gentleman who currently lives alone in a privately owned unit in Auchenflower. Brodie is currently unemployed and receives the disability support pension. Brodie receives a HASP support package which is provided by Open Minds and MACS who provide daily assistance for medication management, domestic tasks, meal preparation and social activities such as PCYC gym, library visits and computer training. MACS visit each evening and supervise Brodie's medication which is kept in a locked box. Brodie has good family support and sees his family regularly. Brodie enjoys going to restaurants and cafes and the movies. He is well linked in with his GP. There is no known alcohol or illicit substance use.Psychiatric HistoryBrodie first came to the attention of psychiatric services in 1986 (age 28yrs) when his mother convinced him to see a psychiatrist. He had developed delusions concerning muscle pain in his thighs. This had been rigorously investigated by orthopaedic surgeons and neurologists with no organic aetiology ever found. The original diagnosis was mono symptomatic delusions / Schizophrenia. Brodie ceased seeing his psychiatrist in 1988 as he felt she had not understood his problems and was not helping him. Prior to this time, he had functioned very highly. He went to a private school and was described as being very intelligent, conscientious and obsessional. Brodie was a good athlete and was training in running to state representative standard. He obtained an honours degree in mathematics and was undertaking a doctorate, until he developed his muscle pain in 1986. Since then he has not continued his education and has not pursued any form of career. Around 1990, Brodie left Australia and travelled the world looking for relief for his somatic concerns. He sold his home (which was given to him by his parents) and severed all ties with family and friends.This enabled him to travel the world seeking a "cure" for his muscle pain. The countries visited included New Caledonia, Finland, Japan, Hong Kong, Italy, Egypt, South America and the United States. It was during his travels in Uruguay in 1992, that he shot and injured two lawyers as a result of untreated persecutory delusions, as described in the Forensic Assessment at the time. Brodie was transferred from a psychiatric facility in Uruguay back to Australia and underwent a protracted admission to the RBWH mental health unit (December 1992 – June 1993) where a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia was confirmed. Following discharge he was managed by the RBWH Community Mental Health Service. Brodie's level of disturbance remained relatively minimal until he required four admissions to the RBWH between 1997 and 1999. He absconded to Noumea in 2000 where he attempted to engage a lawyer. Whilst there, he made a serious suicide attempt inflicting deep lacerations to both wrists. In 2001 when Brodie's treatment history was discussed with a staff psychiatrist at RBWH, the situation was recalled as follows: Brodie had absconded overseas and was unable to be traced, he then made a premeditated attempt on his life was only found as another hotel guest noticed blood seeping out beneath his room door. He was transferred back to Australia three days later and placed under an Involuntary Treatment Order whilst an inpatient at the RBWH before being transferred to the Medium Secure Unit (MSU) of The Prince Charles Hospital. Brodie remained at MSU from January to November 2001 and then transferred to the Community Care Unit (Somerset Villas), RBWH where he has resided until 2013. During the intervening years, he has required two brief inpatient admissions to the RBWH (October 2004 and March 2006).To date, Brodie has had a poor treatment response to a number of antipsychotic medications including Quetiapine, Risperidone, Amisulpride, Olanzapine and Aripiprazole. Brodie was treated with Clozapine for many years, however, had a medical admission in 2015 with LRTI and further deterioration in cardiac function resulting in the need to cease Clozapine. Since Brodie's diagnosis, he has expressed repeatedly that he does not believe he has a mental illness and should not be on medication. As a result of his poor insight, there have been chronic issues around non-adherence with medication, and his illness is such that the risk of harm to himself and others is significant when he is unwell. Serious concerns remain that Brodie would become non-adherent with treatment if he were not under an ITO, leading to deterioration in his physical and mental wellbeing. However, he continues to hope to eventually come off his ITO and all psychotropic medications in the future. Brodie has periodically engaged a number of lawyers, to attempt to challenge his ITO and have it revoked. Brodie was referred to the Community Southern Team, Inner North Brisbane Mental Health Service in August 2013 for ongoing community mental health follow-up. The Southern Team's former Team Manager, K. Carney submitted a notification to the Gun Registration Board.Early Warning Signs:Pacing, becomes dishevelled, rubs his head excessively, mumbling to himself.

Her son used a chainsaw to break into a door between the garage and the house. Nothing untoward was noted in her house. She was later found by Police at Kilcoy. She had gone there to stay in a caravan park. She reported a longstanding desire to relocate to Kilcoy and reported that she had frequently stayed at the caravan park in the past. She indicated later that she had thought she was about to have her driver's licence taken from her and so avoided her OPD appointment with Prof Byrne. This was not the case, as there has been no concern about her driving.She was admitted to the RBWH Mental Health Centre for several days of observation. During this time she underwent multiple mental state examinations and a physical examination. No significant changes in her mental state or behaviour were observed on the ward. She was discharged home. During this admission, it was reiterated to Alison that the conditions of her Forensic Order required her to notify staff whenever she was planning overnight trips away from home. Alison went missing again during the week commencing 8th February 2016 (the exact date is uncertain). She did not answer the telephone when case managers attempted to contact her and she was not at home when they visited. It subsequently emerged that she had once again driven to Kilcoy. On this occasion she had reportedly repeatedly visited a house about 20km outside Kilcoy (near Somerset Dam). It is our understanding that the home owner called QPS and Mrs Anderson was taken to the Caboolture Hospital. She was subsequently transferred to the RBWH on 16th February 2016. It seems that she had visited the house in Kilcoy because she had been planning to purchase it several years ago, prior to the events leading to the Forensic Order. Her previous plan had been to move there with her son Marcus (now deceased).Although no overt psychotic symptoms were observed, it seems likely that this most recent trip to Kilcoy was based on a delusional belief. It is likely that her recent hospitalisation for pulmonary thromboembolism and the associated reduction in dose of clozapine are related to her apparent exacerbation.ADMISSION TO RBWH MHC 16TH FEBRUARY 2016:On admission Alison reported that she had gone to the house outside of Kilcoy because she believed that her son Marcus (who is deceased) was actually still alive and living there under "witness protection". She agreed to an addition of amisulpride to enable us to avoid increasing the clozapine which Alison was so against. She tolerated this admission well without any postural hypotension or dizziness. Her paranoia about the neighbours did settle. Ellen managed this distress through reduced intake of food and use of laxatives, taking up to 10/day. formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Isabella is a 14 year old female presenting with a four year history of anorexia nervosa that appears to have occurred in the context of temperamental and psychological vulnerabilities inclusive of perfectionism and anxiety, low weight-based self-esteem in early childhood, exposure to criticism regarding her shape and weight by peers, and perceived peer rejection. Her index presentation appears to have been immediately precipitated by physical illness and subsequent weight loss that appears to have then be internally and externally reinforced leading to increasing dietary restriction, anorexic behaviours and further weight loss. Her most recent deterioration appears to have occurred in the context of a general decline in her weight coupled with further illness and dietary changes related to her oral health as well as a planned European holiday which further motivated her preoccupation with shape and weight. Isabella's illness appears to be largely maintained by a significant fear of 'fatness' and weight gain, the sense of mastery and achievement that she experiences from restraint and control, which also reduces her internal sense of anxiety, a fear that if she gives up the illness she will lose her perfectionism, control and drive, as well as continued cognitions that support the importance of determining one's value on weight and shape. Family system factors also appear to be maintaining aspects of her illness, including parental difficulty with sitting with their daughters discomfort and high parental control leading to intermittent undermining of treatment and/or minimisation of the severity of the illness. Protectively, however, Isabella is a likeable and intelligent young women who currently has a well developed peer and social support network. Her parents are highly supportive and motivated to assist Isabella in her recovery and despite the relapse, have previously demonstrated an ability to re-feed their daughter.

Phoebe is a 16-year-old female who lives with her mother (Sam), step-father (Shane) and older sister (Alissa, 22). She also has an older biological sister (Caitlin, 21) who lives outside the family home, as well as a step-brother (Utah) and step-sister (Casey, 16). She is enrolled at Dakabin State High School in Grade 11 and attends school full-time, working towards QCE. Phoebe was referred to Pine Rivers CYMHS following two presentations to Emergency Department at TPCH (04/08/2017) and Redcliffe Hospital (13/08/2017) due to concerns about deliberate self-harm, as well as a suicide attempt by intentional overdose (paracetamol and ibuprofen). Phoebe attended a priority choice appointment on 16/08/2017 with Daniel O'Brien (PR CYMHS, Team Leader). Priority new partnership appointment was offered due to risk concerns. Phoebe attended appointment on 23/08/2017 with PSP (Stacey Lynch, Clinical Psychologist) and Dr Shanmugam (Consultant Psychiatrist) where she was subsequently admitted to RBWH AIU due to high risk of suicide attempt and death relating to severe depression. Phoebe was discharged from RBWH AIU to Pine Rivers CYMHS on 17/10/2017 following an 8 week admission. Phoebe has been under the care of Pine Rivers CYMHS for mental health support since October 2017At time of assessment last year, Phoebe presented with low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, nightmares, reduced appetite, withdrawal from social activities, increased feelings of guilt and of being a burden to others. She reported longstanding low mood since primary school, however identified experiencing a deterioration in her mood over the previous 18 months. Phoebe reported ongoing suicidal ideation and has a history of several suicide attempts in 2017 by intentional overdoses and an attempted hanging using shoe laces. Phoebe also has a longstanding history of deliberate self-harm by using sharp objects to cut her arms. Phoebe reported experiencing perceptual disturbances where she would hear a male voice (inside her head) making derogatory comments and telling her to kill herself. She has also described seeing shadows, as well as having experiences of feeling as though someone is sitting on her bed or choking her. Phoebe was unable to recognise any strengths and reported "all I can think about is how much I hate myself". Whilst an inpatient at RBWH AIU Phoebe went through a period where she intentionally restricted her intake, stating that she felt as though it was a way she could have some control and hurt herself. During admission to RBWH the diagnosis of borderline personality disorder or cluster b vulnerability were considered, however at that time it was deemed Phoebe did not meet full DSM-V criteria due to age and symptoms not being able to be considered pervasive. For this reason, Phoebe's presentation has been understood within the context of trauma and interpersonal vulnerabilities.Predisposing Phoebe to mental health difficulties is a prejudicial childhood and family history of mental health difficulties. Whilst mother denied Phoebe experiencing any childhood trauma, Phoebe reported exposure to domestic violence allegedly perpetrated by her mother’s ex-partner. During Phoebe's mental health admission last year she also disclosed historical alleged sexual abuse in Grade 8 (approx. 3 years ago) by a male peer in the year level above her. Phoebe also reported significant bullying during primary school which mother has confirmed. Phoebe described experiences of having rocks thrown at her, as well as her pants being pulled down in front of peers. It is hypothesised that these experiences have had a significant impact on Phoebe’s sense of safety and security in the world, as well as the lens she looks at the world through, particularly how other people interact with her.Phoebe presents as an internalised young person who is understood to be very sensitive to perceived rejection or invalidation. She has articulated that she has never felt secure in her environment, herself or her relationship with others.When feeling rejected or invalidated Phoebe has reported experiencing an urge to show people what she is capable of through engaging in DSH or other "destructive behaviours" such as knocking things over or purposefully being clumsy. Phoebe’s rejection sensitivity also results in perception of poor relationships with peers and feeling as though no one cares about her, including teachers and professionals. Phoebe has also been observed to be vulnerable to the psycho-pathology of other young people, likely understood within the context of poor sense of self. She has articulated that she recognises she will get stuck in an "internal game" where it becomes a "competition" about how bad her mental health can get. Whilst Phoebe has developed a repertoire of distress tolerance strategies when she is triggered she struggles to implement these strategies and will withdraw from her environment. It is hypothesised that a further perpetuating factor for Phoebe's mental health difficulties is her relationships within immediate family. Phoebe described having limited contact with her father and reported that growing up he would often make outlandish statements that were never true (e.g., needing to have a limb amputated). She has reported experiencing her father as manipulative and rejecting, identifying that he only contacts her when he is looking for something from her. Phoebe also has a strained relationship with her step-father who can be dismissive and invalidating of her distress. Step-father has told Phoebe that he has nil interest in being able to understand her mental health difficulties, this has been confirmed by mother. Understandably Phoebe feels unloved and rejected by her step-father who has been in her life for 7 years. Whilst Phoebe’s mother is well-meaning, historically she has struggled to be consistently emotionally available to Phoebe for a range of reasons and at times this led to role reversal where Phoebe took on carer/protective role for her mother. For a young person who is known to be sensitive to perceived rejection or invalidation it can be assumed that attachment ruptures within her parental attachments exacerbate Phoebe’s level of distress.Protectively, Phoebe is a likeable young person who has the capacity to be insightful and reflective when not distressed. She is sensitive and caring of others, for example in primary school she shaved her head to raise money for cancer. Premorbidly, Phoebe’s mother descried her as a social, bubbly and athletic adolescent (played representative basketball in high school). Phoebe is very creative and enjoys using art as a way of expressing herself. She also enjoys listening to music and playing the ukulele. She loves animals and adores her dogs and 3 pet guinea pigs. There has been a significant improvement in Phoebe's functioning over the past 12 months. She now attends school full-time, has a part-time job and has also obtained her learners drivers license. Phoebe's mother is also considered to be a very strong protective factor and has demonstrated her commitment to supporting Phoebe in any way she can (emotionally and practically). Phoebe has not missed one appointment in the past 14 months.

Damien dropped out of high school after year 10, but made friends and held down a job. Damien has reported that previously he has worked two-full time jobs consecutively (when first arrived in Brisbane from Victoria in 2007), working as a machine operator, and on production lines. He reported during this time that he was not getting much sleep due to his work schedule, but was motivated to continue long working hours for the income. He last worked in 2010, in a casual factory work role. He has a history of homelessness (incl. sleeping in his car), and has also lived in a number of backpacker's accommodations, boarding houses etc.His first contact with MHS was in September 2007, while incarcerated at AGCC. He was diagnosed with alcohol abuse disorder and an antisocial personality in 2008 (classified patient at TPCH). There appears to have been no follow up after that, until Damien was again assessed at AGCC (by Dr Mann), and re-admitted to TPCH for further assessment. Eventually it was confirmed that Damien has a psychotic illness requiring treatment. It was also reported by Damien's sister, Rhiannon, that he exhibited odd behaviour while incarcerated at Woodford CC in 2009. He reportedly expressed multiple conspiracy theories, but had been very guarded in revealing such information. He was readmitted to TPCH again in Jan 2009 after refusing treatment in prison. During this later admission to hospital he was commenced on depot medication, before being discharged back to correctional services.Damien has a history of violence towards his step-father and mother. He was charged with assaults in the past, and has a significant forensic history (including assault, burglary x 3, attempt to perverse the course of justice x 2, fraud, entering or remaining in casino contrary to order or direction).Damien's current FO relates to index offence/s of common assault, and unlawful stalking. In July 2012 he was arrested following threatening phone calls he made to a recruitment agency. In September 2012 he was arrested after making threats to a shop assistant over a phone SIM card.The most recent offence is in relation to threatening emails sent to a solicitor who previously represented him. Damien's solicitor referred Damien to MHS, due to concerns that his behaviour appeared to be irrational and driven by persecutory ideation. At this time, Damien was found not to have taken any medication for the preceding 3 years, and had relapsed with his mental illness, paranoid Schizophrenia. Damien was admitted to RBWH under MHA 2000 (ITO made on 25/10/12). Damien's charges were subsequently referred to the MHC, and he was placed on a Forensic Order (due to finding of unsoundness of mind) on 15/06/15.Damien has previously viewed homelessness as a means of saving money, and has difficulties foreseeing future consequences of his actions. He has difficulties with problem-solving and planning, and can be impulsive in his decision making. Due to underlying illness symptoms (paranoia, persecutory beliefs) and limited social problem-solving skills, Damien can misinterpret information given, and can exhibit hostile attribution bias regarding others' intentions against him at times. This can trigger Damien, resulting in agitation which may escalate towards aggression or threatening behaviour.Damien may also react when he feels that he is being treated unfairly, or has been slighted in some way. Damien's insight regarding his illness and need for treatment is chronically limited, and he has a history of disengagement. He continues to express that he doesn't require treatment under the Forensic Order, and perceives the sole purpose of this being as punishment for previous offences, and therefore believes he has been on the Order for long enough. He does not acknowledge that the Order is also in place to ensure regular monitoring and treatment to maintain stability in his mental state. He remains focused on coming off the Forensic Order, and is inconsistent in his reports as to whether he would continue his treatment as a voluntary patient.Damien currently attends all required appointments, and adheres to all required treatment including prescribed monthly depot. He reports no concerns or side effects regarding medication (notes side effects of previous oral medications), and does perceive some benefit of treatment at times.Damien says that he no longer "goes off" at people, and that the treatment helps him to keep his cool and stay calm. He denies any recent incidents of conflict, and there have been no recent observed incidents of aggression. Damien denies any intent to harm others.Damien is not currently using any substances (other than tobacco), and has engaged with the DDC to discuss smoking cessation. He has reduced his smoking, and now intermittently uses NRT (1-2 packets tailor made/ pouches tobacco per fortnight). Damien has stable accommodation and income, and is happy with his current accommodation and lifestyle. He reports ongoing contact with his sister (via phone/ intermittent visits), and enjoys house and pet-sitting for her when her and her children go away on holiday.

formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Anne is a 66 year old female who presents with a variety of symptoms including depressive, manic and psychotic and cognitive disturbance and as such posed a diagnostic dilemma. Adverse childhood with sexual assault and possible family history of mental illness with grandmother committing suicide and son living at home until age 36 with reported anger outbursts is also unusual. Her family report since that admission she has had periods of agitation and being "difficult". Further assessment, collateral and risk factors and chronicity of symptoms indicate most likely diagnosis of schizoaffetive disorder. Anne responded well to antipsychotics with mood stabiliser and showed improvement in pseudodementia further supporting this diagnosis. Poor insight and complex family dynamics favoured depot treatment as the best option for Anne. Requires ongoing management under a TA with case management follow up. Nil imminent risks. There is suspicion the family may be psychologically/physically abusive towards Anne however this has never been demonstrated in front of staff.

Chelsea is a 14-year-old female presenting with significant longstanding history of psychological and inhibited temperament vulnerabilities in the context of trait anxiety, and the development of fears and phobias. Chelsea’s most recent presentation was required due to low weight and medical compromise following successive weight loss (7kg over two months) occurring in the context of emetophobia and secondary starvation.Whilst there was no clear precipitant for the worsening of Chelsea's fears around vomiting, there were several identified exacerbating and maintaining factors. These includedChelsea’s association of internalised anxiety with stomach sensations and increased risk of vomiting facilitated her to become hypervigilant to interoceptive cues. Exposure to stimuli reminiscent of vomiting or anxiety provoking situations likely manifested changes in stomach sensations leading her to adopt overt safety behaviours including gradual deterioration of oral intake, cautiousness of food contamination and avoidance of external threats to reduce her internal sense of anxiety and risk of vomiting. Consequently, the effects of starvation syndrome were also likely to have exacerbated Chelsea’s cognitive rigidity and catastrophic thinking style in relation to contamination, food safety and threats. Cognitive vulnerability increases Chelsea's susceptibility of behaviour modelling of illness and limited insight reduces Chelsea’s ability to interpret and habituate to normal physiological responses and, gather disconfirming evidence for her fear. Family system and psychosocial factors may also be acting to maintain aspects of Chelsea’s anxiety, including parental disharmony, relationship breakdown with her sibling and her father’s unpredictability of vomiting-like behaviours.Protectively, Chelsea is a likeable and polite young woman who loves animals and art work. Chelsea has displayed help seeking behaviours and remission of previous fears and phobias, and continued to express wanting to return to a normal routine and overcome her anxiety.

Luke also had previously mixed with a teenage peer group that was into using illicit substances, especially THC, and he described having some unpleasant experiences with these other boys after getting stoned early on in his using of the substance and association with that group (eg: they had some fights with each other).Precipitating:- It appears as though Luke developed psychotic symptoms secondary to THC use; having started about a year before his presentation to hospital. In that context, Luke may have been exposed to peer derision/bullying in the context of his developing Psychosis.Luke would then later suffer a dramatic deterioration in Mental State, when his 18 yo Brother (with whom he was very close) dies suddenly and tragically in a MBA on 02/12/17.Perpetuating:- There appears to have ongoing sporadic but significant (in terms of quantity) use of THC.Luke also appears to have become non-compliant with medications (eg: Risperidone) early on in his treatment, whilst still in the community.Then later, it is highly likely that there was further covert non-compliance whilst an inpatient, especially during the phase in which he took Clozapine (based on dosing schedule vs Blood levels); this improved with more vigilant nursing observation post-dosing. Luke's plasma Clozapine levels only ever reached the lower end of the Therapeutic Range, at maximum dosing (550 mg per day). This non-compliance with the Clozapine, most likely stemmed from his ownparanoid delusionary system., wherein Luke truly believed that the treating team at RBWH were part of conspiracy to murder him, via poisoning with a cocktail of various psychotropic medications.It also appears that Luke's psychiatric illness was all but refractory, to the positive effects of treatment, with a wide ranging host of Antipsychotic medications and procedures, including:- PO Risperidone (Pre-Admission), and during his admission:- PO Brexipiprazole, PO Aripiprazole (later switched to IM Aripiprazole, and still current), PO Clozapine (over 6 weeks, and up to 550 mg PO daily). Lithium was introduced briefly into Luke's Treatment schedule (the last month of his admission), as it was felt he may have been suffering an ever more-volatile and labile mood (almost cyclothymic). The exact reasons for how or why Luke's psychosis remained so refractory to all the various treatments he was confronted with (both pharmacological and ECT) remains a mystery.Na Benzoate was introduced in the last month and a half as an antipsychotic-enhancer or "lifter", thought in trials to enhance the clinical benefits in terms of positive symptom resolution, to be gained via Antipsychotic medications.Protective:- Luke was one member of a highly supportive and close-knit family, who have consistently stood by him through thick and thin. And that at a time of tremendous personal loss for the family, with the sudden death of 18 yo Son and Brother to Luke, Sam (the 1 year anniversary has just passed). formulationOverallClinicalImpression: Ian is a 34 year man with a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia. He has had past diagnosis including conduct disorder, ADHD and developmental disability. Ian also has very brittle asthma- predominantly allergic. Ian is on a TA, previously having been on a FO when he was at the medium secure unit at TPCH in 2002. He first presented to services at age 15. His treatment was complicated by itinerancy and poly substance abuse. Ian was placed on a FO after being found of unsound mind for the following offences:-Assault occasioning bodily harm - five counts-Failure to appear-three counts.-Contravene requirement.-Loitering to beg - two counts.All of Ian's offences occurred in the context of him being floridly unwell and using substances - cannabis and amphetamines. Ian was transferred to CCU in May 2004. In 2009, he was successful with an application for a HASP and is supported by Richmond Fellowship Qld (RFQ). He has a Department of Housing Unit in Windsor, and receives medication supervision from MACs. Ian has part-time employment with Help employment. His finances were subject to administration by Public Trustee Qld until September 2013 when he had a review by QCAT. He was given the opportunity to manage his own DSP.. This was supported by his treating team and RFQ as Ian has very good money management skills.At baseline, Ian is well mannered and engages well. He can be abrupt to others if he feels that he is being pressured to do something that he doesn't want to do, and this can be perceived as him being aggressive, but this is not the case. He has residual positive symptoms, but is guarded about these. He can often be observed to respond to internal stimuli when he doesn't think anyone can see him. This does not cause him any distress. Ian's self awareness is very limited, evidenced by him speaking very loudly in public places.The negative symptoms of Ian's illness are more prominent. He is chronically disorganised and requires a high level of support with many ADL's. His insight is chronically impaired and he does not believe that he has a mental illness or that he needs to take medication. This is also the case with his asthma, and he believes that it is only 'luck' that prevents him from having asthma attacks and not his preventative medications. He continues to state that if he were not on his TA, he would stop taking his medications.On July 18th 2014, Ian suffered a severe asthma attack. He was able to get help from a neighbour to call an ambulance. When at the RBWH emergency department, Ian was diagnosed with status asthmaticus, requiring intubation, ventilation and paralysis in ICU. Ian was critically ill and he remained in an induced coma for 6 days. He remained on the ventilator for a further 6 days before he was able to be extubated. Extubation was delayed due to him developing a paralytic illeus. He was moved to a medical ward on 3/8/14 and then transferred to GARU for rehabilitation on 1/9/14. Ian was discharged from GARU on 3/9/14. Ian's care was transferred back to MIRT on 23/7/14.Ian's motherlives in Gympie, but came down and stayed at Ian's unit for the period of time that he was unwell. She found out from Ian's neighbours that he had been taking amphetamines again and had been drinking an increasing amount of alcohol. A blood test when he was first admitted confirmed amphetamine use. Ian has stated that he 'likes the feeling' of taking amphetamines, but says that he 'knows this was a stupid thing to do' and that he will not do this again. Ian also needed to be reminded that he cannot consume excessive amounts of alcohol due to the risks of mixing alcohol withClozapine. Whilst in hospital, Ian's mother, mental health clinician and NGO staff worked very closely to ensure that Ian's home environment was cleaned thoroughly to minimise any further risks to his asthma when he returned home. Prior to this admission, Ian had become quite dismissive of support, leading to a deterioration of the cleanliness of his home. A new plan has been devised to ensure that Ian receives the ongoing support that he needs and so far, this is working well. Ian does tend to try to avoid household tasks by attempting to ask to go out before his checklists are completed, but hissupport workers have developed strategies to manage this. The Department of Housing have laid new lino in his unit and painted his unit with mould-resistant paint. Ian's medications are currently supervised by RFQ in the mornings and MACs for evening medication supervision.

He again demonstrated FTD and persecutory delusions that people at the hospital were federal agents and that his ex-partner was involved in the sex trade and that others were injecting her with ICE. He believed that he was receiving messages via his computer from people in Ecuador. His ITO was revoked on d/c.ITO recommenced in November 2016 after he was brought to hospital by QAS on EEO following an OD and an altercation. Persecutory ideation about bikies and being set up by his ex-partner. Commenced on paliperidone depot with improved mental state.On discharge from above TPCH admission, Luke was referred to the RBWH MHS for ongoing care. Soon after (on 20/12/16) he was incarcerated due to breach of DVO against his partner. In prison Mr Rickards was seen by Prison Mental Health Services. The medical record indicates he accepted treatment and had some residual attenuated psychotic symptoms. The consultant psychiatrist who reviewed him in prison recommended ongoing treatment under an involuntary treatment order.Luke was transferred from Prison MHS to TPCH for another admission on 7/7/17 under current TA with a diagnosis of Schizophrenia and relapse in the context of stress associated with his release. He stayed at TPCH for 6 days for optimisation of mental state and risk containment. Psychotic symptoms (paranoia, IOR, persecutory delusions and AH) were documented to still be present at d/c, but better managed and tolerable with his medications (Olanzapine, Paliperidone). Luke has subsequently claimed to have falsified these psychotic symptoms to get out of prison.14/07/2017, Luke's care was transferred to RBWH, Northern Community Care Team. Luke has frequently asked for his depot to be reduced/ceased, stating he has drug induced psychosis and would not become psychotic without medication now he is no longer using drugs. Luke approached Dr Moyle, Private Psychiatrist in August 2017 to take over his care, however, Dr Moyle declined, as he believed Luke's care would be better managed under a case management model. Luke contacted his Case Manager, following this and was "abusive, swearing and name calling".In late October 2017, Luke's depot administration was transferred to his GP. Luke's mental health has remained stable, his interactions with staff have improved and he is working to improve his life. He is engaged with Mylestones Employment and sees a Private Psychologist at Today Psychology, which he is happy with. He plans to go back to University in the future.Luke was seeing his GP on a weekly basis for Hep C treatment, which is now completed. His GP, in September 2017, reports that he feels Luke has made "significant progress in the past year", loosing weight and staying abstinent from Illicit drugs.The DVO taken out by Luke's ex-partner expired in November 2017 and Luke has been seeking access to his son Archer. Luke's depot has been further reduced to Paliperidone 75mgs as of 14/02/2018 and further monitoring is required to ensure stability of his mental health.At his request, Luke saw Dr Ravi Sohal on 12/4/18 for a second opinion regarding diagnosis, treatment and the need for treatment under the MHA. Candice is a 17 year old female who presents with a constellation of symptoms including episodic low mood and emotional dysregulation, anxiety, relational problems, and disordered eating. She also has a history of challenging and oppositional behaviour, temperamental difficulties including rigidity in thinking style and speech and language problems in childhood and it is thought that these factors also contribute to her current presentation and difficulty with emotional regulation. The difficult systemic factors occurring since her parents divorce alongside her transition through adolescenceappear to have been significant precipitating factors with the former thought also to be a significant continuing perpetuating factor in this case. Protectively, Candice is also a young woman who has a keen sense of humour and has demonstrated functional capacity at school and in her work place. She is described as having a strong work ethic and reportedly works hard at school to achieve her future ambitions. Her strong willed temperament can therefore be recognised as a strength in this domain. Her parents also remain supportive and appropriately concerned which remains protective, although it is noted that this is waning and relationships are becoming increasingly strained leading to perceived/real rejection and invalidation. She also has a positive rapport with her community team and a willingness to help-seek.

Eliza is a 15 year old female who was admitted to the Adolescent Mental Health Unit, RBWH, after being brought into hospital on an EEA due to an episode of acute emotional and behavioural disturbance in the home environment characterised by self-harm, headbanging, violent behaviour towards her mother as well as property (requiring restraining by her father), and running from the house and reportedly standing in front of traffic. Eliza presents with marked interpersonal sensitivity and relationship conflict, emotional dysregulation, chronic suicidal ideation and self-harming behaviour, and reports experiencing episodes of dissociation and pseudo-hallucinations. She has perfectionistic standards and poor self-esteem which have at times manifested in disordered eating. With regards to her developmental and personal history, there have been no reports of trauma or abuse and Eliza was described to have functioned well academically, socially, and emotionally throughout her primary school years. On reflection, however, her parents have noted that she was likely a sensitive child and perhaps more prone to anxiety within her temperament. It is also wondered whether Eliza has felt that her emotions have been chronically invalidated by her parents, particularly her father, although this is not definitive. Also predisposing Eliza to mental health difficulties is a strong paternal genetic vulnerability to mood disorders. Eliza first presented to services in early 2018 following an overdose. Whilst she denied a specific precipitant for this event, she described a one year history of worsening low mood. Since this time, Eliza has been unable to return to school which has been highly distressing to her as well as disruptive her her developmental tasks of adolescence. She appears to have become progressively invested in the sick role, and over-identifies as a mental health patient and this may in part be related to the need to maintain her avoidance.

It appears that Kenneth has had troubles with addiction for many years, with this current episode being precipitated largely by the anniversary of his fathers death and the possible need to hide his stress/addiction from his new partner and therefore turning to extra medication in the form of dexamphetamines in an attempt to help focus and concentrate on a day to day basis. Protectively Kenneth spoke highly of his new partner hopefully will encourage him to seek the rehab and psychological help he needs.
